lessons.title: Start here: how this course works
lessons.summary: Your 30-day route, the robot you will program, and how to use the animations, puzzles and practice tools.

blocks.text: Welcome to ROS2Lab! In 30 study days of about an hour you go from "what is a terminal?" to writing complete ROS 2 programs, in Python and C++, that control a delivery robot called **Chiku**. This lesson shows you how every lesson works and how to study well.

items: Know the six weeks of the course and why they come in this order
Try each kind of interactive part once
Set up a study routine that works for you

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: This course is 30 study days in 6 weeks. Each lesson takes about 30 minutes: a little reading, then you **do** things. Doing the practice parts is what makes you learn.
Your route: six weeks, one robot

items: **Week 1, Talk to the robot's computer** (Days 1 to 5): the Ubuntu terminal and Python from zero. Robots run Ubuntu, and you control them by typing.
**Week 2, Build the robot's brain** (Days 6 to 10): Python classes, callbacks, C++, reading real ROS 2 nodes, then installing ROS 2 Jazzy and the lab.
**Week 3, Introduction to ROS** (Days 11 to 15): why robots need a software platform, the history and versions of ROS, ROS 1 vs ROS 2, middleware, DDS and QoS.
**Week 4, Speak ROS 2** (Days 16 to 20): nodes, topics, services, parameters, actions, launch files, packages, TF2 and debugging, hands-on in the practice terminal.

**Week 5, ROS Programming Fundamentals** (Days 21 to 25): 20 chapters, first in Python and then in C++: your own packages and nodes, timers and publishers, subscribers, custom messages, services and clients, actions, parameters, launch files and a mini-project.

**Week 6, Writing your own ROS 2 nodes** (Days 26 to 30): new ideas only, in Python AND C++, with nodes that control a robot: time and logging, open- and closed-loop driving, chaining nodes, messages in code, QoS, safe parameters, launch files for two robots, tf2, executors, lifecycle nodes, components, tests and a patrol project.
A **test** closes each week. Every student gets different questions.

blocks.intro: Here is the whole course in one picture. Each week climbs a layer. Press **Add the next layer** until the stack is complete.

blocks.text: The interactive parts

Lessons mix short reading with things you **do**. Practice parts (terminals, Python, quick checks and puzzles) must be finished to complete a lesson. Animations, "think first" boxes, flashcards and bonus games are optional, but they make ideas stick.

blocks.q: **Think first** boxes ask you to guess before you read the answer. Try it: a robot reads its distance sensor 10 times per second. In one minute, how many readings is that?
blocks.answer: 10 × 60 = **600 readings**. Guessing first, even wrongly, makes you remember the answer much better. That is why these boxes exist.

blocks.title: A tiny program, one line at a time
blocks.intro: **Step through the code** blocks run a program slowly. Press **Step** and watch the yellow line, the memory and the output.
blocks.code:

print(battery)

steps.note: Python stores the number 100 in a box called `battery`.
The right side is worked out first: 100 - 30 = 70. Then the box gets the new value.
`print` shows the value. You just read your first program the way a computer does.

blocks.title: My study plan
items: I will study about an hour a day, at the same time each day.
I will do every practice part myself before pressing "Show me".
I will finish each week's lessons before its test.
I will say each lesson's recap out loud (it really helps).

blocks.text: How to learn well, even when it feels hard
Everybody learns at a different speed. Being slow is **not** a problem; skipping practice is. These habits are proven to help:

items: **Read once, then do.** Read a section slowly, then immediately try the practice part. Doing beats reading again.
**Say it in your own words.** After each lesson, explain the recap to a friend, or to yourself out loud.
**Little and often.** 30 minutes every day is much better than 3 hours on Sunday. Your brain stores what it meets again and again.
**Use the hint buttons without shame.** Hints are part of learning. Then do the same exercise again **without** the hint.
**Come back after a day.** Flip the flashcards of yesterday's lesson before you start today's.

lessons.title: Meet the terminal
lessons.summary: What the terminal is, how to read the prompt, and your first commands.

blocks.text: Meet **Chiku**, the delivery robot you will program in this course. Chiku's brain is a small Linux computer. Today you learn to talk to it the way robot engineers do: by typing commands.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The terminal is a text window. You type a command, press **Enter**, and the computer answers in text. That's all it is.

Robots that run ROS 2 almost always use **Ubuntu**, a free version of Linux. On Ubuntu, engineers control the computer by typing short commands in a window called the **terminal**. ROS 2 is used the same way, so the terminal is the first tool you need.

The terminal is like chatting with a very obedient assistant. You type an instruction and press Enter. The assistant does exactly that, nothing more and nothing less. It never guesses what you meant, so spelling matters.
Opening the terminal
On a real Ubuntu computer, press `Ctrl` + `Alt` + `T`. A window opens with a line like this:
student@ros2lab:~$

items.m: the user name (who is logged in)
the computer's name
short for your home folder, `/home/student`
the computer is ready for your command

blocks.label: Many terminals in one window
blocks.text: The practice terminals in this course look like **Terminator**, a terminal app many ROS 2 engineers use (install it with `sudo apt install terminator`). One window can be split into several terminals: right-click and choose **Split Vertically** (**Ctrl+Shift+E**) or **Split Horizontally** (**Ctrl+Shift+O**), or press **+ New terminal**. **Alt+arrow keys** jump between them, and the **red title bar** shows the terminal your typing goes to. Drag the grey line between two terminals to resize them.
Your first commands
Type a command after the `$` and press **Enter**. Try these in the practice terminal below:

items: `whoami` prints who you are logged in as.
`pwd` (print working directory) prints the folder you are in now.
`ls` (list) shows what is inside the current folder.

blocks.title: Practice terminal: your first commands
blocks.intro: This is a practice terminal. It behaves like Ubuntu, but nothing you type here can harm anything.

tasks.do: Type `whoami` and press Enter.
tasks.hint: Type the letters w h o a m i, then press Enter.

tasks.do: Type `pwd` to see which folder you are in.
tasks.hint: pwd stands for print working directory.

tasks.do: Type `ls` to list what is inside your home folder.
tasks.hint: A small L and a small S.

tasks.do: Type `ls -a` to also see hidden files (their names start with a dot).
tasks.hint: Put a space between ls and -a.

blocks.text: Commands are **case-sensitive**: `ls` works, but `LS` or `Ls` does not. Use small letters unless a lesson shows capitals.
How to read any command, slowly

items: Look at the **first word**: that is the command, the action. `ls` means "list".
Words that start with a **dash** `-` are **options**: they change how the command works. `-l` means "long list, with details".
Other words are **arguments**: what the command should work on, for example a folder name.
So `ls -l Documents` means: **list**, **with details**, **the Documents folder**.
Press **Enter** only when the whole line is typed. Nothing happens before Enter.

blocks.label: The three parts of a command

items.m: the action, always first: `ls`, `cd`, `echo`
starts with `-`, changes the action: `-l`, `-a`
what to act on: a file or folder name, or some text

blocks.title: Practice: more useful first commands

tasks.do: Ask the computer for today's date: `date`
Make the computer say something: `echo Hello Chiku`
Show a **long** list with details: `ls -l`
List what is inside the Documents folder: `ls Documents`
Make a spelling mistake on purpose: `LS`. Read the error, it is harmless.
See every command you typed so far: `history`
Clean the screen: `clear`

blocks.intro: Type each command exactly as shown, then press Enter. Mistakes cannot harm anything here.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Most real robots have **no screen and no mouse**. Engineers connect to them over Wi-Fi and control them only through a terminal (using a tool called `ssh`). Everything you learn in this terminal works on those robots too.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Typing capital letters: `Ls` or `PWD` do not work. Commands are small letters.
Forgetting the space: `ls-l` is wrong, `ls -l` is right.
Pressing Enter too early, before the whole command is typed.
Expecting a reply to every command: some commands (like `cd`) print nothing when they work. Silence means success.

blocks.q: In `ls -l Documents`, what is `-l`?
options: An option: it asks for a long list with details
blocks.why: Words starting with `-` are options that change how the command works.
blocks.hint: Look for the dash.

blocks.q: Type a command that makes the terminal print the word `Ready`.
blocks.why: `echo` prints whatever text you give it.
blocks.hint: echo, a space, then the word.

blocks.q: In the prompt `student@ros2lab:~$`, what does `~` mean?
blocks.why: `~` is a short way of writing your home folder.
blocks.hint: Look at the "Reading the prompt" box above.

blocks.q: Which command shows the folder you are in right now?
blocks.why: `pwd` means print working directory.
blocks.hint: Which command name means print working directory?

blocks.q: Type the command that lists what is inside the current folder.
blocks.why: `ls` means list.
blocks.hint: Two small letters.

items.back: who am I logged in as?

items: The terminal is a window where you type commands and press Enter.
`whoami` tells you who you are, `pwd` tells you where you are, and `ls` shows what is there.
Spelling and capital letters matter.

lessons.title: Folders and paths: moving around (part 1)
lessons.summary: Move between folders with `cd`, and learn absolute and relative paths.

blocks.text: Chiku must find the file with today's delivery list. Files live in folders inside folders, so first you learn to move around.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Folders sit inside folders, like boxes inside boxes. `cd` moves you from one folder to another, and `pwd` tells you where you are standing.
Your files live inside **folders**, which Linux also calls **directories**. Folders can contain other folders, like rooms inside a building.

Think of the computer as a college campus. `/` is the main gate: the top of everything. `/home` is the hostel block, `/home/student` is your room, and `/home/student/Documents` is a cupboard in your room. A **path** is the address that tells the computer how to reach a place.
Two kinds of paths

items: An **absolute path** starts from the main gate `/`. It works from anywhere, for example `/home/student/Documents`.
A **relative path** starts from where you are now. If you are in `/home/student`, then `Documents` points to the same place.

items.m: your home folder
this folder
the folder one level up (the parent)
the top folder of the whole computer

blocks.text: Moving with cd

cd Documents        # go into Documents
cd ..               # go up one level
cd ~                # go back home from anywhere
cd /opt/ros/jazzy   # jump using an absolute path

Press the **Tab** key after typing the first few letters of a folder name. The terminal completes the name for you and avoids spelling mistakes. On a phone, use the **Tab** button under the practice terminal.

blocks.intro: Before the practice terminal, watch what `cd` does to **where you are**.

tasks.do: Go into the `robot_ws` folder: `cd robot_ws`
tasks.hint: Type: cd robot_ws  (try pressing Tab after cd ro)

tasks.do: Go one level deeper, into `src`.
Check where you are with `pwd`.
Go up two levels in one command, back home: `cd ../..`
tasks.hint: Each .. goes up one level. Type: cd ../..

tasks.do: Jump to the ROS 2 folder with an absolute path: `cd /opt/ros/jazzy`
Come back home with `cd ~`
tasks.hint: Type: cd ~  (cd on its own also works)

blocks.intro: Now practise with a game: guide Chiku through the folders using only `cd`.

blocks.q: Which command tells you which folder you are in right now?
blocks.why: `pwd` prints the working directory: where you are.
blocks.hint: print working directory

blocks.q: Type the shortest command that takes you to your home folder from anywhere.
blocks.why: `cd` alone (or `cd ~`) always goes home.
blocks.hint: Two letters are enough.

blocks.q: Match each symbol with its meaning.
blocks.why: These four symbols appear in almost every path.
blocks.hint: ~ is home.

lessons.title: Folders and paths: moving around (part 2)
lessons.summary: Part 2: Walking a path, one step at a time.

blocks.text: Welcome back! In part 1 you worked on: Two kinds of paths, Moving with cd. Now let's finish the job. Chiku must find the file with today's delivery list. Files live in folders inside folders, so first you learn to move around.
Walking a path, one step at a time

items: You start at home: `/home/student` (shown as `~`).
`cd robot_ws` steps **into** the robot_ws folder. Now you are at `/home/student/robot_ws`.
`cd src` steps one more folder **down**: `/home/student/robot_ws/src`.
`cd ..` steps one folder **up** (back out): `/home/student/robot_ws`.
`cd ~` (or just `cd`) jumps **home** from anywhere, like a "go home" button.
`cd /opt/ros/jazzy` starts from the very top `/`, so it works from anywhere.

blocks.title: Treasure hunt: find today's delivery list

tasks.do: Look around your home folder: `ls`
Go into the `deliveries` folder.
List what is inside it.
Go into the `today` folder.
Read the treasure: `cat list.txt`
Check your exact position with `pwd`.
Go back up to `deliveries` with one `..`
Read yesterday's list without moving there, using a relative path: `cat yesterday/list.txt`
Go home in one command.

blocks.intro: Somewhere in your home folder is today's delivery list. Follow the steps to find it.

files.~/deliveries/today/list.txt:
1. Library: 3 books
2. Physics lab: 1 parcel
3. Principal's office: letters

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: `cd..` without a space: always write `cd ..`.
Wrong capital letters: `cd documents` fails when the folder is `Documents`.
Getting lost: type `pwd` to see where you are, and `cd ~` to go home.
Using a relative path from the wrong place: `cd src` only works if `src` is inside the folder you are in now.

blocks.q: Does each path work **from anywhere**, or does it **depend on where you are**?

items.why: It starts with `/`: an absolute path.
No `/` at the start: relative to the current folder.
`~` always means your home folder, so this works from anywhere.
"The folder above" depends on where you are.
Relative: go up one, then into Music.

blocks.why: Paths starting with `/` (or `~`) are absolute and work from anywhere. Everything else is relative to where you are.

blocks.q: You are in `/home/student`. Which command takes you into `/home/student/robot_ws/src`?
blocks.why: From your home folder, `robot_ws/src` means: into robot_ws, then into src.
blocks.hint: Start from where you are, and go in the order robot_ws, then src.

blocks.q: Which of these is an **absolute** path?
blocks.why: Absolute paths always start with `/`, the top folder.
blocks.hint: Which one starts from the main gate?

blocks.q: You are in `/home/student/robot_ws/src`. Type one command to go up **one** level.
blocks.why: `cd ..` moves to the parent folder, `/home/student/robot_ws`.
blocks.hint: Two dots mean one level up. Remember the space after cd.

blocks.text: `cd..` without a space does not work on Ubuntu. Always put a space after `cd`.

blocks.q: You are in `/home/student/deliveries/today`. Where does `cd ../..` take you?
blocks.why: Each `..` goes up one level: today → deliveries → student.
blocks.hint: Count the two dots-pairs: two steps up.

items.back: absolute path: starts at the top

items: `cd folder` goes in, `cd ..` goes up, `cd ~` goes home.
Absolute paths start with `/`. Relative paths start from where you are.
Press Tab to complete names.

lessons.title: Making, copying and deleting (part 1)
lessons.summary: Create folders and files, then copy, move, rename and delete them safely.

blocks.text: Before Chiku can learn new skills, it needs a tidy workspace: folders for code, notes and backups.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `mkdir` makes folders, `touch` makes empty files, `cp` copies, `mv` moves or renames, and `rm` deletes for ever.
Every ROS 2 project lives in a folder called a **workspace**. In this lesson you build one with these commands:

mkdir robot_ws             # make one folder
mkdir -p robot_ws/src      # make folders inside folders (-p = parents)
touch notes.txt            # make an empty file
cp notes.txt copy.txt      # copy a file
cp -r robot_ws backup_ws   # copy a folder with everything inside (-r)
mv copy.txt ideas.txt      # rename (or move) a file
rm ideas.txt               # delete a file
rm -r backup_ws            # delete a folder and everything inside
`-p`, `-r` and `-a` are **options**. They adjust what a command does, like asking for tea "with less sugar": it is still tea, the option changes how it is made.
Linux has **no recycle bin**. `rm` deletes immediately and forever. Read the command twice before pressing Enter, especially with `rm -r`.

tasks.do: Create the folders `ros2_ws/src` in one command: `mkdir -p ros2_ws/src`
Go into `ros2_ws`.
Create an empty file called `README.md`.
List the folder with `ls` to see both items.
Copy the whole `src` folder to `src_backup`.
tasks.hint: Folders need -r. Type: cp -r src src_backup

tasks.do: Rename `README.md` to `notes.md`.
Delete the `src_backup` folder.
tasks.hint: Type: rm -r src_backup  (check the name first!)

blocks.q: Match each command with what it does.

pairs.b: makes a new folder called maps
deletes a folder and everything in it, for ever

blocks.why: mkdir and touch create, cp copies, mv moves or renames, rm deletes with no recycle bin.
blocks.hint: mv moves, cp copies.

blocks.q: What does the `-p` in `mkdir -p ros2_ws/src` do?
blocks.why: Without -p, mkdir fails if ros2_ws does not exist yet.
blocks.hint: p for parents.

blocks.q: Type the command that creates an empty file called `notes.txt`.
blocks.why: `touch` makes an empty file (or updates the date of an existing one).
blocks.hint: t...h, a space, the file name.

blocks.q: Which command deletes a folder `old` and everything inside it?
blocks.why: Folders with things inside need `-r` (recursive). There is no undo.
blocks.hint: r for recursive.

blocks.label: Part 1 done
blocks.text: Great work! Take a short break, then continue with **part 2**: Copy, move or rename? Decide slowly.

lessons.title: Making, copying and deleting (part 2)
lessons.summary: Part 2: Copy, move or rename? Decide slowly.

blocks.text: Welcome back! In part 1 you worked on: Create folders and files, then copy, move, rename and delete them safely. Now let's finish the job. Before Chiku can learn new skills, it needs a tidy workspace: folders for code, notes and backups.
Copy, move or rename? Decide slowly

items: Do you want **two** of the thing afterwards (the old one stays)? Use **cp** (copy).
Do you want the thing in a **new place** (the old place becomes empty)? Use **mv** (move).
Do you want the **same place but a new name**? That is also **mv**: `mv old.txt new.txt`.
Is it a **folder** with things inside? Copy with `cp -r`, delete with `rm -r`. (`mv` works on folders as it is.)
Before any `rm`, type `ls` first and read what is there. There is no undo.

blocks.title: Practice: tidy Chiku's messy Desktop

tasks.do: Go to the Desktop: `cd Desktop`
See the mess: `ls`
Make two folders at once: `mkdir notes maps`
Move the note into the notes folder: `mv todo.txt notes/`
Move the map into the maps folder.
Make a backup copy of the map **inside** maps: `cp maps/lab_map.yaml maps/lab_map_backup.yaml`
Rename the badly named file `untitled.py` to `patrol.py`.
Delete the junk file `junk.tmp`.
Check the tidy result: `ls`

blocks.intro: Chiku's Desktop is a mess. Put each file where it belongs.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: `rm -r` on the wrong folder: always run `ls` first and read the name twice.
`mkdir a/b` when `a` does not exist: use `mkdir -p a/b`.
`cp folder new` without `-r`: folders need `cp -r`.
Thinking `mv` makes a copy: after `mv`, the old name is gone.

blocks.q: Why does `mkdir robot_ws/src` fail when `robot_ws` does not exist yet?
options: mkdir needs -p to also create the missing parent folder
blocks.why: `-p` tells mkdir to create every missing folder on the path.
blocks.hint: Which option creates parent folders?

blocks.q: Which command copies the folder `maps` with everything inside it to `maps_old`?
blocks.why: Folders need `cp -r`. `mv` would move the folder instead of copying it.
blocks.hint: Copying a folder needs one extra option.

blocks.q: Put these commands in order: create a workspace, go into it, make a file there, and check.
items: mkdir -p lab_ws/src
cd lab_ws
touch notes.txt
ls
blocks.why: Create the folder first, go into it, create the file, then check with `ls`.
blocks.hint: You cannot go into a folder before it exists.

blocks.q: You want `report.txt` to be called `report_v1.txt`, in the same folder. Which command?
blocks.why: Renaming is moving to a new name: `mv`. `cp` would leave two files.
blocks.hint: Do you want one file or two afterwards?

items.back: delete a folder and everything in it

items: `mkdir -p` makes folders (and missing parents). `touch` makes an empty file.
`cp -r` copies folders. `mv` moves or renames.
`rm` deletes forever, so check twice.

lessons.title: Reading and editing files
lessons.summary: Look inside files with `cat`, `head` and `tail`, and edit them with `nano`.

blocks.text: Chiku kept a diary (a log file) of its last trip, and something went wrong near the end. Let's read it.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `cat` shows a whole file, `head` the beginning, `tail` the end, and `grep` finds the lines that contain a word. `nano` lets you change a file.
Robots write **log files** that record what happened, and ROS 2 packages are described by small text files. You will often need to look inside a file or change one line.

cat notes.txt         # show the whole file
head -n 5 log.txt     # show the first 5 lines
tail -n 5 log.txt     # show the last 5 lines
less log.txt          # scroll through a long file (press q to quit)
nano notes.txt        # edit a file
`head` is like reading only the first page of a long notebook, and `tail` is like reading only the last page. Robot logs add new messages at the end, so `tail` shows you the newest news.
Editing with nano

items: Type `nano filename` and press Enter. The file opens inside the terminal.
Move with the arrow keys and type your changes.
Press `Ctrl` + `O` to save (O for output), then Enter.
Press `Ctrl` + `X` to exit nano.

blocks.text: In the practice terminal you can also use the **^O Save** and **^X Exit** buttons. The `^` symbol means the Ctrl key.

blocks.title: Practice: read a robot log and edit a file

files.~/robot.log:
boot: ok
motors: ok
camera: ok
lidar: ok
battery: 86%
wifi: connected
mission: start
obstacle: detected
mission: paused
battery: 84%

tasks.do: Show the whole log: `cat robot.log`
Show only the first 3 lines: `head -n 3 robot.log`
Show only the last 2 lines, the newest messages.
Open `hello.py` in nano. Change `robot` to `ROS 2 robot`, save with Ctrl+O, and exit with Ctrl+X.
tasks.hint: Type: nano hello.py  then edit the text, press the ^O Save button, then ^X Exit.

tasks.do: Check your change: `cat hello.py`

blocks.q: Chiku's log file has 5,000 lines and the newest messages are at the bottom. Which command shows only the last 20 lines?
blocks.answer: `tail -n 20 robot.log`. Bonus: `tail -f robot.log` keeps the file open and prints new lines as the robot writes them, which is perfect for watching a running robot.

blocks.text: Searching inside files with grep
Robot logs can have thousands of lines. Reading them all is slow. `grep WORD file` prints **only the lines that contain WORD**. It is one of the most used commands in robotics.

grep ERROR robot.log          # only lines with ERROR
grep -i battery robot.log     # -i: ignore capital/small letters
grep -c WARN robot.log        # -c: just count the matching lines
tail -n 20 robot.log | grep ERROR   # | sends the output of tail into grep
`grep` is like the **Ctrl+F** search box of a web page, but for the terminal. The `|` sign (called a **pipe**) is like a funnel: the output of the first command pours into the second one.

blocks.title: Practice: be a log detective

tasks.do: How many lines does the log have? `wc -l robot.log`
Show only the error lines: `grep ERROR robot.log`
tasks.hint: Type: grep ERROR robot.log  (ERROR in capitals)

tasks.do: Find every battery line, ignoring capitals: `grep -i battery robot.log`
Show the last 4 lines only.
Combine them with a pipe: `cat robot.log | grep WARN`

lessons.title: Permissions and sudo (part 1)
lessons.summary: Read rwx permissions, make a program runnable with `chmod +x`, and use `sudo` safely.

blocks.text: Chiku's new program refuses to start: Permission denied! Time to learn who is allowed to do what.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Each file has a small lock with three switches for three groups of people: **read**, **write** and **run**. `chmod` changes the switches. `sudo` borrows administrator power for one command.
Every file has **permissions** that say who may read it, change it or run it. When you see `Permission denied`, permissions are usually the reason.

ls -l
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student   31 Oct  2 10:15 notes.txt
-rwxr-xr-x 1 student student   64 Oct  2 10:15 move.py
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 Oct  2 10:15 maps

items.m: `d` means a folder, `-` means a file
read: look inside
write: change it
execute: run it as a program
after the first letter: owner (you), group, everyone else

blocks.text: Permissions are like keys to a hostel room. `rwxr-xr-x` means the owner can enter, rearrange and use everything, while others may look in and use things but not change them.
Making a program runnable

./move.py           # bash: ./move.py: Permission denied
chmod +x move.py    # add execute (x) permission
./move.py           # now it runs
sudo: administrator power for one command

Some actions change the whole system, such as installing software. They need administrator rights. Put `sudo` in front of the command; Ubuntu asks for **your** password. Nothing appears on screen while you type the password. That is normal.
`sudo` means "I know exactly what I am doing." Never put `sudo` in front of a command you do not understand, and never use `sudo rm -r`.

blocks.intro: Flip the permission switches and solve the three puzzles. Watch how the letters and the number change together.

blocks.text: Decoding `-rwxr-xr--` one letter at a time

items: Letter 1: `-` means a normal **file** (a `d` would mean a folder).
Letters 2 to 4, `rwx`: the **owner** (you) can read, write and run it.
Letters 5 to 7, `r-x`: the **group** can read and run, but not change it (the `-` means "no").
Letters 8 to 10, `r--`: **everyone else** can only read it.
As numbers: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Owner 4+2+1 = **7**, group 4+1 = **5**, others 4 = **4**, so this is **754**.

tasks.do: Look at the permissions with `ls -l`
Try to run the program: `./move.py`. Read the error.
Make it executable: `chmod +x move.py`
Run it again with `./move.py`
Try `apt install tree` without sudo, and read the error.
Now install it the right way, with sudo.
Run `tree` to see your folders drawn as a tree.

blocks.q: What number is `-rwxr--r--`?
blocks.why: Owner rwx = 7, group r = 4, others r = 4.

blocks.q: Type the command that lets everybody run `move.py`.
blocks.why: `chmod +x` adds the run permission.
blocks.hint: chmod, then +x, then the file.

items: `ls -l` shows permissions: d or -, then rwx for owner, group and others.

lessons.title: Installing software with apt
lessons.summary: Refresh the software list, search for packages, and install ROS 2 tools.

blocks.text: Chiku needs a new tool, the turtle simulator. Installing software on Ubuntu works like an app store.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `apt` is Ubuntu's app store in the terminal. `sudo apt update` refreshes the list of apps, `sudo apt install name` installs one.
On Ubuntu you install software with **apt**, the package manager. It downloads programs from trusted online stores called **repositories**. ROS 2 itself is installed with apt.
apt works like the app store on your phone. `apt update` refreshes the store's catalogue but installs nothing. `apt install` downloads and installs an app. `apt search` looks for apps by name.

sudo apt update                        # refresh the list of software
apt search turtlesim                   # find packages by name
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-turtlesim   # install a package

items.m: apt names of ROS 2 Jazzy packages start like this
apt names use dashes: `ros-jazzy-demo-nodes-py`
inside ROS 2 the same package is called `demo_nodes_py`

blocks.text: On a real computer apt may ask `Do you want to continue? [Y/n]`. Type `y` and press Enter. Adding `-y` at the end answers yes automatically.

tasks.do: Refresh the software list: `sudo apt update`
Search for turtlesim: `apt search turtlesim`
Install it: `sudo apt install ros-jazzy-turtlesim`
Load ROS 2 into this terminal: `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash` (Day 10 explains why).
Start the turtle simulator: `ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node`

blocks.text: What really happens when you type `sudo apt install tree`

items: `sudo` asks for your password, because installing changes the whole computer.
apt looks up `tree` in its **local list** of packages (the list `apt update` downloaded).
It works out what else `tree` needs (its **dependencies**) and shows you the total size.
It downloads the files from the Ubuntu **repository** (an online store of checked software).
It installs them and sets them up. Now the `tree` command exists on your computer.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting `sudo apt update` on a new computer: apt then says it cannot find packages.
Using underscores in apt names: it is `ros-jazzy-demo-nodes-py`, with dashes.
Forgetting `sudo` for install: you get a permission error.

pairs.b: refresh the list of available software (installs nothing)
find packages by name or description

blocks.why: update refreshes the catalogue; install, upgrade and remove change the computer, so they need sudo.
blocks.hint: update only refreshes the list.

blocks.q: What does `sudo apt update` do?
options: Refreshes the list of available software; it installs nothing
Updates the Python code in your workspace
blocks.why: `update` only refreshes the catalogue. `install` actually adds software.
blocks.hint: Think of the app store catalogue.

blocks.q: `sudo apt install ros-jazzy-demo_nodes_py` says Unable to locate package. Why?
options: Package names must be in capitals
blocks.why: apt names use dashes; inside ROS 2 the same package uses underscores.
blocks.hint: Look closely at the symbols between the words.

blocks.why: Installing changes the computer, so it needs sudo.
blocks.hint: sudo apt install ...

items: `sudo apt update` refreshes, `sudo apt install name` installs, and `apt search word` finds packages.
ROS 2 apt packages look like `ros-jazzy-...` with dashes.

lessons.title: Python 1: the robot's notebook (part 1)
lessons.summary: Print messages, store values in variables, tell numbers from text, and ask questions with `input()`.

blocks.text: Chiku keeps a notebook: its name, its battery level, how far it has travelled. In Python, each line of that notebook is a **variable**. Today you write Chiku's first notebook.

items: Print messages with `print()`
Store values in variables
Tell numbers and text apart
Ask the user a question with `input()`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **variable** is a labelled box that remembers a value. `print()` shows things. Text needs quotes, numbers don't.
Your first line of Python
`print()` shows something on the screen. Text goes inside quotes; numbers don't need quotes.

blocks.title: Try it: press Run
blocks.code:
print("Hello, I am Chiku!")
print(2 + 3)
print("2 + 3")

blocks.text: Look at the last two lines: `2 + 3` without quotes is maths (5), but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is just text.
Variables: labelled boxes
A variable is a labelled box in Chiku's notebook. `battery = 80` puts 80 into a box labelled battery. Later you can read the box, or put something new in it.

name = "Chiku"        # text (str)
battery = 80          # whole number (int)
speed = 0.5           # decimal number (float)
is_charging = False   # True or False (bool)
print(name, battery, speed, is_charging)

items.m: whole numbers: 80, -3, 0
numbers with a decimal point: 0.5, 3.14
text in quotes: "Chiku"
True or False (capital T and F)

blocks.text: In Python, `=` means **store**, not "is equal to". `battery = battery - 10` means: take the old battery value, subtract 10, and store the result back in the box.
Nice messages with f-strings

name = "Chiku"
battery = 80
print(f"{name} has {battery}% battery")
Put the letter `f` before the quotes, then write variable names inside `{ }`. Python fills in their values.
Asking questions with input()
`input()` waits for the user to type something and gives it back as **text**. To do maths with it, turn it into a number with `int()` (whole numbers) or `float()` (decimals).

blocks.title: Try it: trip calculator
blocks.goal: Run it once as it is. Then change the program so that the trip uses **20%** battery instead of 10%. With the answers shown, the last line must be `Chiku will be at 60% after the trip`.
blocks.code:
name = input("Robot name: ")
level = int(input("Battery %: "))
print(f"{name} will be at {level - 10}% after the trip")
contains: Chiku will be at 60% after the trip
blocks.retryHint: Inside the f-string, change level - 10 to level - 20.
blocks.solution:
name = input("Robot name: ")
level = int(input("Battery %: "))
print(f"{name} will be at {level - 20}% after the trip")

blocks.q: What type is `3.5`?
blocks.why: A number with a decimal point is a float.
blocks.hint: Does it have a decimal point?

blocks.q: What does this print?
blocks.why: The f-string fills in the value of battery.
blocks.hint: Replace {battery} with its value.
blocks.code:
battery = 90
print(f"Chiku has {battery}%")

lessons.title: Python 2: should the robot stop? (part 1)
lessons.summary: Make decisions with `if`, `elif` and `else`, and repeat actions with `for`, `while` and `break`.

blocks.text: Chiku is driving down the corridor. Its distance sensor says how far the nearest wall is. Chiku must **decide**: go, slow down or stop. And it must **repeat** that check again and again.

items: Compare values with `<`, `>` and `==`
Make decisions with `if`, `elif` and `else`
Repeat with `for` and `while`
Stop a loop early with `break`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `if` lets Chiku choose what to do. `for` and `while` let it repeat. `break` lets it stop repeating early.
Comparisons give True or False

distance = 0.4
print(distance < 0.5)    # True
print(distance == 1.0)   # False

items.m: less than, greater than
less or equal, greater or equal
is equal to (two equals signs)
is not equal to

blocks.text: if, elif and else
`if` works like a traffic signal at a junction: red means stop, yellow means slow down, green means go. Python checks the signals from top to bottom and follows the **first** one that is True.

blocks.label: Colons and spaces
blocks.text: Each `if`, `elif` and `else` line ends with a colon `:`. The lines inside are pushed right by 4 spaces. Python uses those spaces to know what belongs inside.

blocks.title: Your turn: the robot's traffic signal
blocks.goal: Change `distance` so that the program prints `STOP`.
blocks.retryHint: STOP appears only when distance is less than 0.5. Try distance = 0.3.

blocks.text: Repeating with for and while

for i in range(3):        # i = 0, then 1, then 2
    print("Beep", i)

count = 3
while count > 0:          # repeat while this is True
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Lift-off!")
`range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2. Python starts counting at 0, so `range(3)` means three times.
Stopping early with break

blocks.title: Mini-challenge: patrol with a battery check
blocks.goal: Each trip uses 30% battery. Add `break` so Chiku goes home as soon as the battery is below 20, and does not try to reach the Hostel.
blocks.code:
battery = 100
for place in ["Lab", "Library", "Canteen", "Hostel"]:
    battery = battery - 30
    print("Reached", place, "battery", battery)
    if battery < 20:
        print("Low battery, going home")
        # add break on the next line
blocks.expect:
Reached Lab battery 70
Reached Library battery 40
Reached Canteen battery 10
Low battery, going home
blocks.retryHint: Under the print("Low battery, going home") line, add a line with break, indented the same way.
blocks.solution:
battery = 100
for place in ["Lab", "Library", "Canteen", "Hostel"]:
    battery = battery - 30
    print("Reached", place, "battery", battery)
    if battery < 20:
        print("Low battery, going home")
        break

blocks.q: What does `range(4)` give in a for loop?
blocks.why: range starts at 0 and stops before 4.
blocks.hint: Python counts from 0.

blocks.q: What does this print?
blocks.why: 0.7 is not below 0.5, but it is below 1.0, so the elif runs.
blocks.hint: Check the tests from top to bottom.

blocks.text: Great work! Take a short break, then continue with **part 2**: more practice and the quick checks.

lessons.title: Python 2: should the robot stop? (part 2)
lessons.summary: Part 2: more practice, quick checks and the recap.

blocks.text: Welcome back! In part 1 you worked on: Comparisons give True or False, if, elif and else, Repeating with for and while. Now let's finish the job. Chiku is driving down the corridor. Its distance sensor says how far the nearest wall is. Chiku must **decide**: go, slow down or stop. And it must **repeat** that check again and again.

blocks.title: A loop that stops for an obstacle
blocks.code:
readings = [1.2, 0.8, 0.3, 2.0]
for d in readings:
    if d < 0.5:
        print("STOP at", d)
        break
    print("ok", d)
print("done")

steps.note: A list of four distance readings.
First round of the loop: `d` takes the first item, 1.2.
Is 1.2 < 0.5? **False**, so the indented lines under `if` are skipped.
Print and go back to the top of the loop.
Second round: `d` is 0.8.
0.8 < 0.5? False again.
Print, back to the top.
Third round: `d` is 0.3.
0.3 < 0.5? **True!** Now the lines under `if` run.
Print the warning.
`break` leaves the loop **immediately**. 2.0 is never checked, and line 6 is skipped.
The program continues after the loop.

blocks.title: Practice: the battery light
blocks.goal: Write `if` / `elif` / `else` so the program prints the right word. With `battery = 15` it must print `LOW`.
blocks.code:
battery = 15

# print FULL if battery >= 80, OK if battery >= 30, LOW if battery >= 10, otherwise EMPTY
blocks.retryHint: Start with if battery >= 80: then elif battery >= 30: then elif battery >= 10: then else:. Each line ends with a colon, and print lines are pushed right 4 spaces.

blocks.title: Practice: countdown with while
blocks.goal: Make Chiku count down from 5 to 1, then print `Lift-off!`. Each number on its own line.
blocks.code:
count = 5
# while count is greater than 0: print it, then make it 1 smaller

print("Lift-off!")
blocks.solution:
count = 5
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1

print("Lift-off!")
blocks.retryHint: while count > 0:  then (pushed right) print(count) and count = count - 1

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Writing `=` instead of `==` in a test: `if battery = 10:` is an error.
Forgetting the colon `:` at the end of if/elif/else/for/while lines.
Wrong indentation: the lines inside must be pushed right by exactly 4 spaces.
A `while` loop that never ends because the variable never changes.

blocks.q: Which sign means "is equal to" when you compare two values?
blocks.why: `=` stores a value; `==` compares two values.
blocks.hint: Comparing needs two signs.

blocks.q: How many times does this print Beep?
blocks.why: `range(4)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3: four numbers.
blocks.hint: Count the numbers range(4) gives.
blocks.code:
for i in range(4):
    print("Beep")

blocks.q: Put the lines in order: count down from 3, then print Go!
items: count = 3
while count > 0:
print(count)
count = count - 1
print("Go!")
blocks.why: Set the start value, loop while it is above zero, print and reduce inside the loop, then print Go! after the loop.
blocks.hint: The indented lines belong inside the loop.

blocks.q: Python refuses to run this. Tap the line with the mistake.
blocks.code:
distance = 0.3
if distance < 0.5
    print("STOP")
else:
    print("GO")
blocks.why: A line that starts a block (`if`, `else`, `for`, `def`...) must end with a colon `:`.
blocks.hint: Compare line 2 with line 4.

items: Comparisons (`<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`) give True or False.
`if` / `elif` / `else` run the first matching choice.
`for i in range(n)` repeats n times; `while` repeats while a test is True.
`break` leaves a loop early.

lessons.title: Python 3: memory and skills
lessons.summary: Keep many values in lists and dictionaries, and write your own functions.

blocks.text: Chiku must remember a list of places to visit and the readings of its three distance sensors. It also needs reusable **skills**, like checking whether the way is safe.

items: Store many values in a list
Look up values by name in a dictionary
Write and use your own functions

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **list** keeps many values in order. A **dictionary** finds a value by its name. A **function** is a skill you write once and use many times.
Lists: many values in order

places = ["Lab", "Library", "Canteen"]
print(places[0])       # first item: Lab
print(len(places))     # how many: 3
places.append("Hostel")

A list is like a train: coaches in a fixed order, numbered from 0. `append` adds a new coach at the end, and `len` counts the coaches.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: A class is a blueprint; an object is a robot built from it.

blocks.text: One blueprint, many robots: today Chiku gets brothers and sisters.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **class** is a design drawing. An **object** is a real thing built from that drawing. One drawing, many things.
ROS 2 programs are built from **classes**. The word sounds difficult, but the idea is simple, and you already know it from real life.

A **class** is like the blueprint (design drawing) of a robot. One blueprint can build many robots. Each robot built from it is an **object**. All the robots have the same parts, but each one can have its own name and battery level.

class Robot:          # the blueprint
    pass              # (empty for now)

r1 = Robot()          # build robot 1 (an object)
r2 = Robot()          # build robot 2 (another object)
r1.name = "Chiku"
r2.name = "Bolt"
print(r1.name)        # Chiku
print(r2.name)        # Bolt

one thing built from the blueprint (also called an instance)
a value stored inside an object, like `r1.name`
calling the class builds a new object

blocks.text: Every ROS 2 program you will write is a class. The official `turtlesim` simulator, the TurtleBot3 drivers and the Nav2 navigation system are all built from classes, often hundreds of them.

lessons.title: Attributes and __init__
lessons.summary: Give every new object its starting values automatically, with `__init__` and `self`.

blocks.text: Every robot that leaves Chiku's factory should get its name and a full battery automatically.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `__init__` is the setup step that runs **by itself** every time a new object is built. `self` means "the object being built right now".
In the last lesson we added a name after building each robot. That is easy to forget. Python has a special setup step that runs **automatically** whenever an object is built: `__init__`.
`__init__` is like the factory's final checklist. Every robot that leaves the factory gets its name painted on and its battery charged, before anyone uses it.

class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name, battery):
        self.name = name          # store the name inside this robot
        self.battery = battery    # store the battery inside this robot

r1 = Robot("Chiku", 90)
r2 = Robot("Bolt", 40)
print(r1.name, r1.battery)
print(r2.name, r2.battery)

items.m: two underscores, init, two underscores: the setup step
the object being built right now
store the value inside this object

blocks.text: When you write `Robot("Chiku", 90)`, Python builds an empty robot, then runs `__init__` with `self` as the new robot, `name` as "Chiku" and `battery` as 90. You never pass `self` yourself: Python does it for you.
`self` must be the **first** parameter: `def __init__(self, name):`. Forgetting it causes a `TypeError`.

blocks.code:
class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name, battery):
        self.name = name
        self.battery = battery

r1 = Robot("Chiku", 90)
r2 = Robot("Mitra", 40)
print(r1.name, r2.battery)

steps.note: The class (blueprint) is defined. No robot exists yet.
`Robot("Chiku", 90)` makes a new, empty object and calls `__init__` on it.
Inside `__init__`, **self is the new object**. `self.name = name` stores "Chiku" **inside** it.
Same for the battery.
`__init__` is done. The finished object is stored in `r1`. The temporary `name` and `battery` boxes disappear; the values live on inside the object.
The same happens for `r2`, with **its own** values. This time `self` was r2.
Each object keeps its own attributes.

lessons.title: Methods: what an object can do
lessons.summary: Write methods that use and change an object's attributes.

blocks.text: A robot is more than its data: it can move, charge and report. These skills are called methods.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: **Attributes** are what an object has. **Methods** are what it can do. A method is a function inside a class, and it always gets `self` first.
Attributes are what an object **has**. Methods are what an object **can do**. A method is simply a function written inside a class.

blocks.out:

Chiku moved 2 steps
Chiku total distance: 5

blocks.text: Calling `r.move(3)` is like pressing the move button on that particular robot. Inside the method, `self` means "this robot", so Chiku's distance changes and no other robot's does.
You call `r.move(3)` with one value, but the method is written `def move(self, steps)` with two. Python fills in `self` with `r` automatically.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: An object can keep **other objects** inside it, like a robot keeps motors inside it. You reach them with dots: `self.left.spin()`.
Real robots are made of parts: motors, sensors, a battery. In Python, an object can keep other objects as attributes. This is exactly how a ROS 2 node keeps its publishers, subscribers and timers.

Later you will see `self.publisher_.publish(msg)`. It is the same pattern: in this node, take the publisher object, and call its publish method.

lessons.title: Inheritance and super()
lessons.summary: Build a new class on top of an existing one, which is exactly how every ROS 2 node is written.

blocks.text: Chiku's cousin Raju is a delivery robot with a basket. Raju should get everything Chiku has, plus the basket.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: **Inheritance** means a new class starts with everything an old class has, and adds more. `super().__init__()` runs the old class's setup first.
Writing every class from zero would be slow. **Inheritance** lets a new class start with everything an existing class already has, and then add more.

Car makers build a new model on an existing **platform**: the wheels, engine and brakes come from the platform, and the new model adds its own features. The platform is the **parent class**, and the new model is the **child class**.

blocks.out:
Pragyan engine started
Pragyan exploring on 6 wheels
blocks.text:
class Vehicle:                   # parent class
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def start(self):
        print(self.name, "engine started")

class Rover(Vehicle):            # child class: a Rover is a Vehicle
    def __init__(self, name):
        super().__init__(name)   # run the parent's setup first
        self.wheels = 6

    def explore(self):
        print(self.name, "exploring on", self.wheels, "wheels")

r = Rover("Pragyan")
r.start()     # inherited from Vehicle
r.explore()   # Rover's own method

items.m: Rover inherits from Vehicle; the class in brackets is the parent
run the parent's `__init__`, so its setup happens too
a child can write its own version of a parent's method

blocks.text: This is exactly a ROS 2 node

from rclpy.node import Node

class MyFirstNode(Node):                    # inherit from ROS 2's Node class
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('my_first_node')   # set up the node and name it
        self.get_logger().info('Hello from my node!')

`Node` is a parent class written by the ROS 2 team. Your class inherits from it, so your node can do everything a node can do: log messages, publish, subscribe and use timers. `super().__init__('my_first_node')` runs Node's setup and gives your node its name.

lessons.title: Callbacks and timers
lessons.summary: Hand a function over to be called later: the heartbeat of every ROS 2 program.

blocks.text: Chiku must blink its light every second without anyone pressing a button. Timers and callbacks make it happen.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **callback** is a function you hand to someone else to call later. A **timer** calls your function again and again, every few seconds.

In ROS 2 you rarely call your own methods directly. Instead you tell ROS 2: "**call this method for me** every half second", or "when a message arrives". A function handed over to be called later is a **callback**.

It is like giving the college office your phone number and saying "call me when my certificate is ready." You hand over your number; you do not start talking right away. In Python, you hand over the function's name **without brackets**.

def wave():
    print("Waving!")

my_callback = wave      # no brackets: the function itself, not run yet
my_callback()           # now it runs
`wave` (no brackets) means the function itself. `wave()` means "run it **now**". Writing `self.timer_callback()` inside `create_timer(...)` is a very common beginner mistake.
Timers in ROS 2

`self.create_timer(1.0, self.blink)` means: every 1.0 seconds, call `self.blink`. `rclpy.spin(node)` keeps the program alive so the timer can keep firing. (`self.count += 1` is a short way to write `self.count = self.count + 1`.)

blocks.title: A blinking node (the practice simulator runs for 3 seconds)
blocks.goal: Make the timer fire every `0.5` seconds. In 3 seconds it should blink 6 times, so the output contains `Blink 6`.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

class Blinker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('blinker')
        self.count = 0
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.blink)

    def blink(self):
        self.count += 1
        self.get_logger().info(f'Blink {self.count}')

rclpy.init()
node = Blinker()
rclpy.spin(node)
node.destroy_node()
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: Change 1.0 to 0.5 inside create_timer(...).

blocks.intro: What is `rclpy.spin()` actually doing while your node runs? Start it, then make a callback slow.

blocks.text: What happens, second by second

items: `__init__` runs once: it creates the timer and hands over `self.blink` (no brackets). Nothing blinks yet.
`rclpy.spin(node)` starts waiting. It is like a watchman with a clock.
After 1.0 second the clock rings: spin calls `self.blink()` for you. "Blink 1".
After 2.0 seconds it rings again: "Blink 2". And so on, for ever, until you press Ctrl+C.
Your code never calls `blink()` itself. That is the whole idea of a callback.

blocks.q: A timer callback contains `time.sleep(5)` and the timer period is 1 second. What goes wrong?
blocks.answer: Callbacks run **one at a time**. While `sleep(5)` blocks, no other callback can run: the other timers wait, messages pile up and the robot reacts late. Keep callbacks short; never sleep inside them.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Writing `self.blink()` inside `create_timer`: that runs it once immediately and hands over `None`.
Forgetting `rclpy.spin(node)`: the program ends before any timer fires.
Putting slow work (`sleep`, long loops) inside a callback.
Giving two timers the same attribute name, so the first one is replaced.

lessons.title: Reading a real ROS 2 node

blocks.text: Time to read real ROS 2 code. You already know every idea in it.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A real ROS 2 node is just a class that inherits from `Node`, creates a publisher and a timer in `__init__`, and publishes in the timer's callback. You already know every piece.

You now know every idea used in a real ROS 2 Python node: classes, `__init__`, `self`, methods, objects inside objects, inheritance, `super()` and callbacks. Here is the minimal publisher from the official ROS 2 Jazzy tutorial (Apache 2.0 licence):

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String


class MinimalPublisher(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('minimal_publisher')
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10)
        timer_period = 0.5  # seconds
        self.timer = self.create_timer(timer_period, self.timer_callback)
        self.i = 0

    def timer_callback(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = 'Hello World: %d' % self.i
        self.publisher_.publish(msg)
        self.get_logger().info('Publishing: "%s"' % msg.data)
        self.i += 1


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    minimal_publisher = MinimalPublisher()
    rclpy.spin(minimal_publisher)
    minimal_publisher.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
Line by line

items: `import rclpy` brings in ROS 2's Python library.
`from std_msgs.msg import String` gets the String message type: a box with one text field called `data`.
`class MinimalPublisher(Node)`: our node **inherits** from Node (Day 7).
`super().__init__('minimal_publisher')` runs Node's setup and names the node.

`self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(String, 'topic', 10)` stores a publisher **object inside our object** (Day 6). It sends String messages on the topic named `topic`. The 10 is the queue size: how many messages may wait if the network is slow.
`self.create_timer(timer_period, self.timer_callback)` calls `timer_callback` every 0.5 seconds (Day 7). Notice: no brackets.
`self.i = 0` is a counter attribute (Day 6).
`timer_callback` makes a message, fills `msg.data`, publishes it, logs it, and adds 1 to the counter.
`main()` starts ROS 2, builds the node, spins to keep it running, then cleans up and shuts down.

blocks.text: `'Hello World: %d' % self.i` puts the number `self.i` where `%d` is. Modern Python also writes this as `f'Hello World: {self.i}'`.

blocks.text: Adding a listener
A **subscriber** receives messages. Its callback runs once for every message that arrives on its topic. In this playground the talker and the listener run together, so you can see both sides.

blocks.title: Talker and listener together
blocks.goal: Complete `listener_callback` so it logs `I heard: ` followed by the message text. The output should contain `I heard: Hello World: 2`.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String


class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(String, 'chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback)
        self.i = 0

    def timer_callback(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = f'Hello World: {self.i}'
        self.publisher_.publish(msg)
        self.i += 1


class Listener(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('listener')
        self.subscription = self.create_subscription(String, 'chatter', self.listener_callback, 10)

    def listener_callback(self, msg):
        # log the received text here, using msg.data
        pass


rclpy.init()
listener = Listener()
talker = Talker()
rclpy.spin(talker)
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: Replace pass with self.get_logger().info(f'I heard: {msg.data}')

from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String


class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(String, 'chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback)
        self.i = 0

    def timer_callback(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = f'Hello World: {self.i}'
        self.publisher_.publish(msg)

lessons.title: Hello, C++: compile and run
lessons.summary: Write, compile and run your first C++ program, and fix the most common error.

blocks.text: Chiku's motors need very fast decisions, hundreds every second. For speed-critical parts, robot engineers often use **C++**, and many ROS 2 drivers and controllers are written in it. Good news: the ideas are the same as in Python; only the spelling is stricter.

items: Write, compile and run a C++ program
Print with `std::cout`
Create variables with a type
Fix the most common error: a missing semicolon

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: C++ is translated into a fast program **before** it runs (compiling). Write `.cpp`, compile with `g++`, run with `./name`. Every line ends with `;`.

Python reads your recipe and cooks line by line as it reads. C++ first translates the **whole** recipe into machine language (this is called **compiling**), and only then cooks. Translating takes a moment, but the cooking is then very fast.
Your first C++ program

items: Write the code in a file ending in `.cpp`, for example with `nano hello.cpp`.
Compile it: `g++ hello.cpp -o hello`. This makes a program called hello.
Run the program: `./hello`.

tasks.do: Look at the code: `cat hello.cpp`
Compile it: `g++ hello.cpp -o hello`
Run your program: `./hello`
Open `hello.cpp` in nano and change the message to `Hello, ROS 2!`. Save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X.
tasks.hint: Type: nano hello.cpp, change the text between the quotes, then press the ^O Save and ^X Exit buttons.

tasks.do: Run `./hello` again. Is the message new? Then compile again with g++ and run once more.
tasks.hint: The program changes only after you compile again: g++ hello.cpp -o hello, then ./hello

blocks.text: Did you notice? After editing, `./hello` still printed the old message until you compiled again. In C++, you must **compile after every change**.
Variables have a type

wheels = 4
speed = 0.5

right.label: C++

every statement ends with a semicolon
curly brackets group lines (Python uses indentation)
the name tag of C++'s standard tools, as in `std::cout` and `std::string`

blocks.text: Functions with types
A C++ function says the **type of its answer** (`bool`) and the **type of each input** (`double distance`).
Lists in C++: std::vector

right.label: C++

blocks.text: `std::vector` is C++'s list (add `#include <vector>` at the top). In ROS 2 C++ code, a laser scanner's distance readings arrive as a `std::vector<float>`.

blocks.title: A C++ for loop, step by step

steps.note: `int total = 0;` makes a box that can only hold whole numbers (`int`).
The loop starts: `int i = 1`. Check `i <= 3`: true, so enter the body.
total = 0 + 1.
`i++` adds 1 to i. Check 2 <= 3: true.
total = 1 + 2.
i becomes 3. 3 <= 3: still true.
total = 3 + 3.
i becomes 4. 4 <= 3 is **false**, so the loop ends. (`i` only exists inside the loop.)
Print the total: same as Python's `for i in range(1, 4)`.
`return 0;` tells the system the program finished without errors.

items: Using `and`/`or` habits: C++ writes `&&` and `||`.

lessons.title: C++ classes: same blueprint, stricter rules
lessons.summary: Write a C++ class with a constructor, member functions, `public` and `private`, and inheritance.

blocks.text: Remember the Python Robot blueprint from Day 6? Today you build the same blueprint in C++. The ideas are the same; the rules are stricter.

items: Read and write a C++ class with a constructor and member functions
Use `public` and `private`
Recognise inheritance in C++

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A C++ class is the same blueprint idea as Python: a constructor instead of `__init__`, `this->` instead of `self.`, plus `public` (the buttons) and `private` (the insides).

left.label: Python

right.label: C++

items.m: the **constructor**: a function with the class's name, `Robot(...)`
`name_`: C++ code often ends member names with `_`, and doesn't write `self`
the initialiser list: sets members before the constructor's body runs
who may use it: everyone / only the class itself
a C++ class ends with a semicolon

blocks.text: `public` and `private` are like a robot's control panel and its insides. Anyone may press the buttons on the panel (public functions like `move`). Only the robot itself touches its insides (private data like `battery_`), so nobody can set the battery to -50 by mistake.
Inheritance in C++

left.label: Python

right.label: C++

blocks.text: `: public Robot` means DeliveryRobot inherits from Robot. Calling `Robot(name)` in the initialiser list does the job of Python's `super().__init__(name)`.

blocks.q: Match each C++ piece with its Python twin.
blocks.why: Same ideas, stricter spelling: C++ adds types, braces, semicolons and `this->` instead of `self.`.
blocks.hint: this-> is C++'s self.

blocks.q: In C++, which part does the job of Python's `__init__`?
options: The constructor: a function with the same name as the class
blocks.why: The constructor runs automatically when an object is created, like `__init__`.
blocks.hint: Which function has the class's name?

blocks.q: `battery_` is private. Which line gives a compile error?
blocks.why: Private members can only be used inside the class's own functions.
blocks.hint: Which line touches the robot's insides from outside?

blocks.q: What is the parent class in `class Rover : public Robot`?
blocks.why: The class after `: public` is the parent.
blocks.hint: Look after the colon.

blocks.q: Complete the line so that Rover inherits from Robot: `class Rover : ______ Robot {`
blocks.why: `class Child : public Parent` is how C++ writes inheritance.
blocks.hint: It is the same word as the control-panel section.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting the `;` after the class's closing `}`.
Trying to change a private member from outside the class.
Forgetting to call the parent constructor in the initialiser list.

blocks.q: g++ reports an error at the very end of this file. Tap the line that causes it.
blocks.why: A C++ class must end with `};` (a brace **and** a semicolon). Forgetting the semicolon is one of the most common C++ errors.
blocks.hint: Compare the end of the class with the end of a function.

blocks.q: Put this C++ class in order, top to bottom.
items: class Battery {
public:
Battery(int level) : level_(level) {}
int level() { return level_; }
private:
int level_;
blocks.why: Class line, the public buttons (constructor and member functions), the private insides, then `};`.
blocks.hint: public comes before private here, and the class ends with };

blocks.q: Why are member variables often private in C++?
options: So only the class's own functions can change them, keeping the values valid
Because C++ does not allow public variables
So the compiler can skip them
blocks.why: Private data can only be changed through the class's functions, which can check the values (no battery level of -50).
blocks.hint: Think of the robot's control panel and its insides.

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** How is `this->name_` in C++ like `self.name_` in Python?
blocks.answer: Both mean "the `name_` that belongs to **this** object". C++ uses the pointer `this` with an arrow; Python passes the object in as `self` and uses a dot.

items: A C++ class has a constructor (like `__init__`), member functions and member variables.
`public` is the control panel; `private` is the robot's insides.
`class Child : public Parent` inherits; call `Parent(...)` in the initialiser list.

lessons.title: Reading a real ROS 2 C++ node
lessons.summary: Find the class, constructor, publisher, timer and callback inside the official C++ publisher.

blocks.text: You can already read a Python ROS 2 node. A C++ node has exactly the same parts. Today you find each Python idea inside a real C++ node.

items: Find the class, constructor, publisher, timer and callback in an rclcpp node
Read `std::make_shared` and lambdas without fear
Match each C++ line with its Python twin

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The C++ node has the same five parts as the Python one: class, constructor (names the node), publisher, timer and callback, plus a short `main()`.
This is the minimal publisher from the official ROS 2 Jazzy C++ tutorial (Apache 2.0 licence). It sends a message twice per second.
Line by line

items: `class MinimalPublisher : public rclcpp::Node` inherits from Node, like Python's `class MinimalPublisher(Node)`.
`MinimalPublisher() : Node("minimal_publisher"), count_(0)` is the constructor. It names the node, like `super().__init__('minimal_publisher')`, and sets the counter to 0.
`create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>("topic", 10)`: the message type goes inside `< >`, then the topic name and the queue size.
`auto timer_callback = [this]() -> void { ... };` is a **lambda**: a small function without a name, written right where it is needed.
`create_wall_timer(500ms, timer_callback)` calls the lambda every 500 milliseconds, like `create_timer(0.5, self.timer_callback)`.
`RCLCPP_INFO(...)` prints a log message, like `self.get_logger().info(...)`.
The `SharedPtr` members hold the timer and the publisher. They are smart pointers that clean up by themselves.
`main()` starts ROS 2 (`rclcpp::init`), builds the node and keeps it running (`rclcpp::spin`), then stops (`rclcpp::shutdown`).

items.m: builds an object of type T and gives back a smart pointer to it
a lambda: a tiny function without a name; `[this]` lets it use the node's members

left.label: Python callback
left.code:
def timer_callback(self):
    msg = String()
    msg.data = f'Hello, world! {self.i}'
    self.publisher_.publish(msg)
    self.i += 1

right.label: C++ lambda

blocks.q: Which C++ line does the job of Python's `super().__init__('minimal_publisher')`?
blocks.why: The constructor's initialiser list calls the parent `Node(...)` with the node's name.
blocks.hint: Look for the node's name.

blocks.q: In `create_wall_timer(500ms, timer_callback)`, how often is the callback called?
blocks.why: 500 ms is 0.5 seconds, so twice per second.
blocks.hint: 1000 ms make one second.

blocks.q: What is `[this]() -> void { ... }`?
options: A lambda: a small function without a name
blocks.why: Lambdas let you write a callback right where you need it.
blocks.hint: It is a kind of function.

blocks.q: Which rclcpp function keeps the node running, like `rclpy.spin`? Type it with its namespace.
blocks.why: `rclcpp::spin(...)` keeps calling the node's callbacks until you press Ctrl+C.
blocks.hint: rclcpp:: followed by the same word as in Python.

blocks.q: Match each C++ line from the node with its Python twin from Day 7.
blocks.why: rclcpp and rclpy are two doors into the same ROS 2: every C++ call has a Python twin.
blocks.hint: Look for matching words: init, spin, timer, logger, shutdown.

blocks.intro: Topics are one of **three** ways ROS 2 nodes talk. The other two are **services** and **actions**. Play to feel the difference; you will meet them in the official tutorials.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting `<std_msgs::msg::String>` after `create_publisher`: C++ needs the type in angle brackets.
Writing `publish(message)` with a dot on a pointer: publishers are pointers, so use `->`.
Forgetting `using namespace std::chrono_literals;` before writing `500ms`.
An rclcpp node is a class that inherits from `rclcpp::Node`.
The constructor names the node and creates the publisher and timer.
Callbacks are often lambdas: `[this]() { ... }`.
`main()`: init, spin, shutdown.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS 2 Jazzy needs Ubuntu 24.04. Choose one way to get it (WSL2, dual boot, virtual machine or the lab), check the computer, then update Ubuntu.

blocks.label: Start early
blocks.text: Read this lesson a few days before Day 10. Downloads and restarts take time, and it is easier to ask for help early.
Four ways to get Ubuntu 24.04

items: **WSL2 on Windows 11 (recommended for most students):** Ubuntu runs inside Windows. No partitioning, and graphical apps such as RViz work. Open PowerShell as administrator, type the command below, restart, then open Ubuntu from the Start menu.
**Dual boot:** Ubuntu installed next to Windows. Fastest, exactly like the lab, but partitioning can lose data if done wrong. Do it only with a backup and with help.
**Virtual machine (VMware Workstation Player or VirtualBox):** safe and easy to reset, but slower, and 3D tools like Gazebo and RViz can misbehave (especially in VirtualBox).
**College lab PCs:** already set up. Use them if your laptop is old or has less than 8 GB of memory.

blocks.text: wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

blocks.title: Is my computer ready?
items: I checked my memory (RAM): **8 GB or more** is best. If I have less, I will use the lab PCs for Gazebo.
I have about **50 GB of free disk space**.
I checked that **virtualization is enabled** (Task Manager, Performance, CPU shows *Virtualization: Enabled*).
I have a good internet connection for about **3 to 5 GB** of downloads, and my charger is plugged in.

blocks.text: After Ubuntu starts

lsb_release -a                       # should say Ubuntu 24.04
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
Ubuntu asks for **your** password whenever you use `sudo`. Nothing appears while you type it. That is normal: type it and press Enter.
Installing WSL2 on Windows 11, step by step

items: Save your work and plug in the laptop. You need about 20 GB of free disk space.
Click Start, type **PowerShell**, right-click it and choose **Run as administrator**.
Type `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04` and press Enter. Windows downloads Ubuntu (this can take 10 to 20 minutes).
Restart the computer when it asks.
Open **Ubuntu 24.04** from the Start menu. The first time, choose a **user name** (small letters, no spaces) and a **password**. Write them down.
In Ubuntu, run `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y`. Now Ubuntu is ready for ROS 2.

lessons.title: Install ROS 2 Jazzy (part 1)
lessons.summary: Rehearse the official installation in the practice terminal, then install on your own Ubuntu.

blocks.text: This is the big moment: installing ROS 2 Jazzy. First you do a full **dress rehearsal** in the practice terminal, so the real installation has no surprises.

items: Follow the official ROS 2 Jazzy installation steps
Understand what each step does
Test the installation with a talker and a listener

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Installing ROS 2 is: set the language, switch on Universe, add the ROS 2 package source, refresh with `apt update`, install `ros-jazzy-desktop`, then `source` it in every terminal.
The official steps, explained

items: **Language settings (locale):** make sure Ubuntu uses UTF-8 text.
**Universe:** switch on Ubuntu's community software collection, which ROS 2 needs.
**ROS 2 package source:** install a small package called `ros2-apt-source`. It tells apt where ROS 2 packages live and adds their security key.
**apt update:** refresh the catalogue so apt can see the ROS 2 packages.
**Install:** `ros-dev-tools` (build tools) and `ros-jazzy-desktop` (ROS 2 with RViz, rqt and demos).
**Source:** load ROS 2 into the terminal, and add that line to `~/.bashrc`.
**Test:** a talker in one terminal and a listener in another.

blocks.text: Two of the commands are very long. In the rehearsal you may copy them with the **Copy** buttons and paste them into the practice terminal (Ctrl+V).
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F\" '{print $4}')

curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo ${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-${VERSION_CODENAME}})_all.deb"

lessons.title: Install ROS 2 Jazzy (part 2)
lessons.summary: Part 2: Now on your real computer; Test with two terminals; If something goes wrong.

blocks.text: Welcome back! In part 1 you worked on: The official steps, explained. Now let's finish the job. This is the big moment: installing ROS 2 Jazzy. First you do a full **dress rehearsal** in the practice terminal, so the real installation has no surprises.
Now on your real computer

When the rehearsal works, open the terminal on your real Ubuntu 24.04 and run the same commands, one by one. The **Copy** button copies everything below; you can also copy and paste one line at a time.

# 1. Language settings (UTF-8)
locale
sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales
sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8
sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8
export LANG=en_US.UTF-8

# 2. Ubuntu universe repository
sudo apt install software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository universe

# 3. ROS 2 package source (ros2-apt-source)
sudo apt update && sudo apt install curl -y
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F\" '{print $4}')
curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo ${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-${VERSION_CODENAME}})_all.deb"
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb

# 4. Install ROS 2 Jazzy
sudo apt update && sudo apt install ros-dev-tools
sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop

# 5. Load ROS 2 now and in every new terminal
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc
The big install downloads a few gigabytes and can take 10 to 40 minutes. Keep your laptop plugged in, and don't close the terminal until you see the prompt again.
Test with two terminals

items: Terminal 1: `ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker`
Open a second terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T): `ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener`
You should see `I heard: [Hello World: 1]`, then 2, 3 and so on. Press Ctrl+C in both terminals to stop.

blocks.text: If something goes wrong

items: **NO_PUBKEY or 'not signed' errors:** an old setup is in the way. Run `sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ros2.list`, repeat step 3, then `sudo apt update`.
**Unmet dependencies:** run `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade` first, then install again.
**Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend:** Ubuntu is updating in the background. Wait 10 minutes or restart. Never delete lock files.
**ros2: command not found:** run `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash`, and check that the line is in `~/.bashrc`.
**The listener hears nothing:** both terminals need the same `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` (see the next lesson).

blocks.q: Why must you add the ROS 2 package source and run `sudo apt update` **before** `sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop`?
blocks.answer: Ubuntu's own catalogue does not contain ROS 2. Adding the ROS 2 source tells apt **where** to look, and `apt update` downloads the new catalogue. Without both, apt says "Unable to locate package ros-jazzy-desktop".

blocks.q: What does the `ros2-apt-source` package do?
options: Tells apt where to find ROS 2 packages and adds their security key
Upgrades Ubuntu to a new version
blocks.why: It only sets up the package source; the actual install comes after `apt update`.
blocks.hint: It is about where packages come from.

blocks.q: Right after installing ros2-apt-source, `sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop` says `Unable to locate package`. What did you forget?
blocks.why: apt must refresh its catalogue before it can see the new ROS 2 packages.
blocks.hint: The catalogue is old.

blocks.q: Put the main installation steps in order.
items: Set up the UTF-8 locale
Enable the universe repository
Install ros2-apt-source
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
blocks.why: Prepare Ubuntu, add the ROS 2 package source, refresh, install, then load ROS 2.
blocks.hint: Preparation comes first; loading ROS 2 comes last.

Following a Humble or ROS 1 tutorial: check that every package name says `jazzy`.
Testing in a terminal that has not been sourced.
The official order: locale, universe, ros2-apt-source, update, install, source.
Run `sudo apt update` after adding a new package source.

lessons.title: Environment variables, source and ~/.bashrc
lessons.summary: Why a new terminal forgets ROS 2, and how `source` and `~/.bashrc` fix it.

blocks.text: Chiku forgets ROS 2 every time you open a new terminal. Let's fix that for good.

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Every terminal has its own small notebook of settings (environment variables). `source` writes ROS 2's settings into it. A new terminal starts with a clean notebook, so `~/.bashrc` re-writes them automatically.
Every terminal keeps a small set of settings called **environment variables**. Programs read them to learn things like your home folder or which ROS 2 version to use.

echo $HOME                # /home/student
echo $ROS_DISTRO          # empty until ROS 2 is loaded
export ROBOT_NAME=chiku   # create a variable in this terminal
echo $ROBOT_NAME          # chiku
printenv | grep ROS       # show only variables containing ROS

A terminal is like a classroom whiteboard. `export` writes something on the board. Opening a **new** terminal is like walking into a new classroom with a clean board: everything written before is gone.
Loading ROS 2 with source

ROS 2 is installed in `/opt/ros/jazzy`, but a new terminal does not know that. The command `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash` writes all the ROS 2 settings on the board. Without it you get `ros2: command not found`.
Making it automatic with ~/.bashrc
`~/.bashrc` is a hidden file that runs **every time** a new terminal opens. Add the source line to it once, and every new terminal loads ROS 2 by itself:
echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc
Use **two** arrows, `>>`, which add a line at the end of the file. A single `>` replaces the whole file and erases your old settings.
