lessons.summary: Install Gazebo, ros2_control, Nav2, SLAM, TurtleBot3 and MoveIt, prepare rosdep and a workspace, and check everything.

blocks.text: Chiku is ready to graduate from the turtle simulator to real robot tools: **Gazebo** to simulate robots, **Nav2** to drive around a map, and **MoveIt** to move robot arms.

items: Install the lab packages for mobile robots and robot arms

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The lab needs a simulator (Gazebo), driving and mapping tools (Nav2, SLAM, TurtleBot3), an arm planner (MoveIt), and two helpers: rosdep (installs dependencies) and colcon (builds your code).

a small, popular teaching robot with ready-made simulations

blocks.text: ROS 2 Jazzy uses the **new Gazebo (Harmonic)**. Old tutorials that mention `gazebo_ros_pkgs`, Gazebo 11 or Gazebo Classic do not work on Jazzy.

blocks.title: Dress rehearsal: set up the lab

blocks.text: Now on your real computer
Run these commands one by one on your Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 Jazzy installed. Together they download a few gigabytes.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y python3-colcon-common-extensions python3-rosdep python3-vcstool
sudo rosdep init
rosdep update
sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-robot-state-publisher ros-jazzy-joint-state-publisher-gui ros-jazzy-xacro ros-jazzy-tf2-tools ros-jazzy-teleop-twist-keyboard 'ros-jazzy-rqt*'
sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-ros-gz
sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-ros2-control ros-jazzy-ros2-controllers ros-jazzy-gz-ros2-control ros-jazzy-gz-ros2-control-demos
sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup 'ros-jazzy-nav2-minimal-tb*' ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox ros-jazzy-robot-localization ros-jazzy-cartographer-ros 'ros-jazzy-turtlebot3*'
sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-moveit ros-jazzy-moveit-resources-panda-moveit-config ros-jazzy-ur-description
Then add your lab settings to `~/.bashrc`, so every new terminal is ready:

echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc
echo "export TURTLEBOT3_MODEL=burger" >> ~/.bashrc
echo "export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7" >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

In the lab, every student uses a **different** `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` (a number from 0 to 101, given by your instructor), so your robot doesn't listen to your neighbour's commands. Real TurtleBot3 robots in the lab are set up by the instructor following the ROBOTIS e-Manual for Jazzy.

lessons.title: Why robots need a software platform
lessons.summary: The problems every robot team faces, and how a software platform like ROS solves them.

blocks.text: Chiku now has a camera, a LiDAR, two motors, a path planner and a small screen. Five programs must talk to each other all the time. Who writes all that connecting code, and what happens when one part changes?

items: Explain why robots need a software platform
Name five things a platform gives you
Recognise a few other robot platforms

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A robot is a team of small programs. A **software platform** gives that team a common language, ready-made parts and tools, so you don't build everything from zero.
A robot is not one program. It is a **team of small programs**: one reads the camera, one drives the motors, one plans the path, one shows a screen. They must swap data many times every second.

blocks.intro: Press the buttons in order: swap the LiDAR, then use a framework, then swap it again.

blocks.text: What a robot software platform gives you

items.m: a standard message (like a laser scan) whatever brand of sensor you buy
a ready-made way for programs to send data to each other, even on different computers
use packages others have written instead of writing everything again
3-D viewers, recorders, graphs and debuggers that work with every robot
thousands of people sharing code, answers and tutorials

blocks.text: Think of **Indian Railways**. Every train runs on the same gauge of track and follows the same rules, and stops at shared stations. A new train does not need new tracks. In a robot, the programs are the trains, ROS's standard messages are the tracks, and topics are the stations.
Other robot software platforms
ROS is the most widely used platform in research and is growing fast in industry, but it is not the only one:

items: **YARP**: from the iCub humanoid research community in Italy.
**OROCOS**: a European toolkit for real-time control of machines and robot arms.
**Player/Stage**: a 2000s classic, a robot device server plus a 2-D simulator.
**Microsoft Robotics Developer Studio**: a Windows-only platform, now discontinued.
**MOOS-IvP**: popular for underwater and marine robots.
**NVIDIA Isaac**: GPU-accelerated simulation and AI tools. Its Isaac ROS packages are built **on top of** ROS 2, not instead of it.

blocks.text: Chiku buys a new camera: with and without a platform

items: **Without a platform:** the old camera sent pictures in its own format. The face-finder, the screen and the recorder all read that format. The new camera uses a different format, so **all three** programs must be rewritten.
**With ROS:** the camera driver turns any camera's pictures into the standard `sensor_msgs/msg/Image` message on a topic like `/camera/image_raw`.
Swap the camera: install the new camera's ROS driver. It publishes the **same** message on the **same** topic.
The face-finder, screen and recorder **don't change at all**. This is hardware abstraction, and it saves weeks of work.
Bonus: someone else probably already wrote that driver. You download it instead of writing it.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A university lab can take the **same** navigation software (Nav2) that companies use on warehouse and hospital robots, and run it on its own robot. Only the drivers at the bottom change. That reuse is only possible because they share a platform.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Calling ROS an operating system like Windows: it is a framework that runs **on** Ubuntu.
Thinking a platform makes the robot smart by itself: it gives structure and parts; you still write the robot's behaviour.
Writing your own messaging code "to keep it simple": it becomes the hardest part to maintain.

pairs.b: GPU simulation and AI, built on ROS 2

blocks.why: Each platform grew up around a different kind of robot. ROS became the common choice because it is free, open and has the biggest set of reusable packages.

blocks.q: Chiku's team writes their own messaging code instead of using a platform. What will hurt most when they buy a new camera next year?
blocks.answer: Every program that used the old camera's data must be rewritten. With a platform, only the camera's **driver** changes, because it still publishes the same standard image message.

blocks.q: Is each item a **problem a platform solves**, or **not a platform's job**?

items.text: Programs need a common way to send data
items.why: Communication is the core of a platform.

items.why: That is a hardware choice, not software.

items.text: Every lab rewrites the same 3-D viewer
items.why: Shared tools like RViz work for every ROS robot.

options: Middleware plus tools and libraries that run on an OS like Ubuntu
An operating system that replaces Ubuntu
blocks.why: Despite the name, ROS runs **on** an operating system. It is a framework: communication, tools and reusable packages.
blocks.hint: Does ROS replace Ubuntu?

blocks.q: A new LiDAR brand still publishes the same standard `LaserScan` message, so the planner code does not change. This benefit is called:
blocks.why: The standard message hides (abstracts) the hardware differences.
blocks.hint: It hides the details of the hardware.

blocks.q: Which benefit lets you replace the LiDAR brand without changing the planner?
blocks.why: The driver hides the brand's details behind a standard message.
blocks.hint: Which word means "hiding the hardware details"?

items.back: common language + parts + tools for robot programs
swap hardware, keep the rest of the code
download working parts instead of writing them
the most widely used robot software framework

items: A robot is a team of small programs that must share data.
A platform gives hardware abstraction, communication, reuse, tools and community.
ROS is a framework that runs on an OS; other platforms include YARP, OROCOS and MOOS.

lessons.title: What ROS was built to do
lessons.summary: The five original objectives of ROS, and the new goals that led to ROS 2.

blocks.text: In 2007, the people who started ROS wrote down what they wanted it to be. Ten years later, robots had changed: fleets, factories, tiny chips, weak Wi-Fi. So they set new goals, and those goals became ROS 2.

items: List the five original objectives of ROS
Name the new goals that ROS 2 was designed for

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS was built to be: programs talking directly (peer-to-peer), lots of tools, many languages, a thin layer around reusable code, and free for everyone. ROS 2 kept these and added: many robots, small chips, real-time, bad networks and factory use.
The five original objectives

items.m: programs talk directly to each other, not through one central program
many small tools (viewer, recorder, command line) instead of one giant program
write nodes in C++, Python and other languages; they can still talk to each other
put your algorithm in a normal library and add a small ROS wrapper, so it can be reused anywhere
anyone can use, study, change and share it

blocks.label: ROS objectives (from the first ROS paper, 2009)

blocks.text: **Peer-to-peer** is like WhatsApp friends messaging each other directly. **Thin** is like a phone charger with a standard plug: the clever electronics live inside, and the plug (the ROS wrapper) is small.
Why a new version was needed
ROS 1 was built around the **PR2**, a single research robot with powerful computers and excellent Wi-Fi in one lab. Real-world robots needed more, so ROS 2 was designed for:

items: **Teams of many robots** working together.
**Small embedded computers**, even microcontrollers.
**Real-time control** (reacting within a guaranteed time).
**Non-ideal networks**: weak Wi-Fi, lost packets, even satellite links.
**Production use** in factories and products, not just labs.
**Prescribed patterns** for building systems, such as managed start-up and shut-down.

blocks.text: A college hostel mess can feed 50 students. To cater weddings, hospitals and airlines, it needs hygiene certificates, punctuality guarantees and delivery to far places. ROS 1 was the mess; ROS 2 is the catering company.
blocks.label: Think of it like this

blocks.text: Each original objective, with a Chiku example

items: **Peer-to-peer:** the camera node sends images straight to the face-finder node; nothing in the middle has to relay them.
**Tools-based:** instead of one huge program, many small tools: `ros2 topic echo` to see data, `rviz2` to see the robot in 3D, `ros2 bag` to record.
**Multi-lingual:** the motor node can be C++ (fast) and the planner can be Python (quick to write). They still talk.
**Thin:** the clever maths lives in normal libraries (like OpenCV); the ROS part is a small wrapper, so the maths can be reused even without ROS.
**Free and open source:** you can download, read, change and share all of it, which is why a whole world community grew around it.

blocks.answer: If your path-planning code is a normal Python or C++ library with a small ROS wrapper, you can test it without ROS, reuse it in another project, and even move it to a different framework later.

lessons.title: The parts of ROS

blocks.text: Chiku's delivery business has staff (nodes), a kitchen speaker (topics), a cash counter (services), delivery tracking (actions) and a notice board of settings (parameters). Let's open ROS and find each one.

items: Name the five ways ROS programs communicate

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS has three groups of parts: **communication** (nodes, topics, services, actions, parameters), **tools** (the ros2 command, rviz2, rqt, bags, launch) and ready-made **capabilities** (tf2, Nav2, MoveIt 2, ros2_control).
Three groups of parts

items.m: nodes, topics, services, actions, parameters
ros2 command line, rviz2, rqt, ros2 bag, launch
ready-made skills: tf2 (coordinate frames), Nav2 (navigation), MoveIt 2 (arms), perception, ros2_control
one running program with one job (the cook, the cashier)
a continuous stream of messages (the kitchen announcement speaker)
one question, one answer ("what is my bill?")
a long job with progress updates that you can cancel (food delivery tracking)
a setting stored in a node (the notice board: "max speed 20 km/h")

lessons.title: The ROS ecosystem
lessons.summary: Packages, distributions, ROS Index, rosdep, REPs, the community and the big projects around ROS.

blocks.text: Chiku needs a navigation system, an arm planner and a simulator. Good news: thousands of people have already built these and shared them. That giant shared world is the ROS ecosystem.

items: Explain packages and distributions
Use the ecosystem tools: ROS Index, rosdep, REPs
Name the organisations and flagship projects

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The ecosystem is everything around ROS: thousands of **packages** shared by people worldwide, bundled into tested **distributions** (like Jazzy), plus tools to find and install them.

items.m: the unit of sharing: a folder with package.xml and code
a tested set of packages released together (Humble, Jazzy, Lyrical…)
index.ros.org, the search engine for ROS packages
installs the system libraries a package needs
ROS Enhancement Proposal: a design or standards document, like a rule book

blocks.text: The ROS ecosystem is like a city's food scene. **Packages** are dishes. A **distribution** is a fixed thali where every dish is tested to taste good together. **ROS Index** is the food app to find dishes, **rosdep** fetches missing ingredients, and **REPs** are the food-safety rule book.
Who looks after ROS?

items: **OSRF (Open Source Robotics Foundation)**, also called **Open Robotics**: the non-profit that has looked after ROS and Gazebo since 2012.
**OSRA (Open Source Robotics Alliance)**: launched by OSRF in March 2024, so companies and the community govern ROS, Gazebo and Open-RMF together.
**ROS-Industrial**: a consortium that brings ROS into factories.
**The community**: ROS Discourse (forum), Robotics Stack Exchange (questions) and **ROSCon**, the yearly conference.

lessons.title: The ROS story: 2007 to 2026
lessons.summary: From a Stanford project and Willow Garage to ROS 2, OSRA, the end of ROS 1 and Lyrical.

blocks.text: Every famous tool has a story. ROS started as a university project, grew in a robotics lab, became a shared public good, and is now governed by an alliance of companies and volunteers.

items: Tell the story of ROS in a few sentences
Put the key events in order

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS began at Stanford, grew up at Willow Garage (2007), was looked after by the Open Source Robotics Foundation from 2012, was rebuilt as ROS 2 (first release 2017), and is now governed by an alliance of companies and volunteers (OSRA, 2024).

blocks.intro: Press Next stop to ride the timeline.

blocks.text: The story in five sentences

items: Mid-2000s: Stanford researchers build reusable robot software (the STAIR and Personal Robotics projects).
2007: the robotics lab **Willow Garage** takes over the project; the first ROS code is written in November 2007.
2010: **ROS 1.0** and the first distribution, **Box Turtle**. PR2 robots go to research groups, who share their code.
2012–2017: **OSRF** is founded to look after ROS. ROS 2 is announced (2014) and the first release, **Ardent**, arrives in December 2017.
2022–2026: Intrinsic buys OSRF's commercial arm (2022), **OSRA** starts (2024), **ROS 1 ends** (May 2025) and **Lyrical** is released (May 2026).

blocks.text: The people and places behind the story

items: **Stanford University, mid-2000s:** students in two projects (the STAIR robot and the Personal Robotics Program) were tired of rewriting the same robot software. They started building reusable pieces.

**Willow Garage (2007–2014):** a robotics research company in California hired that team, built the **PR2** robot, and gave PR2s to universities on the condition that they share their software. That rule made ROS grow fast.
**TurtleBot (2011):** a cheap, simple ROS robot made ROS affordable for students everywhere.
**OSRF / Open Robotics (2012):** a non-profit created to look after ROS and the Gazebo simulator for everyone.
**ROS 2 (2017 onwards):** a rebuild on DDS for many robots, small chips and products. Humble (2022) and Jazzy (2024) are long-term-support releases.
**2022–2026:** Intrinsic (an Alphabet company) takes over Open Robotics' commercial team in 2022; OSRA is launched in 2024; ROS 1 Noetic reaches end of life in May 2025.

pairs.b: the 2007 lab where ROS grew up
the research robot ROS 1 was designed around
the low-cost robot that brought ROS to students
the non-profit that has looked after ROS since 2012
the 2024 alliance that now governs ROS

blocks.answer: Thousands of working robots and packages were written for ROS 1. Moving them takes time and money, and early ROS 2 releases were missing some features. So both lived together for about 8 years.

options: No: it bought OSRF's commercial company; ROS stays open source, looked after by the non-profit OSRF
Yes, ROS is now owned by Google
Yes, and ROS became paid software
No, ROS was sold to NASA

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** Why do you think Willow Garage *gave away* PR2 robots to universities?
blocks.answer: Because every university that used the PR2 had to share its software. More users meant more shared code, which made ROS better for everyone, which attracted even more users. That snowball is why ROS became the standard.

Because the founder's surname was Turtle

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Every May a new ROS 2 version comes out, named after a turtle, in alphabetical order. Versions from even years are supported for 5 years (LTS). Pick the LTS that matches your Ubuntu.

items.m: a named release of ROS, e.g. Jazzy Jalisco

Each release targets **one Ubuntu LTS**: Humble = 22.04, Jazzy and Kilted = 24.04, Lyrical = 26.04.

items: **Which Ubuntu do I have (or can I install)?** Ubuntu 24.04 → Jazzy (or Kilted). Ubuntu 22.04 → Humble.
**Do I need it for years?** Choose an **LTS** (even year): Humble (to 2027), Jazzy (to 2029), Lyrical (to 2031).
**Do the packages I need support it?** Check index.ros.org for Nav2, MoveIt, your robot's drivers.
**Is my course or lab using one?** Use the same as your team. In this course: **Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04**.

lessons.title: ROS 1 vs ROS 2
lessons.summary: No master, DDS, colcon, Python 3, QoS, security, real-time and more: what changed and why.

blocks.text: You will still meet ROS 1 code in old projects and online answers. Knowing the differences saves hours: you'll spot a ROS 1 tutorial in seconds.

items: Explain why ROS 2 has no master
Name the main differences between ROS 1 and ROS 2
Recognise ROS 1 commands in old tutorials

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS 2 removed the central "master", switched to the industry standard DDS for communication, and added QoS, security, real-time support and Windows/macOS. Commands start with `ros2` instead of `ros...`.

blocks.intro: Compare: press ROS 1 first, then Stop roscore, then ROS 2.

blocks.text: ROS 1 was like a school where every new student must ask the **principal's office** (the master) to find a classroom. If the principal is absent, nobody can find anyone. ROS 2 is like a **WhatsApp group**: everyone joins and finds each other directly.
The big differences

blocks.q: Match each ROS 1 thing with its ROS 2 replacement.

pairs.b: launch files in Python, XML or YAML

blocks.why: If a tutorial uses roscore, catkin_make or rospy, it is ROS 1.

items: **Communication:** ROS 1 had its own TCPROS protocol. ROS 2 uses the industry-standard **DDS**, with **Quality of Service** settings.
**More features:** many nodes in one process (composition), managed lifecycle nodes, **SROS2 security** (encryption and access control), real-time-friendly design.
**More platforms:** Ubuntu and Windows are fully supported; micro-ROS runs on microcontrollers.
**Python 3 only**, modern C++.
**Status:** ROS 1 ended in May 2025; ROS 2 is where all new work happens.

blocks.q: In ROS 1, did topic data travel through the master?
blocks.answer: **No.** The master was only a phone book: it told nodes where to find each other. The data then went directly between nodes. ROS 2 removes even the phone book.

blocks.q: Translate each old ROS 1 command into ROS 2.
blocks.why: If you see `rosrun`, `roslaunch`, `rostopic`, `catkin` or `rospy`, the tutorial is ROS 1.
blocks.hint: Most ROS 2 commands just add a space: ros2 run, ros2 topic...

blocks.q: A classmate found this online and it fails on Jazzy. Tap the line that shows it is a **ROS 1** program.
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

pub = rospy.Publisher('chatter', String, queue_size=10)
rospy.init_node('talker')
blocks.why: `import rospy` is the ROS 1 Python library. ROS 2 uses `import rclpy`, and nodes are written as classes.
blocks.hint: Which library does ROS 2 use in Python?

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Running `roscore` in ROS 2: there is no master any more.
Using `catkin_make`: ROS 2 builds with `colcon build`.
Copying ROS 1 launch files (`.launch` XML with `<launch>` and `type=`) without converting them.

blocks.q: ROS 1 or ROS 2?
What happened in ROS 1 when roscore stopped?
options: New nodes could no longer find each other
blocks.why: The master was a single point of failure. ROS 2 removed it.
blocks.hint: Phone book gone.

blocks.q: Which build tool does ROS 2 use?
blocks.why: colcon builds ament packages.
blocks.hint: You used it on Day 10.

blocks.title: Practice: spot ROS 1 commands

tasks.do: Try the old ROS 1 way: `roscore`. Read the error.
Try `rosrun turtlesim turtlesim_node`. Also gone.
Now the ROS 2 way: load ROS 2, then `ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node`. No master needed!

options: It is a ROS 1 tutorial; ROS 2 has no roscore
blocks.why: Only ROS 1 needed a master started with roscore.
blocks.hint: Is there a master in ROS 2?

items: ROS 2 has no master: DDS discovers nodes automatically.
colcon instead of catkin, rclpy instead of rospy, parameters per node, actions built in.
New: QoS, security, real-time support, Windows, micro-ROS. ROS 1 ended in May 2025.

lessons.title: Middleware: the robot's postal service
lessons.summary: What middleware is, publish/subscribe vs request/response, and the rclpy → rcl → rmw → DDS layers.

blocks.text: Chiku's camera node is on one computer and the viewer on another. Neither knows anything about networks, IP addresses or packets. Something in the middle carries the messages. That something is middleware.

items: Explain what middleware does
Tell publish/subscribe from request/response
Draw the ROS 2 layer stack
Switch the middleware with one variable

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Middleware is the delivery service between your programs. You give it a message and a topic name; it finds the receivers and carries the message, even to another computer.

Middleware is like **India Post**. You write the address (the topic name) and drop the letter (the message). Trucks, trains and sorting offices are the post office's problem. You could switch to a private courier (another middleware) without changing how you write letters.

items.m: one-to-many, continuous, the sender does not know who listens (like FM radio)
one asks, one answers (like a phone call)
ROS MiddleWare interface: a standard plug between ROS and the middleware below it

blocks.intro: Send a message, then change the middleware and send again.

blocks.text: One message's journey, layer by layer

items: **Your node** calls `self.pub.publish(msg)` with a Twist message.
**rclpy** (or rclcpp) turns that Python call into a call to **rcl**, the common C library under both languages.
**rcl** hands it to **rmw**, the plug that connects to whichever middleware is installed.
**rmw** gives it to **DDS** (Fast DDS by default in Jazzy). DDS turns the message into bytes.
DDS sends the bytes over the **network** (or shared memory on the same computer) to every matching subscriber.
On the other side the same layers run upwards, and the subscriber's callback receives a normal Twist message.

blocks.q: Put the layers in order, from your code (top) to the network (bottom).
items: Your node
rclpy or rclcpp
rcl
rmw
DDS (for example Fast DDS)
Network
blocks.why: Your code → client library → shared C core → the plug → the middleware → the wires.
blocks.hint: rcl is the shared core written in C.

blocks.text: Because of the **rmw** plug, the middleware can be swapped without changing a single line of your code. In Jazzy the default is **eProsima Fast DDS**; **Eclipse Cyclone DDS** and **RTI Connext** are also fully supported, and **Zenoh** (not DDS) can be tried too.

export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp   # needs: sudo apt install ros-jazzy-rmw-cyclonedds-cpp
ros2 doctor --report | grep middleware
Use the **same middleware on every computer** of a robot system. Different DDS vendors can sometimes talk to each other, but it is not guaranteed, and Zenoh never talks to DDS.

blocks.title: Practice: check and switch the middleware

tasks.do: See which middleware is chosen: `echo $RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` (empty means the default, Fast DDS)
Switch to Cyclone DDS: `export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp`
Run a health check: `ros2 doctor`

blocks.q: Which pattern is like FM radio?
blocks.why: A station broadcasts; anyone tuned in hears it; it doesn't know who listens.
blocks.hint: One sender, many listeners.

blocks.q: What do you change to switch the middleware?
blocks.why: Your code stays the same thanks to the rmw plug.
blocks.hint: Nothing in your code.

blocks.q: Two robots in one lab: robot A uses Fast DDS, robot B uses Cyclone DDS. A's topics sometimes don't appear on B. Why, and what is the fix?
blocks.answer: Different DDS vendors are **not guaranteed** to work together perfectly. Set the **same** `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` on every computer of the system (or leave all on the default), then restart the nodes.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Thinking you must write network code in ROS 2: the middleware does it.
Mixing middleware between computers of one robot system.
Confusing rmw (the plug) with DDS (the actual messenger).

items.back: common C library under rclpy and rclcpp

blocks.q: Match each layer with its job.

pairs.b: the Python / C++ door into ROS 2
shared C code under both languages
the plug for the chosen middleware
finds receivers and moves the bytes

blocks.why: From top to bottom, each layer hides the details of the one below.
blocks.hint: Top: your code. Bottom: the network.

items: Middleware carries messages so your code doesn't deal with networks.
Layers: your node → rclpy/rclcpp → rcl → rmw → DDS → network.
Switch with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION; use the same one everywhere. Jazzy's default is Fast DDS.

lessons.title: Why use ROS 2
lessons.summary: Support until 2029, security, real-time, embedded chips, a huge ecosystem and industry backing.

blocks.text: A company asks Chiku's team: "Why should we build our warehouse robot on ROS 2?" Here are the answers, with the reason behind each.

items: Give five solid reasons to use ROS 2
Avoid overclaiming

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Choose ROS 2 because it is supported for years, can be secure, can do real-time control, runs even on tiny chips, has a huge library of ready-made parts, and is used by industry. But be honest about its limits.
Five reasons, explained slowly

items: **Long support.** Jazzy (2024) gets fixes until May 2029. A company can build a product on it and not worry about it disappearing next year.
**Security when you need it.** SROS2 can encrypt messages and control which node may talk on which topic. Important for robots in hospitals, homes and factories.
**Real-time friendly.** With a real-time Linux kernel and careful code, ROS 2 can run motor control loops that must react within a fixed time.
**Tiny chips too.** micro-ROS brings ROS 2 to microcontrollers (like an ESP32 or STM32), so even a small sensor board can publish topics.
**A huge, shared toolbox.** Nav2 for driving, MoveIt 2 for arms, ros2_control for motors, Gazebo for simulation, and thousands of drivers. You build on them instead of from zero.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: ROS 2 is used in university labs, in warehouse and delivery robots, in agriculture, and even in space robotics through the **Space ROS** project. Learning it is learning a skill robot companies hire for.
When ROS 2 might NOT be the right choice

items: A tiny toy with one motor and one sensor: plain Arduino code is simpler.
A hard real-time safety system (for example a car's brakes) that needs certified software: ROS 2 can be part of the system, but the safety layer needs special certified tools.
A team with no Linux experience and a deadline next week: learn the basics first (like you are doing now).

blocks.title: Practice: a quick health check of ROS 2

tasks.do: Load ROS 2.
Run the built-in health check: `ros2 doctor`
Count how many packages are installed: `ros2 pkg list | wc -l`
Check the version: `echo $ROS_DISTRO`

blocks.intro: Before starting any project, engineers check that ROS 2 is healthy.

items.back: LTS releases get 5 years of updates; Jazzy until May 2029
SROS2 adds encryption, authentication and access control (you must switch it on)
designed so real-time control is possible with a real-time OS and careful code
Nav2, MoveIt 2, ros2_control and Gazebo are all ROS 2-first, backed by companies through OSRA

blocks.q: Which ROS 2 feature answers each need?

items.text: "Our hospital robot's data must be encrypted"
"We need updates for the next 4 years"

items.why: Access control is part of SROS2.

blocks.text: Be precise when you talk about ROS 2. Security is **not** on by default, and real-time behaviour needs a real-time OS and careful design: ROS 2 makes them **possible**.

blocks.q: Why is ROS 1 a poor choice for a new project in 2026?
options: It reached end of life in May 2025
blocks.why: No more updates or security fixes.
blocks.hint: Think of the timeline.

blocks.q: A startup builds a hospital delivery robot that must work for 5 years. Which plan is best?
options: ROS 2 Jazzy (LTS), with SROS2 security switched on
blocks.why: An LTS release gives years of fixes, and a hospital robot needs security switched on.
blocks.hint: Think: support length and security.

blocks.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: ROS 2 can be secured with SROS2, but security must be switched on
ROS 2 is secure by default with no setup
ROS 2 only runs on big computers
ROS 2 makes any code real-time automatically
blocks.why: Security and real-time are possible, not automatic.
blocks.hint: Watch out for "automatically" and "by default".

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Saying ROS 2 is "secure by default": SROS2 must be switched on.
Saying ROS 2 is "real-time" by itself: it needs a real-time OS and careful code.
Choosing a short-support release for a long product.

blocks.q: Is ROS 2 a good fit for each project?

items.text: A university robot that uses a lidar, a camera and navigation
items.why: Lots of sensors and ready packages: perfect.

items.text: A blinking LED on an Arduino
items.why: Too small: plain Arduino code is simpler.

items.text: A warehouse robot fleet for 5 years

items.why: Needs certified safety software; ROS 2 can sit above it, not replace it.

items.text: A farm robot with a robot arm

blocks.why: ROS 2 shines when there are many parts to connect; it is overkill for tiny single-purpose gadgets.

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** Give one honest limit of ROS 2 that you would tell a company.
blocks.answer: For example: security (SROS2) must be switched on and set up; real-time needs a real-time OS and careful code; and the team needs Linux skills. Being honest builds trust.

items: ROS 2: long LTS support, security (SROS2), real-time friendly, micro-ROS, huge ecosystem.

lessons.title: DDS: how nodes find each other
lessons.summary: The DDS standard, automatic discovery (SPDP and SEDP), domains and ROS_DOMAIN_ID.

blocks.text: In the lab, 30 students start their robots on the same Wi-Fi. Suddenly a student's arrow keys move someone else's turtle! Today you learn why, and the one-line fix.

items: Explain what DDS is
Describe the two discovery steps
Choose a safe ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Work out a domain's port

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: DDS lets programs find each other automatically: each one announces "I'm here" (SPDP), then they swap the list of topics they read and write (SEDP), and matching ones connect. `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` keeps different groups apart.

**DDS (Data Distribution Service)** is an international standard (from the Object Management Group) for publish/subscribe communication. It is used in aircraft, defence, finance and factories. ROS 2 uses it underneath, so your nodes get a proven, industrial-strength messenger.

items.m: your program's membership card in a domain
what a ROS publisher becomes inside DDS
what a ROS subscription becomes inside DDS
the standard wire protocol DDS sends over the network

blocks.intro: Try: all domains 0, then change Laptop 3 to 5, then try 300.

blocks.text: Discovery in two steps

items: **SPDP (participant discovery):** every program regularly shouts "I am here, domain N" on the network.
**SEDP (endpoint discovery):** programs that heard each other swap details of their writers and readers: topic name, type and QoS. Matching ones connect, and data flows.

blocks.text: A college WhatsApp group: "XYZ joined the group" is step 1. Posts like "I'm selling notes" and "I'm buying notes" are step 2, and matching people then chat directly. The **domain ID** is which group you are in.
Domains and ROS_DOMAIN_ID

items: Programs only see programs in the **same domain**. The default is **0**.
Set it per terminal: `export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7` (add it to `~/.bashrc` to keep it).
Safe values on Linux: **0 to 101** (the maximum is 232).
Port rule of thumb: discovery uses **7400 + 250 × domain ID**. Domain 1 → 7650, domain 2 → 7900.

blocks.q: A lab has 30 students on one Wi-Fi network, all using the default domain. What will happen, and what is the fix?
blocks.answer: All 30 robots are in domain 0, so every node sees every other node, and keys may move other students' turtles. Fix: each bench gets its **own ROS_DOMAIN_ID** between 1 and 101, written in `~/.bashrc`.

tasks.do: Check your domain: `echo $ROS_DOMAIN_ID` (empty means 0)
Move to domain 7: `export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7`
Make it permanent: `echo "export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7" >> ~/.bashrc`
The ros2 command keeps a background helper (the daemon) that remembers old discoveries. Restart it after changing domains: `ros2 daemon stop`

blocks.q: Which discovery port does ROS_DOMAIN_ID=4 use? (7400 + 250 × domain)
Laptop A uses domain 3 and laptop B uses domain 5. Can B's listener hear A's talker?
options: No, different domains never see each other
blocks.why: Same domain = same group.
blocks.hint: Different groups.

blocks.q: Which domain IDs are the safe choice on Linux?
blocks.why: Above 101 can clash with other programs' ports.
blocks.hint: Up to about 100.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Two lab benches on the same domain: their robots hear each other. Give each bench its own `ROS_DOMAIN_ID`.
Changing `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` in only one terminal of a robot system.
Using a domain above 101 on Linux: stick to 0–101.

blocks.q: Match each DDS word with its meaning.

pairs.b: a separate group; only the same domain can talk
one program taking part in DDS
the variable that picks your group

blocks.why: Discovery: announce yourself, swap your topic lists, then talk directly.
blocks.hint: SP = participant, SE = endpoint.

blocks.q: Which discovery port does ROS_DOMAIN_ID=10 use? (7400 + 250 × domain)
blocks.hint: Multiply first: 250 × 10.

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** Your robot and your friend's robot both use domain 0 on the lab Wi-Fi. What will happen, and what is the one-line fix?
blocks.answer: They discover each other, so your keyboard could drive their robot. Fix: give each a different domain, e.g. `export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7` (and add it to `~/.bashrc`).

items: DDS is the industry-standard messenger under ROS 2.
Discovery: SPDP (I'm here) then SEDP (my readers and writers), then data flows.
ROS_DOMAIN_ID separates groups: use 1–101, one per lab bench; port = 7400 + 250 × ID.

lessons.title: Quality of Service (QoS)
lessons.summary: Reliability, durability, history and depth; ROS 2 QoS profiles; and the compatibility rule.

blocks.text: Chiku's camera sends 30 images a second over weak Wi-Fi. Should a lost image be sent again? And when a new screen joins late, should it get the last map? QoS settings decide.

items: Explain the main QoS policies
Pick a QoS profile for a job
Predict whether a publisher and subscriber connect

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: QoS settings decide **how** messages are delivered: try again or not (reliability), keep the last one for latecomers or not (durability), and how many to keep (depth). The publisher must offer at least what the subscriber asks for.

items.m: RELIABLE: resend until delivered. BEST_EFFORT: send once; a lost message is gone
VOLATILE: no old messages for late joiners. TRANSIENT_LOCAL: keep the last messages for late joiners
KEEP_LAST with depth N (a queue of N messages), or KEEP_ALL
advanced timing rules: the maximum gap between messages, how long a message stays valid, how 'alive' is checked

blocks.text: Think of the Mumbai **dabbawalas**. **Reliable**: if a tiffin is missed, they come back for it. **Best effort**: they move on, and tomorrow's tiffin will come anyway. **Transient local**: the tiffin is left with the watchman for the person who arrives late.
Ready-made profiles

items: **Default** (what `10` gives you): RELIABLE, VOLATILE, keep last 10.
**Sensor data**: BEST_EFFORT, VOLATILE, keep last 5. For cameras and LiDAR: fresh data beats complete data.
**Services and parameters**: RELIABLE.

blocks.intro: Try: RELIABLE → RELIABLE, then BEST_EFFORT publisher → RELIABLE subscriber, then the late joiner test.

blocks.text: The compatibility rule

A subscriber **requests** a QoS, a publisher **offers** one. They connect only if **the publisher offers at least what the subscriber requests**. If not, ROS 2 prints an "incompatible QoS" warning and **delivers nothing**, which is one of the most common reasons why nodes don't talk.

blocks.q: Will this publisher → subscriber pair connect?

items.why: Offering more than requested is fine.
The subscriber wants guaranteed delivery that the publisher doesn't offer.
The subscriber wants old messages the publisher doesn't keep.

blocks.title: QoS lab: why is the viewer silent?
blocks.goal: The camera uses BEST_EFFORT, but the viewer asks for RELIABLE (the default `10`). Run it and read the warning. Then make the **viewer** use `qos_profile_sensor_data` so it prints `viewer got frame 1`.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy, qos_profile_sensor_data
from std_msgs.msg import String

rclpy.init()
camera = Node('camera')
viewer = Node('viewer')
pub = camera.create_publisher(String, 'image', QoSProfile(depth=5, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.BEST_EFFORT))
viewer.create_subscription(String, 'image', lambda msg: print('viewer got', msg.data), 10)
pub.publish(String(data='frame 1'))
blocks.retryHint: Change the last argument of create_subscription from 10 to qos_profile_sensor_data.
blocks.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy, qos_profile_sensor_data
from std_msgs.msg import String

rclpy.init()
camera = Node('camera')
viewer = Node('viewer')
pub = camera.create_publisher(String, 'image', QoSProfile(depth=5, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.BEST_EFFORT))
viewer.create_subscription(String, 'image', lambda msg: print('viewer got', msg.data), qos_profile_sensor_data)
pub.publish(String(data='frame 1'))

blocks.title: QoS lab: the late joiner
blocks.goal: The map is published **before** the planner exists. Make **both** sides use `TRANSIENT_LOCAL` durability so the late planner still prints `planner got map v1`.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, DurabilityPolicy
from std_msgs.msg import String

rclpy.init()
qos = QoSProfile(depth=1, durability=DurabilityPolicy.VOLATILE)
map_server = Node('map_server')
pub = map_server.create_publisher(String, 'map', qos)
pub.publish(String(data='map v1'))

planner = Node('planner')   # starts later
planner.create_subscription(String, 'map', lambda m: print('planner got', m.data), qos)
rclpy.spin_once(planner)
blocks.retryHint: Change DurabilityPolicy.VOLATILE to DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL in the qos line.
blocks.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, DurabilityPolicy
from std_msgs.msg import String

rclpy.init()
qos = QoSProfile(depth=1, durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL)
map_server = Node('map_server')
pub = map_server.create_publisher(String, 'map', qos)
pub.publish(String(data='map v1'))

planner = Node('planner')   # starts later
planner.create_subscription(String, 'map', lambda m: print('planner got', m.data), qos)
rclpy.spin_once(planner)

Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: A RELIABLE subscriber on a BEST_EFFORT camera topic: nothing arrives. Use the sensor-data profile on the subscriber.
Expecting a late subscriber to get old messages with VOLATILE durability.

keep the last message for latecomers
keep the last 10 in the queue

items: QoS policies: reliability, durability, history/depth (+ deadline, lifespan, liveliness).

modules.description: The core ideas of ROS 2, hands-on in a practice terminal: nodes, topics, messages, services, parameters, actions, launch files, packages, TF2 and debugging tools. Ends with a mini-project.

lessons.title: What ROS 2 really is
lessons.summary: The big picture: why robots are built from many small programs, and where ROS 2 sits.

blocks.text: Chiku can already run Python and C++ programs. But a real delivery robot has to read its lidar, plan a route, drive its wheels, watch its battery and talk to people, **all at the same time**. Today you see how ROS 2 organises all of that.

items: Explain what ROS 2 is (and what it is not)
Name the parts of the ROS 2 graph: nodes, topics, services, actions, parameters
Say why robots are built from many small programs

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS 2 is a set of tools that lets many small programs (**nodes**) work together as one robot. They talk on **topics** (streams), **services** (questions) and **actions** (long jobs), and are tuned with **parameters**.

**ROS 2** (Robot Operating System 2) is a free set of **libraries and tools** for building robot software. Despite the name, it is **not** an operating system: it runs on top of Ubuntu, like any other program. Its job is to let many small programs work together as one robot.

blocks.intro: Build Chiku's software stack from the ground up. Read the caption after each layer.

blocks.text: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen. One cook makes rotis, one makes curry, one washes plates, and a manager calls out orders. No single person does everything; they **shout short messages** to each other. A robot built with ROS 2 works the same way: each small program does one job and they pass messages.
The ROS 2 graph
All the programs of a robot, and the connections between them, form the **ROS 2 graph**. You will meet every part of it this week:

items.m: one small program with one job, such as the lidar driver or the obstacle stopper
a named channel for a **stream** of messages, like `/scan`. Many can listen.
a question with exactly one answer, like "spawn a turtle" or "add these two numbers"
a long job with feedback and a final result, like "drive to the kitchen". It can be cancelled.
a named setting of a node, like `max_speed`, that you can change while it runs

blocks.q: Why not write Chiku's whole brain as **one giant program**? Think of two reasons before you look.
blocks.answer: 1. **Crashes stay small**: if the camera program crashes, the wheels and the safety stop keep working. 2. **Reuse and teamwork**: one student can write the lidar node while another writes the planner, and you can download ready-made nodes (Nav2, SLAM, MoveIt) instead of writing them. Bonus: the nodes can even run on **different computers** and still talk.

blocks.text: Chiku's graph, one node at a time

items: The **lidar node** reads the laser sensor and publishes distances on the topic `/scan`, 10 times a second.
The **obstacle node** subscribes to `/scan`. If something is closer than its `stop_distance` parameter, it publishes "stop" on `/cmd_vel`.
The **motor node** subscribes to `/cmd_vel` and turns the wheels.
The **map node** offers a service `/save_map`: ask once, the map is saved, it replies "done".
The **navigator node** offers an action `/navigate_to_pose`: "go to the library", with progress updates on the way.
Together these nodes and connections are the **ROS 2 graph**. Tools like `rqt_graph` draw it for you.

items: Thinking ROS 2 replaces Ubuntu: it runs on top of it.

blocks.hint: Nodes are separate programs.

goal, feedback, result; can be cancelled

lessons.title: Nodes: the robot's team members
lessons.summary: Start nodes with `ros2 run`, list them, inspect them with `ros2 node info`, and rename one.

blocks.text: Before Chiku drives in the real world, engineers practise with **turtlesim**: a tiny simulator where a turtle plays the robot. It is made of real ROS 2 nodes, so every command you learn here works on any robot.

items: Start a node with `ros2 run <package> <executable>`
See running nodes with `ros2 node list`
Read `ros2 node info` and rename a node with `--ros-args --remap`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `ros2 run <package> <program>` starts a node. `ros2 node list` shows who is running, and `ros2 node info` shows everything one node publishes, listens to and offers.
Programs in ROS 2 come in **packages** (folders of related programs). To start one, you name the package and the program inside it:

ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node      # package turtlesim, program turtlesim_node
ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key   # drive it with the arrow keys

On a real computer each `ros2 run` keeps its terminal busy, so you open **one terminal per node** (and source ROS 2 in each). The practice terminal below works the same way: a started node keeps its terminal busy until **Ctrl+C**, so press **+ New terminal** (or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**) to type more commands.

blocks.title: Practice: start and inspect nodes
blocks.intro: This terminal pretends to be Ubuntu with ROS 2 Jazzy installed. Nothing is running yet.

tasks.do: Load ROS 2 into this terminal: `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash`
Start the turtle simulator: `ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node`

Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**, then load ROS 2 with `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash`). Then: start the keyboard driver: `ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key`
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal, source ROS 2, then: Type: ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key

tasks.do: Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**, then load ROS 2 with `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash`). Then: list the running nodes: `ros2 node list`
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal, source ROS 2, then: Type: ros2 node list

tasks.do: Look inside the simulator node: `ros2 node info /turtlesim`
tasks.hint: Type: ros2 node info /turtlesim  (with the / in front)

tasks.do: Start a **second** simulator with a new name: `ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node --ros-args --remap __node:=my_turtle`
Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**, then load ROS 2 with `source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash`). Then: list the nodes again. You should see three.
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal, source ROS 2, then: Type: ros2 node list

blocks.text: Reading `ros2 node info`

`ros2 node info` is a node's **ID card**: every topic it listens to (Subscribers) and talks on (Publishers), every service it offers (Service Servers) and every action it can do (Action Servers). You do not need to understand every line yet; look for the **turtle1** lines.
Why rename a node or give it a namespace?

items: Two programs with the **same node name** confuse ROS 2: logs mix and tools can't tell them apart.
`--ros-args --remap __node:=my_turtle` changes only the **name** of the node.
`--ros-args --remap __ns:=/robot2` puts the node, **and all its topics**, inside a folder-like **namespace**: `/robot2/turtle1/cmd_vel`.
Namespaces let you run two identical robots side by side without their topics mixing.
No code changes: the same program, started with different arguments.

blocks.title: Practice: two robots side by side

tasks.hint: Copy it exactly: __ns has two underscores

tasks.do: Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**). Then: list the nodes: `ros2 node list`
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal then: Type: ros2 node list

tasks.do: List the topics. Notice the two different cmd_vel topics.
Look inside the keyboard node: `ros2 node info /teleop_turtle`
Which programs does the turtlesim package contain? `ros2 pkg executables turtlesim`

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting `--ros-args` before `--remap`.
One underscore in `__node` or `__ns`: you need two.
Forgetting the `/` at the start of node names: `ros2 node info /turtlesim`.
Mixing up package and program: `ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node`, package first.

blocks.q: Match each section of `ros2 node info /turtlesim` with what it tells you.

pairs.b: the turtle **listens** for speed commands here
the turtle **tells everyone** where it is
you can **ask** it to create a new turtle
you can give it a **long job**: turn to an angle

blocks.why: A node's info lists its whole public face: what it hears, says, answers and does.
blocks.hint: Subscribers listen, publishers talk, service servers answer, action servers do long jobs.

blocks.q: In `ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key`, what is `turtlesim`?
blocks.why: The pattern is `ros2 run <package> <executable>`.
blocks.hint: ros2 run, then the package, then the program.

blocks.q: Two nodes have the same name. What should you do?
blocks.why: Node names should be unique; duplicates confuse tools and logs. Remapping changes the name without touching the code.
blocks.hint: You did it in the practice terminal.

blocks.q: Type the command that lists all running nodes.
blocks.why: `ros2 node list` prints one node name per line.
blocks.hint: ros2, then node, then list.

items: `ros2 run <package> <executable>` starts a node.
`ros2 node list` shows running nodes; `ros2 node info /name` shows what a node publishes, subscribes, serves and does.
`--ros-args --remap __node:=new_name` renames a node without changing its code.

lessons.title: Topics: publish and subscribe
lessons.summary: How nodes stream data on topics, and how to spy on them with `ros2 topic`.

blocks.text: Chiku's lidar measures distances 10 times every second. Three different nodes need that data. How does the lidar send it to all of them without knowing who they are?

items: Explain publish and subscribe
Use `ros2 topic list`, `info`, `echo` and `hz`
Spot the most common topic bug: a wrong name

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A topic is a named radio channel. Publishers broadcast on it, every subscriber tuned to exactly that name hears every message, and nobody needs to know who else is there.

A topic is like an FM radio station. The station (**publisher**) broadcasts on one frequency, say 91.1. Anyone who tunes to exactly 91.1 (**subscriber**) hears every song. The station never knows how many radios are listening, and a radio tuned to 91.2 hears nothing.

blocks.intro: Press the buttons in order. Watch where each message goes, then try the typo button.

items.m: the part of a node that **sends** messages on a topic
the part of a node that **receives** every message on a topic and runs a callback
the shape of each message, for example `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist`. Publisher and subscriber must use the same type.

blocks.text: Topics are **many-to-many**: a topic can have several publishers and several subscribers. Nodes find each other automatically by the topic **name** and **type**. No node needs to know the others exist.

blocks.title: Practice: spy on turtlesim's topics
blocks.intro: turtlesim and the keyboard driver are already running in other (pretend) terminals, and ROS 2 is loaded.

tasks.do: List all topics: `ros2 topic list`
Show their message types too: `ros2 topic list -t`
Who uses the speed topic? `ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel`
Read one message of the turtle's position: `ros2 topic echo --once /turtle1/pose`
How often is the position published? `ros2 topic hz /turtle1/pose`
Now make a typo on purpose: `ros2 topic echo /turtle1/Pose` (capital P). What happens?
tasks.hint: Type it with a capital P: /turtle1/Pose

blocks.text: A wrong topic name gives **no error**: your subscriber simply hears nothing. When data does not arrive, always check the name with `ros2 topic list` first. Names are case-sensitive, and `/scan` and `scan` can differ inside namespaces.

blocks.q: The obstacle stopper never receives laser data, although `/scan` is busy. Tap the line with the bug.
blocks.why: The topic is `/scan` with a small s. `/Scan` is a different (empty) topic, so the callback never runs.
blocks.hint: Compare the topic name with the one the lidar uses.

blocks.q: Two nodes publish on the same topic `/cmd_vel`: the keyboard driver and an autopilot. What does the wheel node receive?
blocks.answer: **Both** streams of messages, mixed together, and it obeys whichever arrived last. The robot jerks between the two commands. That is why real robots use a **multiplexer** node (`twist_mux`) that picks one source by priority.

blocks.q: What does `ros2 topic echo /turtle1/pose` do?
options: Prints every message published on that topic
blocks.why: `echo` subscribes and prints what arrives. It is the quickest way to check that data is flowing.
blocks.hint: echo repeats what it hears.

blocks.q: A lidar publishes on `/scan`. Three nodes subscribe to `/scan`. How many copies of each message are delivered?
options: 1, only the first subscriber gets it
0, the lidar must name each receiver
It depends on the order they started
blocks.why: Every subscriber of the topic gets its own copy.
blocks.hint: Remember the radio: everyone tuned in hears the song.

blocks.q: Type the command that shows the **message type** and the number of publishers and subscribers of `/scan`.
blocks.why: `ros2 topic info` shows the type and how many publishers and subscribers the topic has.
blocks.hint: ros2 topic ____ /scan

blocks.intro: Tune each robot part to the right topic.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: A typo in the topic name: no error, just silence. Check with `ros2 topic list`.
Two publishers on one command topic: the robot obeys whichever came last.
Forgetting the `/` or adding an extra one: `/scan` and `scan` can differ inside namespaces.

items.back: receives every message on a topic

items: A topic is a named stream. **Publishers** send, **subscribers** receive, and they never need to know each other.
Every subscriber gets every message; topics are many-to-many.
`ros2 topic list / info / echo / hz` let you inspect topics. A wrong name fails silently.

lessons.title: Messages: what travels on a topic
lessons.summary: Read message types with `ros2 interface show`, then drive the turtle with `ros2 topic pub`.

blocks.text: To make Chiku drive, some node must send it a speed command. But in what format? "Go a bit faster" is not something a motor driver understands. ROS 2 messages have a **fixed shape**, so every node agrees on what the numbers mean.

items: Read a message definition with `ros2 interface show`
Understand `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist` (linear and angular speed)
Publish a message from the terminal with `ros2 topic pub`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Every topic carries one **message type**: a form with named boxes. `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist` has `linear` speed and `angular` turning speed. You can send one by hand with `ros2 topic pub`.
A **message type** is like a form with named boxes. `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist` is the standard speed command for mobile robots. It has two groups of three numbers:

$ ros2 interface show geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
Vector3  linear      # speed along x (forward), y (sideways), z (up), in m/s
	float64 x
	float64 y
	float64 z
Vector3  angular     # turn speed around x, y, z, in rad/s
	float64 x
	float64 y
	float64 z
A wheeled robot on the floor only needs two boxes: `linear.x` (how fast forward) and `angular.z` (how fast to turn left; negative turns right). Like driving a scooter: throttle and handlebar.

blocks.intro: Move the sliders and predict the path before you press Publish.

items.m: package `geometry_msgs`, a **msg** (message) called `Twist`
package `turtlesim`, a **srv** (service) called `Spawn`
package `turtlesim`, an **action** called `RotateAbsolute`

blocks.text: Without `--once`, `ros2 topic pub` keeps publishing once per second until you press Ctrl+C. Add `--rate 10` to publish 10 times per second.
Planning a square, before typing anything

items: A Twist with `linear.x = 2.0` (and nothing else) drives the turtle **2 metres straight** in about one second.
A Twist with only `angular.z = 1.57` turns it **left by about 90 degrees** (1.57 radians is a quarter turn).
A square is: forward, turn, forward, turn, forward, turn, forward.
We use `--once` so each command sends exactly **one** message.
First we change the pen colour with a **service**, so the square shows up in red.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Missing quotes around the `{...}` values: the shell splits them up. Always wrap them in double quotes.
Writing `z: 90`: turning uses **radians**; a quarter turn is about 1.57.
Forgetting `--once`: the command keeps publishing every second.
Using the wrong type name: it is `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist`.

blocks.q: Match each Twist message with what the robot does.

pairs.b: drives forward in a left curve

blocks.why: `linear.x` is forward speed (negative = backwards) and `angular.z` is turning speed (positive = left, negative = right).
blocks.hint: Positive angular.z turns left.

blocks.q: In `geometry_msgs/msg/Twist`, which field makes a ground robot **turn**?
blocks.why: A ground robot turns around the vertical z axis.
blocks.hint: Turning is angular; the floor robot turns around the up axis.

blocks.q: Type the command that prints the fields of the message type `turtlesim/msg/Pose`.
blocks.why: `ros2 interface show` prints any message, service or action definition.
blocks.hint: ros2 interface ____ turtlesim/msg/Pose

items: Every topic carries one **message type**: a fixed set of named fields.
`Twist` = `linear` (m/s) + `angular` (rad/s); a ground robot uses `linear.x` and `angular.z`.
`ros2 interface show` reads a type; `ros2 topic pub` sends a message by hand.

lessons.title: Write a publisher and a subscriber
lessons.summary: Write Python nodes that publish speed commands and react to incoming messages.

blocks.text: Typing commands by hand is fine for testing, but Chiku must drive by itself. Time to write nodes that publish and subscribe in Python.

items: Create a publisher and publish from a timer callback
Create a subscriber whose callback runs for every message
Find the classic publisher and subscriber mistakes

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A publisher fills a message and calls `publish()`, usually inside a timer callback. A subscriber gives ROS 2 a callback that runs once for every message that arrives.

A publisher node has three parts you already know from Week 2: `create_publisher` (an object inside the node), `create_timer` (a callback every N seconds) and the callback that **fills a message and publishes it**. Step through it and watch the memory.

blocks.title: A driver node, one timer tick at a time

steps.note: `Driver()` runs `__init__`. First, `super().__init__('driver')` sets up the node and names it **driver**.
A **publisher** object is created and stored in `self.pub`: type `Twist`, topic `/turtle1/cmd_vel`, queue size 10.
A timer will call `self.drive` every 0.5 s. Nothing is published yet! `__init__` is finished; `rclpy.spin` now waits.
0.5 s later, spin calls `drive()`. A new, empty Twist message is made: all fields start at 0.0.
Fill the forward speed.
Fill the turn speed.
**Publish.** Every subscriber of `/turtle1/cmd_vel` (the turtle) gets a copy. `drive()` ends; 0.5 s later it runs again.

blocks.title: Drive the turtle in a circle (practice simulator, 3 seconds)
blocks.goal: Change `angular.z` so the turtle turns while it drives (any value that is not 0). The output must show a **non-zero** `angular.z`, and the pretend turtle reports where it ended up.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class Driver(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('driver')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.drive)

    def drive(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 1.0
        msg.angular.z = 0.0   # change me
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        self.get_logger().info(f'linear.x={msg.linear.x} angular.z={msg.angular.z}')


rclpy.init()
node = Driver()
rclpy.spin(node)
node.destroy_node()
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: Change msg.angular.z = 0.0 to, for example, msg.angular.z = 1.0. Keep the line that publishes.

blocks.text: Subscribing
A subscriber needs a callback with **one parameter**, the message. ROS 2 calls it automatically for every message that arrives, so you never call it yourself:

self.sub = self.create_subscription(Float64, '/battery', self.on_battery, 10)
#                                    type     topic       callback       queue

def on_battery(self, msg):
    self.get_logger().info(f'Battery: {msg.data}')

blocks.title: A battery monitor (practice simulator, 3 seconds)
blocks.goal: Finish `Monitor`: (1) subscribe to `/battery`, (2) in `on_battery`, log a warning `Low battery: ...` when `msg.data` is below `20.0`. The output should contain `Low battery: 18.0`.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Float64


class Battery(Node):          # pretend battery: publishes a falling level
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery')
        self.level = 30.0
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Float64, '/battery', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)

    def tick(self):
        self.level -= 3.0
        self.pub.publish(Float64(data=self.level))


class Monitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('monitor')
        # 1. subscribe to '/battery' (type Float64) with self.on_battery

    def on_battery(self, msg):
        # 2. if msg.data is below 20.0, log a warning: Low battery: <level>
        pass


rclpy.init()
monitor = Monitor()
battery = Battery()
rclpy.spin(battery)
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: In __init__: self.sub = self.create_subscription(Float64, '/battery', self.on_battery, 10). In on_battery: if msg.data < 20.0: self.get_logger().warn(f'Low battery: {msg.data}')
blocks.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Float64


class Battery(Node):          # pretend battery: publishes a falling level
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery')
        self.level = 30.0
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Float64, '/battery', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)

    def tick(self):
        self.level -= 3.0
        self.pub.publish(Float64(data=self.level))


class Monitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('monitor')
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Float64, '/battery', self.on_battery, 10)

    def on_battery(self, msg):
        if msg.data < 20.0:
            self.get_logger().warn(f'Low battery: {msg.data}')


rclpy.init()
monitor = Monitor()
battery = Battery()
rclpy.spin(battery)
rclpy.shutdown()

items: Calling the subscriber callback yourself: ROS 2 calls it.
Forgetting to fill a field: new messages start with zeros.
Using different topic names or types on the two sides.

blocks.title: Practice: count what you hear
blocks.goal: Make the listener count messages. In `on_msg`, add 1 to `self.count` and log `got 1`, `got 2`... In 3 seconds (talker every 0.5 s) the output must contain `got 6`.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String

class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, 'chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)

    def tick(self):
        self.pub.publish(String(data='hello'))

class Counter(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('counter')
        self.count = 0
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(String, 'chatter', self.on_msg, 10)

    def on_msg(self, msg):
        pass   # add 1 to self.count, then log f'got {self.count}'

rclpy.init()
counter = Counter()
talker = Talker()
rclpy.spin(talker)
rclpy.shutdown()

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String

class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, 'chatter', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.tick)

    def tick(self):
        self.pub.publish(String(data='hello'))

class Counter(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('counter')
        self.count = 0
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(String, 'chatter', self.on_msg, 10)

    def on_msg(self, msg):
        self.count += 1
        self.get_logger().info(f'got {self.count}')

rclpy.init()
counter = Counter()
talker = Talker()
rclpy.spin(talker)
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: self.count += 1  then  self.get_logger().info(f'got {self.count}')

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** Why do we store the count in `self.count` and not in a normal variable inside `on_msg`?
blocks.answer: A normal variable inside `on_msg` is created fresh every time the callback runs, so it would always restart at 0. `self.count` lives inside the node object and remembers its value between messages.

items: Publisher: `create_publisher(Type, 'topic', 10)`, then fill a message and `publish()` it, usually from a timer callback.
Subscriber: `create_subscription(Type, 'topic', self.callback, 10)`; the callback gets each message.
Pass callbacks **without brackets**, and call `super().__init__` first.

lessons.title: Services: ask a question, get an answer
lessons.summary: Call services from the terminal, then write a service server and client in Python.

blocks.text: Chiku needs a second robot friend in the simulator. It does not need a stream of data for that: it needs to **ask once** ("please create a turtle at 2, 2") and get **one answer** ("done, it is called turtle2").

items: Explain request and response, and when to use a service instead of a topic
Use `ros2 service list`, `type` and `call`
Write a service server callback in Python

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A service is one question and one answer. The client asks and waits; the server's callback fills the response and returns it.
A service is like ordering at a shop counter: you ask for one thing, you **wait** at the counter, and you get one answer. A topic is the shop's radio playing all day, whether anyone asked or not.

blocks.text: A service type has two parts separated by `---`: the **request** (what you send) and the **response** (what comes back):

$ ros2 interface show turtlesim/srv/Spawn
float32 x
float32 y
float32 theta
string name # Optional.  A unique name will be created and returned if this is empty
---
string name

blocks.text: Writing a service server
The server's callback receives the **request** and an empty **response**. It fills the response and must **return** it. The client sends a request with `call_async()` and waits for the result.

blocks.title: An adding service and its client
blocks.goal: Complete `add`: set `response.sum` to `request.a + request.b` and log it. The output should contain `Answer: 5`.
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts


class Adder(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('adder')
        self.srv = self.create_service(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints', self.add)

    def add(self, request, response):
        # fill response.sum, log it, and return the response
        return response


rclpy.init()
server = Adder()

# A client (normally in another node or program)
client = server.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints')
client.wait_for_service()
request = AddTwoInts.Request(a=2, b=3)
future = client.call_async(request)
rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(server, future)
print('Answer:', future.result().sum)
rclpy.shutdown()
blocks.retryHint: Add: response.sum = request.a + request.b  (before return response)
blocks.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts


class Adder(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('adder')
        self.srv = self.create_service(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints', self.add)

    def add(self, request, response):
        response.sum = request.a + request.b
        self.get_logger().info(f'{request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}')
        return response


rclpy.init()
server = Adder()

# A client (normally in another node or program)
client = server.create_client(AddTwoInts, 'add_two_ints')
client.wait_for_service()
request = AddTwoInts.Request(a=2, b=3)
future = client.call_async(request)
rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(server, future)
print('Answer:', future.result().sum)
rclpy.shutdown()

blocks.q: You call a service, but no node offers it. What happens?
options: The client waits ("waiting for service to become available...")

Using a service for a stream of data: use a topic.
Calling a service that nobody offers: the client waits for ever. Check with `ros2 service list`.
A service is **one request, one response**; the client waits for the answer.
Service types have a request part and a response part, separated by `---`.

lessons.title: Actions: long jobs with feedback
lessons.summary: Send goals, watch feedback and get results with `ros2 action`, and choose between topics, services and actions.

blocks.text: "Chiku, deliver this file to the HOD's office." That takes two minutes. With a service, Chiku's brain would freeze for two minutes, with no news and no way to say "stop, wrong office!". Actions fix this.

items: Explain goal, feedback, result and cancel
Use `ros2 action list`, `info` and `send_goal`
Choose correctly between topics, services and actions

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: An action is a long job: you send a **goal**, receive **feedback** while it works, then get one **result**. You can cancel it half-way.

An action is like ordering food on a delivery app. You place the order (**goal**), the app keeps you updated: preparing, picked up, 2 km away (**feedback**), then "delivered" (**result**). You can **cancel** while it is on the way.

blocks.intro: Send the goal and watch all three parts. Then try cancelling halfway.

blocks.text: An action type has **three** parts separated by `---`: goal, result, feedback.

$ ros2 interface show turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute
# The desired heading in radians
float32 theta
---
# The angular displacement in radians to the starting position
float32 delta
---
# The remaining rotation in radians
float32 remaining

blocks.text: What happens when you send a rotate goal

items: The client sends the **goal**: "face 3.14 radians" (turn around).
The server **accepts** it and gives it an ID number.
While the turtle turns, the server sends **feedback**: how much is still left to turn.
When it faces the right way, the server sends the **result** (how far it turned) and the status **SUCCEEDED**.
If you cancel before that, the status is **CANCELED** instead.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Using a service for a job that takes many seconds: the caller waits blind and can't cancel.
Forgetting the action type after the name.
Expecting feedback without `--feedback` on the command line.

blocks.q: Topic, service or action? Sort Chiku's jobs.

items.why: Takes time, needs progress updates and must be cancellable: action.
A quick question with one answer: service.

items.text: "move the arm to pick the parcel"
items.why: Long, with feedback: action (MoveIt uses actions).

blocks.why: Stream: topic. Quick question: service. Long job with progress and cancel: action.
blocks.hint: How long does it take? Does it keep coming? Do you need progress?

blocks.q: What can an action client do that a service client cannot?
options: Get feedback while waiting, and cancel the job
blocks.why: Both send a request and get a result, but only actions stream feedback and can be cancelled.
blocks.hint: Think of the delivery app.

blocks.q: In the action type, which part is sent **many times** while the job runs?
blocks.why: One goal, many feedback messages, one result.
blocks.hint: The "2 km away" updates.

blocks.intro: Ten more robot situations. Pick the right way to talk.

items: An action = **goal**, then **feedback** while it runs, then one **result**; it can be **cancelled**.
`ros2 action list / info / send_goal [--feedback]`.
Topic for streams, service for quick questions, action for long jobs.

lessons.title: Launch files: start everything at once
lessons.summary: Start many nodes, with their settings, from one command with `ros2 launch`.

blocks.text: Chiku now has a lidar node, a motor node, an obstacle stopper and a battery monitor. Opening four terminals and typing four commands every morning is slow and error-prone. Launch files start the whole robot with **one command**.

items: Explain what a launch file does
Read a Python launch file
Start one with `ros2 launch <package> <file>`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A launch file is a recipe that starts many nodes at once, each with its name, namespace and settings. One command (`ros2 launch`) starts them all; one Ctrl+C stops them all.

blocks.intro: Compare the two ways of starting Chiku.

blocks.text: In ROS 2, launch files are usually **Python** files ending in `.launch.py`. They contain one function, `generate_launch_description()`, which returns a list of nodes to start. This is the real `multisim.launch.py` idea from the official tutorial, with one parameter added:

items: `package` and `executable`: the same two words you give `ros2 run`.
`namespace`: puts each simulator's topics under its own prefix, so `/turtlesim1/turtle1/cmd_vel` and `/turtlesim2/turtle1/cmd_vel` do not mix.
`name`: the node's name (like `--remap __node:=`).
`parameters=[{...}]`: start-up settings (like `-p`).

blocks.title: Practice: launch two simulators
blocks.intro: Nothing is running yet. ROS 2 is loaded.

tasks.do: Launch: `ros2 launch turtlesim multisim.launch.py`
Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**). Then: see both nodes: `ros2 node list`
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal then: Type: ros2 node list

tasks.do: See the namespaced topics: `ros2 topic list`
Drive only the first turtle: publish a Twist to `/turtlesim1/turtle1/cmd_vel` (with `--once`).

blocks.q: Match each launch-file line with the terminal command it replaces.
blocks.why: Every option you could type after `ros2 run` has a matching field in a launch file.
blocks.hint: Look for the same words: package, namespace, name, parameter.

blocks.q: Your robot needs 6 nodes. Each needs 2 settings. How many things must you type correctly every morning **without** a launch file, and how many **with** one?
blocks.answer: Without: 6 terminals, 6 `ros2 run` lines and 12 settings, typed every day (one typo and the robot misbehaves). With: **one** line, `ros2 launch my_robot bringup.launch.py`. The launch file remembers everything for you.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Running `ros2 launch` on a file that was never installed: build and source first.
Two nodes with the same name in one launch file.
Forgetting the commas between `Node(...)` entries in a Python launch file.

blocks.q: Put the lines of a tiny launch file in order.
items: from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch_ros.actions import Node
def generate_launch_description():
return LaunchDescription([
Node(package='demo_nodes_py', executable='talker'),
Node(package='demo_nodes_py', executable='listener'),
blocks.why: Imports first, then the function that returns a LaunchDescription holding the nodes.
blocks.hint: Imports, function, return, nodes, close the list.

blocks.q: Why do the two simulators in `multisim.launch.py` use different `namespace` values?
options: So their topics get different prefixes and do not mix
Because two nodes cannot run at once
Namespaces are required in every launch file
blocks.why: With namespaces, each turtle has its own `/turtlesimN/turtle1/cmd_vel`.
blocks.hint: Look at the topic list in the practice terminal.

blocks.q: Type the command that starts the launch file `chiku.launch.py` from the package `chiku_bringup`.
blocks.why: `ros2 launch <package> <launch_file>`, just like `ros2 run <package> <executable>`.
blocks.hint: ros2 launch, then the package, then the file.

items.back: the function a Python launch file needs

blocks.q: This Python launch file fails with a SyntaxError. Tap the line with the mistake.
blocks.code:
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch_ros.actions import Node

def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node')
        Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtle_teleop_key'),

blocks.hint: Look at the end of each Node(...) line.

blocks.q: What does one Ctrl+C do in the terminal that runs `ros2 launch`?
options: Stops every node the launch file started
Nothing, you must close each node separately
blocks.why: The launch system watches all its nodes and stops them together.
blocks.hint: One command started them; one key stops them.
