blocks.text: Write (on paper or in nano) a launch file that starts **two** talkers with different names, `talker_a` and `talker_b`. Which field gives each one its own name?

items: A launch file starts many nodes, with names, namespaces and parameters, from one command.
Python launch files define `generate_launch_description()` returning a `LaunchDescription` of `Node(...)`s.
Run them with `ros2 launch <package> <file>`; one Ctrl+C stops them all.

blocks.text: So far Chiku ran other people's packages. Today you make **your own** package, the way every ROS 2 project starts.

items: Explain workspace, package, build, install and overlay

blocks.text: Your code lives in packages inside a workspace's `src` folder. `colcon build` builds them into `install`, `source install/setup.bash` loads them, then `ros2 run` works. Build, source, run.

items.m: a folder, such as `~/ros2_ws`, that holds your packages in its `src/` folder

lessons.title: Coordinate frames and TF2
lessons.summary: Why every robot part has its own coordinate frame, and how TF2 converts between them.

blocks.text: Chiku's lidar sees a box "1.2 m in front of me". The map node needs to know where that box is **in the room**. The answer depends on where Chiku is standing and which way it is facing. This is the job of **TF2**.

items: Explain what a coordinate frame is
Name the usual frames: map, odom, base_link, laser
Say what TF2 does for you

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Every part of the robot sees the world from its own point of view (its **frame**). TF2 keeps track of how all the frames sit relative to each other and converts positions between them.

"The canteen is 50 m to your left" is only useful if I know where you are and which way you face. "The canteen is next to the main gate" works for everyone. Each description is a **frame**. TF2 is the friend who converts between them instantly.

blocks.intro: Drive and turn the robot. The obstacle does not move; watch which numbers change.

blocks.label: Frames you will meet on every mobile robot

items.m: the fixed frame of the whole building; it never moves
where the robot thinks it is from wheel turns; smooth, but slowly drifts
the robot's own body: x forward, y left, z up
the lidar, fixed on the robot, a little in front of base_link

blocks.text: Frames form a **tree**: `map → odom → base_link → laser`. Nodes publish how each frame sits relative to its parent on the topics `/tf` (moving parts) and `/tf_static` (fixed parts, like the lidar mount). Any node can then ask TF2: "where is this point in the map frame?"

ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map base_link     # print the robot's position in the map, again and again
ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames              # draw the frame tree into frames.pdf

blocks.q: The lidar is bolted to Chiku. When Chiku drives forward 1 m, does the `base_link → laser` transform change?
blocks.answer: **No.** The lidar moves with the body, so its position relative to `base_link` stays the same: that transform is **static** (published once on `/tf_static`). What changes is `odom → base_link` (and `map → odom`), because the whole robot moved in the room.

blocks.text: A worked example with numbers

items: The lidar is mounted **0.3 m in front** of the robot's centre (`base_link`).
The lidar sees a box **1.2 m straight ahead of the lidar**. In the `laser` frame the box is at x = 1.2.
From the robot's centre, the box is 0.3 + 1.2 = **1.5 m ahead**. In the `base_link` frame, x = 1.5.
The robot stands at x = 2.0 on the map, facing along the map's x axis.
So on the **map**, the box is at 2.0 + 1.5 = **3.5**. TF2 does exactly this adding (and the rotating, when the robot is turned) for you, thousands of times a second.

blocks.q: The robot is at map x = 4.0, facing along +x. The lidar (0.3 m ahead of base_link) sees a wall 1.0 m ahead. Where is the wall on the map?
blocks.why: 4.0 (robot) + 0.3 (lidar mount) + 1.0 (reading) = 5.3.
blocks.hint: Add the three distances along the same direction.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting the sensor's mounting offset: the laser is not at the robot's centre.
Mixing degrees and radians when turning frames.
Publishing a moving transform on `/tf_static`: static is only for parts bolted together.

blocks.q: In the `base_link` frame, which direction is +x?
options: Forward, the way the robot faces
blocks.why: ROS convention (REP 103): x forward, y left, z up. Red, green, blue in RViz.
blocks.hint: The red arrow in the animation.

blocks.q: Which frame never moves?
options: odom drifts, so it is the fixed one
blocks.why: map is fixed to the building. base_link and laser move with the robot.
blocks.hint: Which one is glued to the building?

blocks.q: Match the frame relation with how often it changes.

pairs.b: all the time, as the wheels turn
now and then, when localisation corrects drift

blocks.why: Fixed mounts are static transforms; motion is published continuously; localisation (AMCL, SLAM) corrects drift between map and odom.
blocks.hint: What is bolted, what drives, what corrects?

items.back: a point of view with its own x, y, z

blocks.title: Practice: be TF2 for a moment
blocks.goal: Finish `to_map(robot_x, mount, reading)` so it returns where a point seen by the lidar is on the map (robot facing along the map's x axis): robot position + lidar mount offset + reading. The program prints `3.5` and `5.3`.
blocks.code:
def to_map(robot_x, mount, reading):
    return 0   # add the three distances

print(to_map(2.0, 0.3, 1.2))
print(to_map(4.0, 0.3, 1.0))
blocks.retryHint: return round(robot_x + mount + reading, 2)   (round avoids 5.300000000000001)

blocks.q: Static (never changes) or moving transform?

items.why: The lidar is fixed to the body.

items.text: shoulder → elbow of a moving arm

blocks.why: Bolted parts are static; anything that moves or is corrected is published again and again.

items: A frame is a point of view with its own x, y, z axes.
Mobile robots use the tree `map → odom → base_link → laser`; x is forward, y left, z up.
TF2 keeps the tree on `/tf` and `/tf_static` and converts points between frames for you.

lessons.title: Your debugging toolbox
lessons.summary: Record and replay data with `ros2 bag`, see the graph with rqt_graph, and pick the right tool for each problem.

blocks.text: Chiku bumped into a chair at 3 pm, but by 3:05 nobody can reproduce it. Engineers solve this by **recording** everything the robot heard and **replaying** it at their desk.

items: Record, inspect and replay topics with `ros2 bag`
Know when to use rqt_graph, echo, hz, node info and ros2 doctor
Follow a simple debugging checklist

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: When something doesn't work, check in order: is ROS 2 loaded, is the node running, is the topic name right, is data arriving, and do the types match. `ros2 bag` records data so you can replay a problem later.
A rosbag is the robot's **dashcam**. It records the messages on chosen topics, with their exact times, into a folder. Playing it back publishes the same messages again, as if the robot were live.

blocks.title: Practice: record and replay a drive
blocks.intro: turtlesim and teleop are running. Imagine you are driving the turtle with the arrow keys in the teleop window.

tasks.do: Record the speed commands and the position into a bag called `drive`: `ros2 bag record -o drive /turtle1/cmd_vel /turtle1/pose`
What is inside? `ros2 bag info drive`
Replay it: `ros2 bag play drive`. The turtle repeats the drive.
Check where the replay left the turtle: `ros2 topic echo --once /turtle1/pose`
Run a quick health check: `ros2 doctor`

blocks.text: Seeing the graph

On your own Ubuntu, type `rqt_graph` (or `ros2 run rqt_graph rqt_graph`). A window draws every node as an oval and every topic as an arrow between them. It is the fastest way to see a missing or misspelt connection.

blocks.q: Each symptom has a best first tool. Match them.

pairs.b: `ros2 topic list` and `ros2 topic info` (is the name right? is anyone publishing?)
`ros2 topic hz` (is the data arriving fast enough?)

pairs.a: "I want to see how all nodes connect."
"The bug only happened once, in the corridor."
pairs.b: `ros2 bag record`, then `ros2 bag play` at your desk

blocks.why: Start with the cheapest question: does the topic exist, does data flow, how fast, and who is connected?
blocks.hint: Silent subscriber: check names first.

blocks.title: Debugging mission: why is the listener silent?

tasks.do: Is the listener running? `ros2 node list`
Which topic does it listen to? `ros2 node info /listener`
Is anyone publishing on /chatter? `ros2 topic info /chatter`
Found it: nobody publishes! Start a talker: `ros2 run demo_nodes_py talker`
Open a **new terminal** (press **+ New terminal** or split with **Ctrl+Shift+E**). Then: confirm data now flows: `ros2 topic hz /chatter`
tasks.hint: The node you started keeps its terminal busy, like on Ubuntu. Press + New terminal then: Type: ros2 topic hz /chatter

blocks.intro: A student says: "My listener prints nothing!" Investigate step by step, like a detective.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Guessing instead of checking: run the checklist in order.
Forgetting to source in the new terminal you opened for debugging.
Recording a bag without the topics you need: name them, or use `-a` for all.

blocks.title: When something does not work, check in this order
items: Did I **source** ROS 2 and my workspace in **this** terminal?
Is the node running? `ros2 node list`
Is the topic name exactly right? `ros2 topic list`
Is data arriving? `ros2 topic echo --once` and `ros2 topic hz`
Do the message types match? `ros2 topic info`
Can I see it on the graph? `rqt_graph`

blocks.q: What does `ros2 bag play drive` do?
options: Publishes the recorded messages again with their original timing
Shows the size of the bag
blocks.why: Playing a bag republishes the recorded topics, so your nodes can be tested without the robot.
blocks.hint: The dashcam replay.

blocks.q: **Explain it back.** A bug happened only once, in the corridor. Why is recording a bag better than trying to make it happen again?
blocks.answer: The bag stores every message with its exact time, so you can replay the **same** situation at your desk as many times as you like, step through it, and test your fix against it. Making the bug happen again might take days.

blocks.q: Your subscriber prints nothing. What do you check FIRST?
options: The topic name with `ros2 topic list`
blocks.why: Start with the cheapest check: does the topic exist with exactly that name?
blocks.hint: Silent subscriber: names first.

items: `ros2 bag record -o name topics...`, `ros2 bag info name`, `ros2 bag play name`.
`rqt_graph` shows the whole graph; `topic echo / hz / info` and `node info` check the details.
Debug in order: sourced? running? right name? data flowing? right type?

lessons.title: Mini-project: design Chiku's ROS 2 graph
lessons.summary: Put the whole week together: design the graph of a delivery robot, then build one node that uses a parameter, two publishers and a service.

blocks.text: The college wants Chiku to carry files between departments. You are the robot's software architect. First you design the graph on paper, then you write the heart of it.

items: Choose topics, services, actions and parameters for real features
Read a graph and predict what breaks
Write a node that combines a parameter, publishers and a service

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Design first: streams become topics, quick questions become services, long jobs become actions, settings become parameters. Then one node can own several of each.
Part 1: design the graph

blocks.q: For each feature, choose how it should be built.

items.text: lidar distances to the obstacle stopper

items.why: Long, needs progress and cancel: an action (Nav2's `navigate_to_pose`).

items.text: how close an obstacle may get before stopping
"open the parcel box" (takes half a second)
items.why: Quick, with a yes/no answer: service.

items.text: the robot's name shown on its screen
"is the battery OK to start a trip?"

blocks.why: Streams on topics, quick questions as services, long jobs as actions, settings as parameters. That is 90% of ROS 2 design.
blocks.hint: Stream? Quick question? Long job? Setting?

blocks.q: In your design, the obstacle stopper subscribes to `/scan` and publishes to `/cmd_vel`. The navigation stack **also** publishes to `/cmd_vel`. What problem will you see, and how do real robots solve it?
blocks.answer: Two publishers fight over the wheels: the robot jerks between "go" and "stop". Real robots send each source to its own topic (e.g. `/cmd_vel_nav`, `/cmd_vel_safety`) and use a **multiplexer** node (`twist_mux`) or a velocity smoother that chooses by priority. Safety wins.

blocks.text: Part 2: build the heart of Chiku

This node uses everything from the week: a **parameter** (`max_speed`), two **publishers** (`/turtle1/cmd_vel` and `/battery`), a **timer** callback and a **service** (`battery_ok`, type `std_srvs/srv/Trigger`, whose response has `success` and `message`).

blocks.title: Chiku's main node (practice simulator, 3 seconds)
blocks.goal: TODO 1: drive at the `max_speed` parameter (this playground starts the node with `-p max_speed:=0.8`). TODO 2: fill the service response. The output should contain `battery_ok -> True battery 70.0`.

        self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 0.5)
        self.battery = 100.0
        self.cmd_pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.bat_pub = self.create_publisher(Float64, '/battery', 10)
        self.srv = self.create_service(Trigger, 'battery_ok', self.check_battery)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.step)

    def step(self):
        self.battery -= 5.0
        self.bat_pub.publish(Float64(data=self.battery))
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 0.0   # TODO 1: use the max_speed parameter
        msg.angular.z = 0.3
        self.cmd_pub.publish(msg)

        # TODO 2: success is True when battery is above 20.0;
        #         message is f'battery {self.battery}'
        return response

chiku = Chiku()
rclpy.spin(chiku)
client = chiku.create_client(Trigger, 'battery_ok')

blocks.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Float64
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from std_srvs.srv import Trigger


class Chiku(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('chiku')
        self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 0.5)
        self.battery = 100.0
        self.cmd_pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.bat_pub = self.create_publisher(Float64, '/battery', 10)
        self.srv = self.create_service(Trigger, 'battery_ok', self.check_battery)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.step)

    def step(self):
        self.battery -= 5.0
        self.bat_pub.publish(Float64(data=self.battery))
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = self.get_parameter('max_speed').value
        msg.angular.z = 0.3
        self.cmd_pub.publish(msg)

    def check_battery(self, request, response):
        response.success = self.battery > 20.0
        response.message = f'battery {self.battery}'
        return response


rclpy.init()
chiku = Chiku()
rclpy.spin(chiku)
client = chiku.create_client(Trigger, 'battery_ok')
answer = client.call(Trigger.Request())
print('battery_ok ->', answer.success, answer.message)
rclpy.shutdown()

def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        Node(package='chiku_drivers', executable='lidar'),
        Node(package='chiku_brain', executable='obstacle_stop',
             parameters=[{'stop_distance': 0.4}],
             remappings=[('/scan', '/laser_scan')]),
        Node(package='chiku_drivers', executable='motors'),
    ])

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Two publishers fighting over `/cmd_vel`: use separate topics and a multiplexer.
A remapping on only one side of a connection.

lessons.title: Python: your first package and node
lessons.summary: Create a Python package with ros2 pkg create, understand every file in it, write a node class that follows the five steps, register it, build it with colcon and run it.
lessons.dayTitle: Your first package, node and publisher

blocks.text: In Week 4 you drove turtles with nodes that other people wrote. From today, **you** write the robot's software. Chiku's team gives you an empty workspace and one job: make a node that wakes up and says hello. It sounds small, but every robot program in the world starts exactly like this: a **package** to hold the code, and a **node** inside it.

items: Create a Python package with `ros2 pkg create`
Say what package.xml, setup.py and setup.cfg are for
Write a node class that follows the five steps (init, create, spin, destroy, shutdown)
Register the node, build it, source it and run it

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **package** is a folder that ROS 2 knows how to build. A **node** is a Python class that talks to ROS 2. To run your node you need four things: the package, the code, one line in **setup.py** that gives the program a name, and a build with **colcon**.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A package is like a labelled lunch box. The **label** (package.xml) says whose box it is and what is inside. The **food** is your code. The **instructions** on the lid (setup.py) say how to serve it. colcon is the cook who reads the label and the instructions and puts the meal on the table (the install folder).
Step 1: create the package

cd ~/ros2_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python --license Apache-2.0 chiku_py --dependencies rclpy

items: `--build-type ament_python`: this package contains Python code (C++ packages use `ament_cmake`, next chapter).
`--license Apache-2.0`: the open-source licence. Without it ROS 2 writes "TODO" in package.xml.
`chiku_py`: the package name. Lower-case letters, numbers and underscores only. It must come **before** `--dependencies`.
`--dependencies rclpy`: your code will use rclpy (the ROS 2 Python library), so ROS 2 writes `<depend>rclpy</depend>` into package.xml for you.

blocks.text:
chiku_py/                    <- the package folder
├── package.xml              <- ID card: name, version, dependencies
├── setup.py                 <- build recipe: which programs to install
├── setup.cfg                <- tells ROS 2 where the programs go
├── resource/chiku_py        <- an empty marker file (do not delete)
├── chiku_py/                <- YOUR Python code lives in here
│   └── __init__.py          <- makes the folder a Python module
└── test/                    <- ready-made style tests

Two folders are called `chiku_py`: the **package** folder and, inside it, the **Python module** folder where your .py files go. This confuses everybody the first time. Your node file goes in `chiku_py/chiku_py/`.
blocks.label: Why two chiku_py folders?

blocks.text: Step 2: write the node

blocks.label: Write code in VS Code
blocks.text: Engineers write ROS 2 code in **Visual Studio Code** (free; on Ubuntu install it with `sudo snap install code --classic`). Open the whole workspace with `cd ~/ros2_ws` and `code .`: the **Explorer** on the left shows every package, folder and file. Click a file to edit it, press **Ctrl+S** to save, and **Ctrl+J** shows VS Code's own terminal panel. In the live terminal below, type `code ..` from `~/ros2_ws/src` (or press **Open VS Code**): a practice copy of VS Code opens above the terminal, and every file you save there is the same file the terminal, colcon and ros2 run use. nano still works too.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException


class HelloNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('hello_node')          # give the node its name
        self.get_logger().info('Hello! Chiku is awake.')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)                       # 1. start ROS 2 in this program
    node = HelloNode()                          # 2. create the node
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)                        # 3. keep it alive, run callbacks
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):   # Ctrl+C lands here
        pass
    node.destroy_node()                         # 4. destroy the node
    rclpy.try_shutdown()                        # 5. shut ROS 2 down


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `import rclpy` and `from rclpy.node import Node`: bring in the ROS 2 Python library and its Node class.
`class HelloNode(Node):`: our class **inherits** from Node, so it gets everything a node can do (logging, timers, publishers...).
`super().__init__('hello_node')`: run Node's own set-up first and give the node its name. This name is what `ros2 node list` shows.
`self.get_logger().info(...)`: print a log line with the time and the node's name.
`def main(args=None):` is the function `ros2 run` calls. Inside it are the **five steps** every ROS 2 program follows: init, create, spin, destroy, shutdown.
`rclpy.spin(node)` waits and runs callbacks until you press **Ctrl+C**. The `try / except` catches Ctrl+C quietly instead of printing a long error.

blocks.text: Step 3: give the program a name (setup.py)

Read the line from left to right: the **program name** you type after `ros2 run chiku_py ...`, then `=`, then **package.module:function**. So `chiku_py.hello_node:main` means "the main function in chiku_py/hello_node.py".
Step 4: build, source, run

Always build from the **workspace** folder (`cd ~/ros2_ws`), then `source install/setup.bash` in every terminal that should know your package, then `ros2 run`. `--symlink-install` links your .py files instead of copying them, so a small code change works without building again.

lessons.title: C++: your first package and node
lessons.summary: Create a C++ package, read its CMakeLists.txt, write the same hello node in rclcpp, tell CMake to compile and install it, build it and run it. Learn the C++ words you need on the way.
lessons.dayTitle: Your first package, node and publisher

blocks.text: Chiku's motor controller must react within a few milliseconds, so the team writes it in **C++**, the language of fast robot code. Good news: a C++ node follows **the same five steps** as your Python node. The difference is that C++ is **compiled**: colcon must turn your .cpp file into a program before you can run it.

items: Create a C++ package with `ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_cmake`
Read the C++ node line by line: include, class, constructor, main
Add the three CMake lines: add_executable, target_link_libraries, install
Build, run, and know that every C++ change needs a new build

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: **Compiled** means: a program called the compiler reads your whole .cpp file **once** and turns it into a fast machine-code program. colcon runs the compiler for you. **CMakeLists.txt** tells it which files to compile and where to install the result. Change the code? Build again.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Python is like reading a recipe aloud while you cook: you can change a step and carry on. C++ is like a factory: first the machine is **built** from the plans (compile), then it produces very fast. If you change the plans, you must build the machine again.
Step 1: create the package

cd ~/ros2_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_cmake --license Apache-2.0 chiku_cpp --dependencies rclcpp

chiku_cpp/                   <- the package folder
├── package.xml              <- ID card: name, version, dependencies
├── CMakeLists.txt           <- build recipe: what to compile and install
├── include/chiku_cpp/       <- header files (.hpp), empty for now
└── src/                     <- YOUR C++ code (.cpp files) lives in here
Step 2: write the node
The C++ words, one by one

items: `#include "rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp"`: like Python's import. It brings in rclcpp, the ROS 2 C++ library.
`class HelloNode : public rclcpp::Node`: "HelloNode **is a** Node". This is C++ inheritance, the same idea as `class HelloNode(Node):`.
`public:` the parts below can be used from outside the class.
`HelloNode() : Node("hello_node")`: the **constructor** (C++'s __init__). The part after the colon gives the node its name, like `super().__init__('hello_node')`.
`RCLCPP_INFO(get_logger(), "...");`: a log line. Every C++ statement ends with a **semicolon** `;`.
`int main(int argc, char ** argv)`: every C++ program starts in main. argc and argv carry the command-line words, which rclcpp::init reads.

`auto node = std::make_shared<HelloNode>();`: create the node. ROS 2 C++ keeps nodes in **shared pointers** (smart pointers that free memory by themselves). `auto` lets the compiler work out the type.
`rclcpp::spin(node);`, `node.reset();`, `rclcpp::shutdown();`: spin, destroy, shut down. `return 0;` tells Ubuntu "all went well".

blocks.title: Follow the C++ program

steps.note: `ros2 run chiku_cpp hello_node` starts the program in main().
Step 1: connect to ROS 2.
Step 2: create the node inside a shared pointer...
...the constructor runs and names it hello_node...
...and logs the greeting.
Step 3: wait for events until Ctrl+C.
After Ctrl+C: node.reset() releases the node (step 4), shutdown() closes ROS 2 (step 5), and main returns 0.

blocks.text: Step 3: tell CMake what to build

add_executable(hello_node src/hello_node.cpp)
target_link_libraries(hello_node rclcpp::rclcpp)
install(TARGETS hello_node DESTINATION lib/${PROJECT_NAME})

items: `add_executable(hello_node src/hello_node.cpp)`: compile this .cpp file into a program called hello_node.
`target_link_libraries(hello_node rclcpp::rclcpp)`: connect the program to the rclcpp library (otherwise: "undefined reference" errors).
`install(TARGETS hello_node DESTINATION lib/${PROJECT_NAME})`: copy the program to install/chiku_cpp/lib/chiku_cpp, where `ros2 run` looks.

blocks.text: Put the three lines **above** the `if(BUILD_TESTING)` block and above `ament_package()`, which must stay the last line. Many tutorials write `ament_target_dependencies(hello_node rclcpp)` instead of target_link_libraries; it still works in Jazzy, but target_link_libraries is the modern way.

items.title: Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (C++)

lessons.title: Python: a timer and a publisher drive the turtle
lessons.summary: Add a timer and a publisher to a Python node, fill a Twist message, and make turtlesim draw a circle with your own code. Check it with ros2 topic tools.
lessons.dayTitle: Your first package, node and publisher

blocks.text: Saying hello is nice, but Chiku is a robot: it must **move**. In Week 4 you made the turtle move by typing `ros2 topic pub`. Now your node will do it by itself, 10 times per second, forever: a **timer** wakes the node up, and a **publisher** sends the motor command.

items: Create a timer with `create_timer(period, callback)`
Create a publisher with `create_publisher(Type, topic, 10)`
Fill a geometry_msgs/Twist message field by field
Run the node and check its messages with ros2 topic info and echo

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **timer** is an alarm clock inside your node: every 0.1 s it calls your function (the **callback**). A **publisher** is a loudspeaker on one topic. In the callback you build a **Twist** message (how fast to drive and turn) and publish it. turtlesim listens on `/turtle1/cmd_vel` and moves.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A coach in a rowing boat shouts "stroke!" every two seconds. The shout is the **message**, the rhythm is the **timer**, the megaphone is the **publisher**, and the rowers are the **subscribers**. The coach does not wait for an answer; he just keeps shouting.

blocks.intro: First build a Twist by hand: see which field makes the robot go forward and which makes it turn.

blocks.text: The Twist message

ros2 interface show geometry_msgs/msg/Twist

Vector3  linear     # linear.x = forward speed in m/s
    float64 x
    float64 y
    float64 z
Vector3  angular    # angular.z = turning speed in rad/s (left is positive)
    float64 x
    float64 y
    float64 z
The node

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class CircleDriver(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('circle_driver')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)    # 10 Hz, like a real robot
        self.get_logger().info('Driving in a circle. Press Ctrl+C to stop.')

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 1.0      # forward, metres per second
        msg.angular.z = 0.5     # turn left, radians per second
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = CircleDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist`: import the message type. (geometry_msgs must also be a dependency in package.xml.)
`self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)`: a publisher for Twist messages on that topic. 10 is the **queue size**: how many messages may wait if the network is slow.
`self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)`: call on_timer every 0.1 seconds, which is 10 times per second (10 Hz). Pass the method **without brackets**.
`msg = Twist()`: a new message with every field at 0.0.
`msg.linear.x = 1.0` and `msg.angular.z = 0.5`: drive forward at 1 m/s while turning left at 0.5 rad/s. Together: a circle.
`self.pub.publish(msg)`: send it. Every subscriber of /turtle1/cmd_vel receives it.

blocks.title: The first 0.2 seconds of the node's life
blocks.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class CircleDriver(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('circle_driver')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)    # 10 Hz, like a real robot
        self.get_logger().info('Driving in a circle. Press Ctrl+C to stop.')

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 1.0      # forward, metres per second
        msg.angular.z = 0.5     # turn left, radians per second
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = CircleDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

steps.note: __init__: create the publisher.
Create the timer. Nothing happens yet: timers only fire while the node spins.
Log the start message.

lessons.dayTitle: Your first package, node and publisher

blocks.text: The C++ team wants their own circle driver, because their motor nodes are all C++. You already know **what** the node must do: a timer that publishes a Twist 10 times per second. This chapter is about **how C++ writes it**: a few new symbols (`->`, `::`, `100ms`, `std::bind`) that look scary at first and are simple once you have seen them twice.

items: Create a publisher with `create_publisher<T>(topic, 10)`
Create a timer with `create_wall_timer(100ms, ...)` and std::bind
Store publishers and timers in member variables (name_)
Add geometry_msgs to CMake and build

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The C++ node does exactly what the Python one does. The new parts are: the message type goes in **angle brackets** `<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>`; time is written as `100ms`; the callback is connected with **std::bind**; and the publisher and timer must be kept in **member variables**, or C++ throws them away at the end of the constructor.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Think of a hotel key card. `pub_` is the card you keep in your pocket for as long as you stay. If you leave it at the reception desk (a local variable that ends with the constructor), your door no longer opens: the timer stops ticking, silently.
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "geometry_msgs/msg/twist.hpp"`: the C++ header for Twist. Note the **snake_case** file name: Twist becomes twist.hpp.
`using namespace std::chrono_literals;`: lets you write times like `100ms`, `1s` or `500ms`.
`create_publisher<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>("/turtle1/cmd_vel", 10)`: the type goes in < >. `::` means "inside": Twist inside msg inside geometry_msgs.
`create_wall_timer(100ms, std::bind(&CircleDriver::on_timer, this))`: every 100 ms, call on_timer **on this object**. std::bind glues the method and the object together.
`geometry_msgs::msg::Twist msg;`: a message with all fields 0. `msg.linear.x = 1.0;` uses a dot, because msg is a normal object.
`pub_->publish(msg);`: an **arrow**, because pub_ is a pointer (a SharedPtr). Rule: pointer -> arrow, normal object -> dot.
`private:` and the two lines at the bottom: the member variables. The trailing underscore in `pub_` and `timer_` is a ROS 2 habit that says "this belongs to the object".

lessons.title: Python: a subscriber that listens to the robot
lessons.summary: Subscribe to turtlesim's pose, keep the newest message in the node, add up the distance travelled, and report it once per second from a timer.

blocks.text: Yesterday Chiku drove, but it had no idea where it was. Today we give it **eyes**. turtlesim publishes the turtle's **pose** (x, y and heading) about 60 times per second on `/turtle1/pose`. A node that **subscribes** to that topic always knows where the robot is, and can work out how far it has travelled.

items: Create a subscription with `create_subscription(Type, topic, callback, 10)`
Write a callback that receives each message
Keep the newest message in the node and use it in a timer
Handle the moment before the first message arrives

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **subscription** says to ROS 2: "every time a message arrives on this topic, call this function and give it the message". The function is the **callback**. Keep it short: usually it just **stores** the message. A timer can use the stored message at its own, calmer pace.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A weather station sends a reading every few seconds. Your phone app does not redraw the screen for every reading: it **keeps the newest one** and shows it when you look. Receiving the readings is the subscription; looking at the screen is the timer.
What is inside a turtlesim/msg/Pose?

float32 x                  # metres, from 0 to about 11.09
float32 y
float32 theta              # heading in radians, -pi to pi, 0 = facing right
float32 linear_velocity
float32 angular_velocity
The node

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class PoseMonitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('pose_monitor')
        self.last = None            # the previous pose we received
        self.distance = 0.0         # metres travelled so far
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.report)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            self.distance += math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
        self.last = msg

    def report(self):
        if self.last is None:
            self.get_logger().warn('No pose yet. Is turtlesim running?')
            return
        p = self.last
        self.get_logger().info(
            f'x={p.x:.2f} y={p.y:.2f} theta={p.theta:.2f} travelled={self.distance:.2f} m')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = PoseMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `from turtlesim.msg import Pose`: the message type we listen to.
`self.last = None`: nothing has arrived yet. `None` means "no value".
`self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)`: type, topic, callback (no brackets!), queue size.
`on_pose(self, msg)`: ROS 2 calls it with every new Pose. If there was a previous pose, add the straight-line step between them: `math.hypot(dx, dy)` is Pythagoras.
`self.create_timer(1.0, self.report)`: once per second, report the newest values.
`if self.last is None:` warn and `return` early, so the report never uses a pose that does not exist yet.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class Watch(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('pose_watch')
        self.warned = False
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.drive)

    def drive(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 1.0
        self.pub.publish(msg)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if msg.x > 9.0 and not self.warned:
            self.warned = True
            self.get_logger().warn(f'near the right wall at x={msg.x:.1f}')


rclpy.init()
rclpy.spin(Watch())
rclpy.try_shutdown()

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class PoseMonitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('pose_monitor')
        self.last = None            # the previous pose we received
        self.distance = 0.0         # metres travelled so far
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.report)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            self.distance += math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
        self.last = msg

    def report(self):
        if self.last is None:
            self.get_logger().warn('No pose yet. Is turtlesim running?')
            return
        p = self.last
        self.get_logger().info(
            f'x={p.x:.2f} y={p.y:.2f} theta={p.theta:.2f} travelled={self.distance:.2f} m')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = PoseMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.summary: Write the pose monitor in C++: create_subscription with std::bind and a placeholder, a callback that takes a const reference, std::optional for "no message yet", and printf-style logging.

blocks.text: The C++ team wants the same eyes for their motor node. You know the plan: store the newest pose in the callback, report it from a timer. In C++ you meet three new friends: `std::placeholders::_1` (a gap where the message goes), `const Pose & msg` (read the message without copying it) and `std::optional` (a box that may still be empty).

items: Create a subscription with `create_subscription<T>(topic, 10, callback)`
Read a callback that takes `const T & msg`
Use std::optional to handle "no message yet"
Log numbers with printf-style formats like %.2f

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The C++ subscription works exactly like the Python one. `std::bind(&PoseMonitor::on_pose, this, std::placeholders::_1)` means: "call on_pose on this object, and put the message in place of _1". The callback receives `const Pose & msg`: a **reference** (no copy, fast) that is **const** (you cannot change it by mistake).

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: `std::optional<Pose>` is like a parcel box at your door: it is either **empty** or holds **one** parcel. Before the first pose arrives the box is empty. `if (last_)` asks "is there a parcel?", and `last_->x` opens it and looks inside.
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "turtlesim/msg/pose.hpp"` and `using turtlesim::msg::Pose;`: the using line lets you write just `Pose` instead of `turtlesim::msg::Pose`.
`create_subscription<Pose>("/turtle1/pose", 10, ...)`: in C++ the order is **topic, queue size, callback** (in Python it was type, topic, callback, queue size).
`std::bind(&PoseMonitor::on_pose, this, std::placeholders::_1)`: _1 is the gap that ROS 2 fills with each message.
`void on_pose(const Pose & msg)`: `void` = returns nothing; `const Pose &` = read-only reference, no copy.
`std::optional<Pose> last_;`: empty at start. `last_ = msg;` fills it. `if (!last_)` is true while it is still empty.
`RCLCPP_INFO(get_logger(), "x=%.2f ...", last_->x, ...)`: **printf style**. Each `%.2f` is replaced by the next number, with 2 decimals. `%%` prints a percent sign.

steps.note: Constructor: subscribe. last_ is an empty optional.
The first Pose arrives.
Empty: no previous pose, so no distance yet.
Store it. The box is no longer empty.
After 1 s the timer calls report().
Not empty, so we print the newest values.

lessons.summary: Design RobotStatus.msg, build it in an interfaces package (rosidl), check it with ros2 interface show, and publish it from a Python node that reads live data.

blocks.text: The operator's screen needs Chiku's **name, position, battery and whether it is moving**, all in one message, twice per second. No standard message has exactly those fields. So you design your own: `RobotStatus.msg`. Real robot teams do this all the time: a warehouse robot, a drone or a farm robot each has message types made for its own job.

items: Write a .msg file: one `type name` line per field
Create an interfaces package and add the rosidl lines to CMakeLists.txt and package.xml
Build it and check it with `ros2 interface show`
Import, fill and publish it from Python

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A `.msg` file is a list of fields, one per line: **type** then **name**. A tool called **rosidl** turns it into a Python class and a C++ struct when you build. Then you use it like any other message: `from my_robot_interfaces.msg import RobotStatus`.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A form at the doctor's: name, age, weight, "do you smoke? yes / no". Somebody designed that form once, and now everybody fills it in the same way. A .msg file is a form for robots, and rosidl prints copies of it for every language.

blocks.intro: From one .msg file, rosidl generates code for Python and C++.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose
from my_robot_interfaces.msg import RobotStatus


class StatusPublisher(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('status_publisher')
        self.pose = Pose()
        self.battery = 100.0
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(RobotStatus, 'chiku/status', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(0.5, self.on_timer)        # 2 Hz

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.pose = msg

    def on_timer(self):
        self.battery = max(0.0, self.battery - 0.1)
        msg = RobotStatus()
        msg.name = 'chiku'
        msg.x = self.pose.x
        msg.y = self.pose.y
        msg.battery = self.battery
        msg.moving = abs(self.pose.linear_velocity) > 0.01 or abs(self.pose.angular_velocity) > 0.01
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = StatusPublisher()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

blocks.text: rosidl made a C++ struct called `my_robot_interfaces::msg::RobotStatus`, in a header file whose name is the type in **snake_case**: robot_status.hpp. You fill it like any struct: `msg.name = "chiku";`. float64 fields are C++ `double`; float32 fields are C++ `float`.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: The same person can be written as "Chiku Robot" on a passport, "chiku_robot" as a username and "ROBOT, Chiku" on a list. One message, several spellings, and each place expects its own.
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "my_robot_interfaces/msg/robot_status.hpp"`: CamelCase RobotStatus becomes snake_case robot_status.hpp.
`using my_robot_interfaces::msg::RobotStatus;`: write `RobotStatus` instead of the long name.

`[this](const turtlesim::msg::Pose & msg) { pose_ = msg; }`: a **lambda**. `[this]` lets it use the node's members; the part in ( ) is the message; the { } body stores it. Good for one-line callbacks.
`float battery_ = 100.0f;` and `battery_ - 0.1f`: the `f` makes the number a float, matching the float32 field. `std::max(0.0f, ...)` never goes below zero.
`std::fabs(...)` is the absolute value of a floating point number; `||` means "or".

lessons.title: Python: a service server that switches the robot on and off
lessons.summary: Write a service server with create_service: read the request, fill the response, return it. Use it to switch a driving timer on and off, and call it from the terminal.
lessons.dayTitle: Services: ask the robot, get an answer

blocks.text: Safety rule in Chiku's warehouse: the robot must **not** drive the moment its software starts. An operator must press "go" first, and must be able to press "stop" at any time. That is a perfect job for a **service**: a short question with an answer. "Enable driving?" "OK, driving." "Disable?" "OK, stopped."

items: Read a service type: request, ---, response
Create a service server with `create_service(Type, name, callback)`
Write the callback: read the request, fill the response, **return** it
Call the service with `ros2 service call` and see the robot react

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **service server** waits for requests. When one arrives, your callback gets the **request** and an empty **response**. It does something quick, fills the response, and returns it. Here `request.data` is true or false; we store it, and the driving timer checks it 10 times per second.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A light switch with a little lamp: you press it (request: on), the lamp lights up (response: OK, on). The switch does not stay pressed for an hour; it switches and it is done. Long jobs with progress reports are **actions** (Day 24).
The service type we use

ros2 interface show std_srvs/srv/SetBool

bool data      # request: e.g. enable or disable
---
bool success   # response: did it work?
string message # response: informational text

Every service type has two parts separated by `---`: the **request** (what the client sends) and the **response** (what the server answers). std_srvs/srv/SetBool is a standard type, perfect for anything that is switched on or off.
The node

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from std_srvs.srv import SetBool


class SwitchableDriver(Node):
    """Drives in a circle, but only while enabled. A service turns it on and off."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('switchable_driver')
        self.enabled = False
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.srv = self.create_service(SetBool, 'chiku/enable', self.on_enable)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info('Ready. Call /chiku/enable with data: true to start.')

    def on_enable(self, request, response):
        self.enabled = request.data
        response.success = True
        response.message = 'driving' if self.enabled else 'stopped'
        self.get_logger().info(f'enable = {self.enabled}')
        return response                                   # never forget this line

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        if self.enabled:
            msg.linear.x = 1.0
            msg.angular.z = 0.8
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SwitchableDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `from std_srvs.srv import SetBool`: the service type. (std_srvs goes into package.xml as a dependency.)
`self.enabled = False`: start disabled, for safety.
`self.create_service(SetBool, 'chiku/enable', self.on_enable)`: type, service name, callback. Without a leading / the name becomes `/chiku/enable`.
`def on_enable(self, request, response):` gets both objects. `request.data` is what the client sent.
Fill `response.success` and `response.message`, then **return response**. Forget the return and the client never gets an answer.
`on_timer` publishes a moving Twist only while `self.enabled` is True; otherwise a zero Twist (stand still).

        self.speed = 1.0

        response.success = True

lessons.summary: Write the switchable driver in C++: create_service<T>, a callback that receives shared pointers to the request and the response and fills the response in place, two placeholders, and the ? : operator.
lessons.dayTitle: Services: ask the robot, get an answer

blocks.text: The C++ team copies the safety switch into their driver. The idea is the same as in Python; the difference is how the answer travels back. In Python the callback **returns** the response. In C++ the callback gets the response as a **pointer** and fills it **in place**; it returns nothing at all.

items: Create a service server with `create_service<T>(name, callback)`
Read a callback that takes `std::shared_ptr<T::Request>` and `std::shared_ptr<T::Response>`
Use two placeholders, _1 and _2, in std::bind
Read the ternary operator `condition ? a : b`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: ROS 2 creates the request and the response for you and hands your callback a **pointer** to each. You read `request->data` and write `response->success` and `response->message`. When your function ends, ROS 2 sends the response. That is why the C++ callback is `void`.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A form at a counter: the clerk gives you the request form (already filled by the customer) and a blank answer form. You write on the answer form and put it in the tray. You don't hand back a new sheet; you filled the one you were given.
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "std_srvs/srv/set_bool.hpp"` and `using std_srvs::srv::SetBool;`: SetBool becomes set_bool.hpp (snake_case again).

`create_service<SetBool>("chiku/enable", std::bind(&SwitchableDriver::on_enable, this, std::placeholders::_1, std::placeholders::_2))`: the callback takes **two** things, so std::bind needs two gaps, _1 (request) and _2 (response).
`const std::shared_ptr<SetBool::Request> request`: a pointer to the request. `request->data` reads the bool (arrow: it is a pointer).
`std::shared_ptr<SetBool::Response> response`: a pointer to the empty response. `response->success = true;` fills it.
`enabled_ ? "driving" : "stopped"`: the **ternary operator**: if enabled_ then "driving" else "stopped". Python writes `'driving' if enabled else 'stopped'`.
`rclcpp::Service<SetBool>::SharedPtr srv_;`: keep the service in a member, or it disappears at the end of the constructor.

blocks.title: One call: data = true

steps.note: The member starts false: the robot stands still.
A request arrives. ROS 2 calls on_enable with two pointers.
Arrow: read data through the pointer.
Fill the response in place...
...enabled_ is true, so the message is "driving". No return: ROS 2 sends the response now.
On the next timer tick the Twist gets speeds: the turtle drives.

lessons.title: Python: a service client that asks turtlesim for help
lessons.summary: Write client programs: wait for a service, send a request with call_async, wait for the future in main(), read the answer. Spawn a turtle, then let an artist node draw a triangle with three services.
lessons.dayTitle: Services: ask the robot, get an answer

blocks.text: turtlesim offers services: `/spawn` makes a new turtle, `/<turtle>/set_pen` changes its pen colour, `/<turtle>/teleport_absolute` jumps it to a point. In Week 4 you called them by hand with `ros2 service call`. Today a program calls them for you, in a blink. This is how robot programs use each other's abilities: as **clients**.

items: Create a client and wait until the server exists
Send a request with `call_async` and get a **future**
Wait for the answer in main() with `spin_until_future_complete`
Know why a blocking call inside a callback freezes the node

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A client sends a request and immediately gets a **future**: a promise that the answer will come. Then you wait for it with `rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future)` and read `future.result()`. Simple programs do this in main().

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Ordering at a food counter: you pay and get a ticket with a number (the **future**). Then you wait until your number is called (spin_until_future_complete) and collect your food (future.result()). The kitchen works while you wait.
The five steps of a client

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from turtlesim.srv import Spawn


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = Node('spawn_client')                             # a plain node: no class of our own needed
    client = node.create_client(Spawn, '/spawn')            # 1. make a client for the /spawn service
    while not client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0):     # 2. wait until turtlesim offers it
        node.get_logger().info('waiting for /spawn ... is turtlesim running?')
    request = Spawn.Request()                               # 3. fill in the request
    request.x = 2.0
    request.y = 8.0
    request.theta = 0.0
    request.name = 'chiku2'
    future = client.call_async(request)                     # 4. send it (do not wait here)
    rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future)          # 5. now wait for the answer
    node.get_logger().info(f'turtlesim made a turtle called {future.result().name}')
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `node = Node('spawn_client')`: a plain node. For a short program we do not need our own class.
**1.** `create_client(Spawn, '/spawn')`: a client for that service and type.
**2.** `wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0)` returns False after 1 s if the server is not there yet; the while loop keeps waiting and says why.
**3.** `Spawn.Request()` and fill its fields: x, y, theta, name.
**4.** `call_async(request)` sends it and returns a future at once.
**5.** `spin_until_future_complete(node, future)` spins until the answer is in; `future.result().name` is the name turtlesim gave the new turtle.

blocks.text: Level 2: one node, three services

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from turtlesim.srv import Spawn, SetPen, TeleportAbsolute


class TurtleArtist(Node):
    """A client node: asks turtlesim to spawn a turtle, change its pen and teleport it."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('turtle_artist')
        self.spawn = self.create_client(Spawn, '/spawn')
        while not self.spawn.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0):
            self.get_logger().info('waiting for /spawn ... is turtlesim running?')

    def call(self, client, request):
        future = client.call_async(request)                # send, do not block
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(self, future)     # wait here in main(), not in a callback
        return future.result()

    def draw_triangle(self):
        res = self.call(self.spawn, Spawn.Request(x=2.0, y=2.0, theta=0.0, name='artist'))
        self.get_logger().info(f'spawned {res.name}')
        pen = self.create_client(SetPen, '/artist/set_pen')
        tele = self.create_client(TeleportAbsolute, '/artist/teleport_absolute')
        pen.wait_for_service()
        tele.wait_for_service()
        self.call(pen, SetPen.Request(r=255, g=200, b=0, width=4, off=0))
        for x, y in [(8.0, 2.0), (5.0, 7.0), (2.0, 2.0)]:
            self.call(tele, TeleportAbsolute.Request(x=x, y=y, theta=0.0))
            self.get_logger().info(f'line to ({x}, {y})')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = TurtleArtist()
    node.draw_triangle()
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

`turtle_artist` puts the same five steps in a small helper method, `call()`, and uses it for three different services: spawn the artist turtle, give it a yellow pen, then teleport it to three corners. Each teleport draws a straight line.

Never wait for an answer **inside** a callback (a timer or a subscription) with a blocking call like `client.call(request)`: the answer can only be delivered by spin, and spin is busy running your callback. The node freezes forever. In main() it is safe.

blocks.q: This node freezes forever the first time its timer fires. Which line causes it?
blocks.code:
def on_timer(self):
    req = Spawn.Request(x=1.0, y=1.0, theta=0.0, name='t2')
    result = self.spawn_client.call(req)
    self.get_logger().info(result.name)
blocks.why: A blocking call() inside a callback waits for an answer that spin can never deliver, because spin is busy running this very callback.
blocks.fix: In a callback use `future = self.spawn_client.call_async(req)` and `future.add_done_callback(self.on_spawned)`; the answer then arrives in on_spawned.
blocks.hint: Who delivers the answer while on_timer is running?

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Waiting with a blocking call inside a callback: the node freezes.
Not waiting for the service: the request goes nowhere.
Forgetting that each turtle has its own services (/artist/set_pen, not /set_pen).
Reading future.result() before the future is done (it is None).
A client creates, waits, fills, sends (call_async) and waits for the future.
In main() wait with spin_until_future_complete.
Never block inside a callback; use add_done_callback there.

lessons.summary: Write the spawn client in C++: rclcpp::Node::make_shared without a class, create_client<T>, wait_for_service(1s), a request in a shared pointer, async_send_request, spin_until_future_complete and FutureReturnCode.
lessons.dayTitle: Services: ask the robot, get an answer

blocks.text: The C++ team needs a program that sets up the warehouse: spawn the helper turtles at the right places before work starts. A short C++ program that calls turtlesim's `/spawn` service is perfect. Same five steps as in Python; you will recognise every one of them.

items: Create a node without writing a class: `rclcpp::Node::make_shared("name")`
Create a client and wait for the server: `create_client<T>`, `wait_for_service(1s)`
Send a request with `async_send_request` and wait with `spin_until_future_complete`
Check the result with `rclcpp::FutureReturnCode::SUCCESS`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: For a short program you don't need your own node class: `rclcpp::Node::make_shared("spawn_client")` makes a ready node. The request lives in a shared pointer (`std::make_shared<Spawn::Request>()`), so you fill it with arrows: `request->x = 2.0;`. The future's `get()` gives a pointer to the response.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Sending a parcel: you fill in a delivery form (the request), hand it in and get a tracking number (the future), then wait until the tracking says "delivered" (SUCCESS) and read the receipt (future.get()).
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "turtlesim/srv/spawn.hpp"` and `using turtlesim::srv::Spawn;`: the service type.
`auto node = rclcpp::Node::make_shared("spawn_client");`: a node without our own class, inside a shared pointer. So its methods use arrows: `node->create_client<Spawn>("/spawn")`.
`while (!client->wait_for_service(1s))`: `!` means NOT. Keep waiting, one second at a time, while the service is missing.
`auto request = std::make_shared<Spawn::Request>();` then `request->x = 2.0;` ...: fill the request through its pointer.
`auto future = client->async_send_request(request);`: send it; the future arrives at once.
`rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, future) == rclcpp::FutureReturnCode::SUCCESS`: wait, then check it worked. `future.get()->name.c_str()` reads the name for %s.

items: A wrong service name: the client waits forever. Check with ros2 service list.
Using a dot on pointers: `request.x` instead of `request->x`.

lessons.title: Python: an action that drives a distance, with progress
lessons.summary: Write DriveDistance as an action: a server that accepts or rejects goals, publishes feedback while it drives and returns a result, and a client that sends a goal, prints progress and can cancel.

blocks.text: "Chiku, drive 2 metres forward." That takes a few seconds. The operator wants to see the progress ("1.5 m to go..."), be able to **cancel** halfway, and get a final report. A service cannot do that: it answers once and has no progress. An **action** can. Today you write both sides: the robot (server) and the operator's program (client).

items: Read an .action file: goal --- result --- feedback
Write a server: accept or reject a goal, publish feedback, finish with succeed() or canceled()
Write a client: send a goal, print feedback, read the result
Send goals from the terminal with ros2 action send_goal --feedback

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: An action has three parts. The **goal** says what to do (drive 2 m at 0.5 m/s). **Feedback** reports progress many times (remaining: 1.5 m). The **result** is sent once at the end (drove 2.0 m). The server may **reject** a goal, and the client may **cancel** it while it runs.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Ordering a parcel online: you place the order (goal), the shop can refuse it ("we don't deliver there"), you get tracking updates (feedback), you can cancel before it arrives, and at the end you get "delivered" (result).

blocks.text: The server: the robot's side

import time

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.action import ActionServer, CancelResponse, GoalResponse
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException, MultiThreadedExecutor
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from my_robot_interfaces.action import DriveDistance


class DriveDistanceServer(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('drive_distance_server')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.server = ActionServer(
            self, DriveDistance, 'chiku/drive_distance',
            execute_callback=self.execute,
            goal_callback=self.on_goal,
            cancel_callback=self.on_cancel)
        self.get_logger().info('Action server /chiku/drive_distance is ready')

    def on_goal(self, goal_request):
        if goal_request.distance <= 0.0 or not 0.0 < goal_request.speed <= 2.0:
            self.get_logger().warn('Rejected: distance must be > 0 and speed in (0, 2]')
            return GoalResponse.REJECT
        return GoalResponse.ACCEPT

    def on_cancel(self, goal_handle):
        self.get_logger().info('Cancel requested')
        return CancelResponse.ACCEPT

    def execute(self, goal_handle):
        goal = goal_handle.request
        driven = 0.0
        feedback = DriveDistance.Feedback()
        result = DriveDistance.Result()
        while driven < goal.distance:
            if goal_handle.is_cancel_requested:
                self.pub.publish(Twist())              # stop the robot first
                goal_handle.canceled()
                result.distance_driven = driven
                return result
            cmd = Twist()
            cmd.linear.x = goal.speed
            self.pub.publish(cmd)
            time.sleep(0.1)                            # 10 Hz
            driven = min(goal.distance, driven + goal.speed * 0.1)
            feedback.remaining = goal.distance - driven
            goal_handle.publish_feedback(feedback)
        self.pub.publish(Twist())
        goal_handle.succeed()
        result.distance_driven = driven
        self.get_logger().info(f'Done: drove {driven:.2f} m')
        return result


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = DriveDistanceServer()
    executor = MultiThreadedExecutor()     # so cancel requests are handled while execute() runs
    executor.add_node(node)
    try:
        executor.spin()
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `ActionServer(self, DriveDistance, 'chiku/drive_distance', execute_callback=..., goal_callback=..., cancel_callback=...)`: one object, three callbacks.
`on_goal`: check the goal first. Distance must be positive and speed between 0 and 2; otherwise `GoalResponse.REJECT`.
`on_cancel`: return `CancelResponse.ACCEPT` to allow cancelling.
`execute`: the real work. A loop drives in steps of 0.1 s, adds up the distance and publishes **feedback** each step.
Inside the loop: if `goal_handle.is_cancel_requested`, stop the robot, call `canceled()` and return the result so far.
At the end: stop the robot, `goal_handle.succeed()`, fill and return the **result**. `MultiThreadedExecutor` in main() lets a cancel request arrive while execute() is still looping.

blocks.text: The client: the operator's side

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.action import ActionClient
from my_robot_interfaces.action import DriveDistance


class DriveDistanceClient(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('drive_distance_client')
        self.declare_parameter('distance', 2.0)
        self.declare_parameter('speed', 0.5)
        self.declare_parameter('cancel_after', 0.0)      # seconds; 0 = never cancel
        self.client = ActionClient(self, DriveDistance, 'chiku/drive_distance')
        self.goal_handle = None

    def send(self):
        self.client.wait_for_server()
        goal = DriveDistance.Goal()
        goal.distance = self.get_parameter('distance').value
        goal.speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value
        self.get_logger().info(f'Sending goal: {goal.distance} m at {goal.speed} m/s')
        future = self.client.send_goal_async(goal, feedback_callback=self.on_feedback)
        future.add_done_callback(self.on_goal_response)

    def on_goal_response(self, future):
        self.goal_handle = future.result()
        if not self.goal_handle.accepted:
            self.get_logger().warn('Goal rejected')
            rclpy.shutdown()
            return
        self.get_logger().info('Goal accepted')
        self.goal_handle.get_result_async().add_done_callback(self.on_result)
        wait = self.get_parameter('cancel_after').value
        if wait > 0.0:
            self.cancel_timer = self.create_timer(wait, self.cancel)

    def on_feedback(self, feedback_msg):
        self.get_logger().info(f'remaining: {feedback_msg.feedback.remaining:.2f} m')

    def cancel(self):
        self.cancel_timer.cancel()
        self.get_logger().info('Changed my mind: cancelling')
        self.goal_handle.cancel_goal_async()

    def on_result(self, future):
        res = future.result()
        self.get_logger().info(f'Result: drove {res.result.distance_driven:.2f} m (status {res.status})')
        rclpy.shutdown()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = DriveDistanceClient()
    node.send()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

The client never blocks. `send_goal_async(goal, feedback_callback=...)` returns a future; when the server has decided, **on_goal_response** runs; while it drives, **on_feedback** runs many times; at the end **on_result** prints the status and shuts down. Status numbers: **4** = SUCCEEDED, **5** = CANCELED, **6** = ABORTED.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.action import ActionServer, ActionClient
from my_robot_interfaces.action import DriveDistance


class Server(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('drive_distance_server')
        self.battery_m = 1.0
        ActionServer(self, DriveDistance, 'chiku/drive_distance', self.execute)

    def execute(self, goal_handle):
        driven = 0.0
        result = DriveDistance.Result()
        while driven < goal_handle.request.distance:
            if driven >= self.battery_m:
                goal_handle.abort()
                result.distance_driven = driven
                return result
            driven += 0.25
        goal_handle.succeed()
        result.distance_driven = driven
        return result

blocks.why: The server never marks the goal as finished. A goal that returns without succeed(), canceled() or abort() ends as ABORTED.

blocks.q: Put the life of an action goal in order
items: the client sends the goal
the server's goal callback accepts it
execute() drives and publishes feedback
goal_handle.succeed()
the client's result callback prints the result
blocks.why: Send, accept, work with feedback, mark it done, deliver the result.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting `succeed()`: the goal ends as ABORTED.
Not stopping the robot when a goal is cancelled.
Expecting cancel requests during a long execute() with a single-threaded executor (use MultiThreadedExecutor).
Typing the action type without /action/: my_robot_interfaces/DriveDistance.
Actions are long jobs with feedback and cancel.
The server checks goals, works in execute(), publishes feedback and ends with succeed, canceled or abort.
The client sends a goal and gets three kinds of callback: response, feedback, result.
Test with ros2 action list -t and ros2 action send_goal --feedback.

items.title: Writing an action server and client (Python)

lessons.title: C++: an action that drives a distance, with progress
lessons.summary: Write the DriveDistance server in C++ with rclcpp_action: handle_goal, handle_cancel, handle_accepted, an execute() that runs in its own thread, rclcpp::Rate, feedback and result in shared pointers.

blocks.text: The C++ motor team owns the real wheels, so the drive-a-distance action must live in their C++ node. The C++ server has the same three decisions as the Python one (accept? allow cancel? do the job), plus one important rule: the long job runs in its **own thread**, so the node stays free to hear a cancel request.

items: Create a server with `rclcpp_action::create_server<T>(this, name, goal_cb, cancel_cb, accepted_cb)`
Read the three callbacks and what they return
Run the job in a std::thread and loop with rclcpp::Rate
Finish with succeed(result) or canceled(result)

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `handle_goal` says ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE or REJECT. `handle_cancel` says ACCEPT or REJECT. `handle_accepted` starts the job, but must return **quickly**, so it starts a **thread** that runs `execute()`. In execute(), `rclcpp::Rate rate(10)` and `rate.sleep()` make the loop run 10 times per second.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A restaurant: the waiter takes your order (handle_goal), can take back an order (handle_cancel), and hands the order to the kitchen (handle_accepted) and goes back to the tables at once. The kitchen (a separate thread) cooks. If the waiter cooked himself, nobody could call him while the food was on the stove.
The new C++ pieces

items: `#include "rclcpp_action/rclcpp_action.hpp"` and `my_robot_interfaces/action/drive_distance.hpp`: the action library and the generated action type.
`using DriveDistance = ...;` and `using GoalHandle = rclcpp_action::ServerGoalHandle<DriveDistance>;`: short names for long types.
`create_server<DriveDistance>(this, "chiku/drive_distance", goal_cb, cancel_cb, accepted_cb)`: `using namespace std::placeholders;` lets us write just _1 and _2.
`handle_goal(const rclcpp_action::GoalUUID &, std::shared_ptr<const DriveDistance::Goal> goal)`: every goal has an ID (UUID); we don't need it, so it has no name. `goal->distance` reads the goal.
`std::thread{std::bind(&DriveDistanceServer::execute, this, goal_handle)}.detach();`: start execute() in a new thread and let it run on its own.

In execute(): `goal_handle->is_canceling()` checks for cancel; `publish_feedback(feedback)` sends progress; `succeed(result)` ends it. Feedback and result live in shared pointers (`std::make_shared<...>()`).

blocks.title: Follow one goal through the C++ server

steps.note: handle_goal checks the goal: it is fine.
Accepted. ROS 2 now calls handle_accepted.
Start execute() in its own thread; handle_accepted returns at once.
The job begins: a loop at 10 Hz.
After each 0.1 s step: how much is left...
...sent to the client as feedback.
Distance reached: the goal SUCCEEDED, with the result.

blocks.q: This C++ server cannot hear cancel requests while it drives, and the node feels frozen. Which line is the problem?
blocks.why: execute() loops for seconds. Called directly, it blocks the executor: no cancel requests and no other callbacks until it ends.
blocks.fix: Run it in its own thread: `std::thread{std::bind(&DriveDistanceServer::execute, this, goal_handle)}.detach();`
blocks.hint: How long does execute() take?

blocks.q: Python server vs C++ server
blocks.why: Same decisions, different spelling. C++ hands the result to succeed(); Python returns it.
blocks.hint: Read both sides slowly, then try again.

blocks.q: Why does `handle_accepted` start a new thread instead of calling execute() directly?
options: So the callback returns at once and the node can still handle cancel requests and other callbacks
blocks.why: A callback that runs for seconds blocks everything else in the node.
blocks.hint: Who would hear a cancel request?

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Calling execute() directly in handle_accepted.
Forgetting to stop the robot (publish a zero Twist) before canceled(result).
Using `goal.distance` with a dot: goal is a shared pointer, so `goal->distance`.
Forgetting rclcpp_action in package.xml and `rclcpp_action::rclcpp_action` in target_link_libraries.

items.back: run the job in the background

items: C++ action servers have three callbacks: goal, cancel, accepted.
handle_accepted must return quickly: run execute() in a std::thread.
Feedback and result are shared pointers; finish with succeed(result) or canceled(result).
The C++ client collects its callbacks in SendGoalOptions.

lessons.title: Python: parameters, change the robot without changing the code
lessons.summary: Declare parameters with default values, read them in the node, change them live with ros2 param set, start a node with -p values or a YAML file, and save the current values with ros2 param dump.

blocks.text: Chiku's customers keep asking for small changes: "drive slower in our shop", "turn faster", "call the robot Bolt". Changing the code and rebuilding every time? No. Good robot code keeps such settings as **parameters**: named values that you can set when the node starts, or change while it runs.

items: Declare a parameter with a default: `declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)`
Read it: `get_parameter('speed').value`
Change it live with `ros2 param set` and see the robot react
Set values at start with `-p` or a YAML file; save them with `ros2 param dump`

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **parameter** is a setting that belongs to one node, with a name, a type and a value. You **declare** it (with a default) when the node starts, and you **read** it when you need it. Because speed_driver reads its parameters in every timer tick, `ros2 param set` changes the robot's driving at once.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: The settings menu of a phone: brightness, volume, ringtone. The phone's software does not change; you change the settings, and the phone behaves differently. Parameters are the settings menu of a node.

blocks.intro: Change a parameter live and watch the node react.

blocks.text:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class SpeedDriver(Node):
    """Drives in a circle. The speeds are PARAMETERS, so you can change them without editing code."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('speed_driver')
        self.declare_parameter('robot_name', 'chiku')     # name, default value
        self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)              # forward speed, m/s
        self.declare_parameter('turn', 0.5)               # turn rate, rad/s
        name = self.get_parameter('robot_name').value
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info(f'{name} is ready to drive')

    def on_timer(self):
        speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value        # read the newest value every tick
        turn = self.get_parameter('turn').value
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = speed
        msg.angular.z = turn
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SpeedDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items: `self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)`: create the parameter `speed` with default 1.0. The default also fixes the **type**: 1.0 is a double, 'chiku' is a string.
`self.get_parameter('robot_name').value`: read the current value.
In `on_timer` we read speed and turn **every tick**, so a change made with `ros2 param set` is used 0.1 s later.
Declare every parameter **before** you use it: reading an undeclared parameter raises an error.

blocks.text: Three ways to set a parameter

# 1. while the node runs
ros2 param set /speed_driver speed 2.5

# 2. when it starts, on the command line
ros2 run chiku_control speed_driver --ros-args -p speed:=0.5 -p robot_name:=bolt

# 3. when it starts, from a YAML file
ros2 run chiku_control speed_driver --ros-args --params-file config/speed.yaml

tabs.code:
# Parameters for speed_driver. The first line is the NODE name.
speed_driver:
  ros__parameters:
    robot_name: "chiku"
    speed: 1.5
    turn: 1.0
tabs.note: First line: the **node name**. Then `ros__parameters:` with **two** underscores. Then the values, indented with spaces (never Tab).

blocks.q: `ros2 param set /speed_driver speed 2.0` says it worked, but the turtle keeps the old speed. Which line is the problem?
blocks.code:
def __init__(self):
    super().__init__('speed_driver')
    self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)
    self.speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value
    self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)

def on_timer(self):
    msg = Twist()
    msg.linear.x = self.speed
blocks.why: The value is read only once, in __init__. Later changes are stored in the parameter, but the timer keeps using the old copy in self.speed.
blocks.fix: Read it in the timer: `msg.linear.x = self.get_parameter('speed').value`, like speed_driver.py.
blocks.hint: When is the parameter read?

blocks.q: `ros2 param set /speed_driver speed 2` fails with **expected 'Type.DOUBLE' got 'Type.INTEGER'**. How do you fix the command?
options: Write 2.0: speed was declared as a double
blocks.why: The default 1.0 made speed a double. 2 is an integer; 2.0 is a double.
blocks.hint: What type did the default give it?

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
