`ros_parameters` with one underscore in YAML: the values are ignored.
A YAML file whose first line is not the node's name: the values are not applied.
Setting an integer on a double parameter: write 2.0.

lessons.summary: Declare and read parameters in rclcpp: declare_parameter with a default, get_parameter(...).as_double() and as_string(), live changes, YAML files, and the extra qos_overrides parameters every C++ node has.

blocks.text: The C++ motor node needs the same settings menu: speed, turn rate, robot name. Parameters work the same way in C++, and the terminal commands are exactly the same. What changes is how C++ asks for the value: you must say which **type** you want back, for example `.as_double()`.

items: Declare parameters in the constructor: `declare_parameter("speed", 1.0)`
Read them with `get_parameter("speed").as_double()` and `.as_string()`
Change them live and from a YAML file
Recognise the qos_overrides parameters that rclcpp adds

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `declare_parameter("speed", 1.0)` creates the parameter (and returns its value, if you want it). `get_parameter("speed")` gives you a Parameter object; `.as_double()`, `.as_int()`, `.as_bool()` or `.as_string()` turns it into a normal C++ value of that type.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A vending machine: you put in a coin and must press the right button for what you want. `.as_double()` is the "number with decimals" button; `.as_string()` is the "text" button. Press the wrong one (as_int on a double) and the machine refuses with an error.
The new C++ pieces

items: `declare_parameter("robot_name", "chiku");`: a string parameter. `declare_parameter("speed", 1.0);`: a double (1.0 has a decimal point; 1 would make it an integer!).
`std::string name = get_parameter("robot_name").as_string();`: read it as text.
`RCLCPP_INFO(get_logger(), "%s is ready to drive", name.c_str());`: `%s` needs a C-style string, so add `.c_str()`.
`double speed = get_parameter("speed").as_double();` inside on_timer: read the newest value every tick, so live changes work.
Calling `.as_int()` on a double parameter throws an exception and stops the node: the type must match.

blocks.text: To test Chiku you now open three terminals: turtlesim, the driver with its parameters, the pose monitor. Every single time. Real robots run 10 to 50 nodes, so nobody starts them by hand. A **launch file** is a list of the nodes to start, with their settings, and `ros2 launch` starts them all with **one command**.

items: Write a Python launch file with LaunchDescription and Node
Give a node a name, parameters and output='screen'
Read the same launch file in XML
Install launch files with data_files in setup.py, then ros2 launch

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A Python launch file is a Python file with one function, `generate_launch_description()`, that returns a **LaunchDescription**: a list of `Node(...)` actions. Each Node says which package and executable to start, and optionally its name, parameters and where its output goes.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A school assembly has a running order: "choir, then the head teacher's speech, then the prize giving". Nobody shouts instructions to each person; the running order is written once and everybody follows it. The launch file is the robot's running order.

from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch_ros.actions import Node


def generate_launch_description():
    return LaunchDescription([
        Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node', name='sim'),
        Node(package='chiku_control', executable='speed_driver', output='screen',
             parameters=[{'speed': 2.0, 'turn': 1.0}]),

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class SpeedDriver(Node):
    """Drives in a circle. The speeds are PARAMETERS, so you can change them without editing code."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('speed_driver')
        self.declare_parameter('robot_name', 'chiku')     # name, default value
        self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)              # forward speed, m/s
        self.declare_parameter('turn', 0.5)               # turn rate, rad/s
        name = self.get_parameter('robot_name').value
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info(f'{name} is ready to drive')

    def on_timer(self):
        speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value        # read the newest value every tick
        turn = self.get_parameter('turn').value
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = speed
        msg.angular.z = turn
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SpeedDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class PoseMonitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('pose_monitor')
        self.last = None            # the previous pose we received
        self.distance = 0.0         # metres travelled so far
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.report)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            self.distance += math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
        self.last = msg

    def report(self):
        if self.last is None:
            self.get_logger().warn('No pose yet. Is turtlesim running?')
            return
        p = self.last
        self.get_logger().info(
            f'x={p.x:.2f} y={p.y:.2f} theta={p.theta:.2f} travelled={self.distance:.2f} m')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = PoseMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.title: Python mini-project: Chiku's battery monitor
lessons.summary: Put the week together: a node with a subscriber, a publisher of your own message, a service, two parameters and a timer, configured from YAML and started from a launch file. Then operate it like a robot engineer.
lessons.dayTitle: Launch files and your first robot project

blocks.text: The warehouse manager has a problem: Chiku sometimes stops in the middle of an aisle with an empty battery. Your mission: write a **battery monitor** that knows how far Chiku has driven, publishes the battery level, warns the operator in time, and can be recharged. You have every brick already. Today you build the house.

items: Turn a list of requirements into one node
Combine a subscriber, a publisher, a service, parameters and a timer
Start everything from a launch file with a YAML configuration
Operate the robot from the terminal: watch, tune, warn, recharge

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A robot program is mostly **plumbing around a small brain**. The brain here is one line: `level = level - metres * drain`. The plumbing: a pose subscriber (how far did we drive?), a BatteryStatus publisher, a recharge service, two parameters and a 1 Hz timer.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Building with LEGO: no new bricks today. You use the bricks you made this week (subscriber, publisher, custom message, service, parameters, launch) and follow the plan. The plan is the requirements list.
The requirements

items: Publish a pretend battery level on `/chiku/battery` once per second, as **my_robot_interfaces/msg/BatteryStatus**.
The battery empties as the turtle drives: **drain_per_metre** percent for every metre (a parameter).
Log a **WARN** once when the level drops below **low_level** (a parameter).
Offer a **/chiku/recharge** service (std_srvs/srv/Trigger) that fills the battery to 100 %.
Start turtlesim, speed_driver and battery_monitor with **one launch file** that reads **one YAML file** for both nodes.

blocks.text: The node

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose
from std_srvs.srv import Trigger
from my_robot_interfaces.msg import BatteryStatus


class BatteryMonitor(Node):
    """Mini-project: a pretend battery that empties as Chiku drives."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery_monitor')
        self.declare_parameter('drain_per_metre', 2.0)    # percent used for every metre driven
        self.declare_parameter('low_level', 20.0)         # warn below this percentage
        self.level = 100.0
        self.last = None                                  # previous pose
        self.warned = False
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(BatteryStatus, 'chiku/battery', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_service(Trigger, 'chiku/recharge', self.on_recharge)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info('Battery monitor ready: 100.0 %')

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            metres = math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
            drain = self.get_parameter('drain_per_metre').value
            self.level = max(0.0, self.level - metres * drain)
        self.last = msg

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = BatteryStatus()
        msg.robot_name = 'chiku'
        msg.percentage = self.level
        msg.voltage = 10.0 + 2.6 * self.level / 100.0       # 10.0 V empty ... 12.6 V full
        msg.is_charging = False
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        low = self.get_parameter('low_level').value
        if self.level < low and not self.warned:
            self.get_logger().warn(f'Battery low: {self.level:.1f} %. Please recharge!')
            self.warned = True

    def on_recharge(self, request, response):
        self.level = 100.0
        self.warned = False
        response.success = True
        response.message = 'battery full again'
        self.get_logger().info('Recharged to 100 %')
        return response


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = BatteryMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class Battery(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery_monitor')
        self.declare_parameter('drain_per_metre', 10.0)
        self.level, self.last, self.warned = 100.0, None, False
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.on_timer)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            metres = math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
            drain = self.get_parameter('drain_per_metre').value
            self.level = max(0.0, self.level - metres * drain)
        self.last = msg

    def on_timer(self):
        self.get_logger().info(f'battery {self.level:.0f} %')
        if self.level < 20.0 and not self.warned:
            self.get_logger().warn('Battery low. Please recharge!')
            self.warned = True


class Driver(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('speed_driver')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.go)

    def go(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 2.0
        msg.angular.z = 1.0
        self.pub.publish(msg)


rclpy.init()
ex = rclpy.executors.SingleThreadedExecutor()
for n in (Battery(), Driver()):
    ex.add_node(n)
ex.spin()

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose
from std_srvs.srv import Trigger
from my_robot_interfaces.msg import BatteryStatus


class BatteryMonitor(Node):
    """Mini-project: a pretend battery that empties as Chiku drives."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery_monitor')
        self.declare_parameter('drain_per_metre', 2.0)    # percent used for every metre driven
        self.declare_parameter('low_level', 20.0)         # warn below this percentage
        self.level = 100.0
        self.last = None                                  # previous pose
        self.warned = False
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(BatteryStatus, 'chiku/battery', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_service(Trigger, 'chiku/recharge', self.on_recharge)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info('Battery monitor ready: 100.0 %')

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            metres = math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
            drain = self.get_parameter('drain_per_metre').value
            self.level = max(0.0, self.level - metres * drain)
        self.last = msg

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = BatteryStatus()
        msg.robot_name = 'chiku'
        msg.percentage = self.level
        msg.voltage = 10.0 + 2.6 * self.level / 100.0       # 10.0 V empty ... 12.6 V full
        msg.is_charging = False
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        low = self.get_parameter('low_level').value
        if self.level < low and not self.warned:
            self.get_logger().warn(f'Battery low: {self.level:.1f} %. Please recharge!')
            self.warned = True

    def on_recharge(self, request, response):
        self.level = 100.0
        self.warned = False
        response.success = True
        response.message = 'battery full again'
        self.get_logger().info('Recharged to 100 %')
        return response


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = BatteryMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class SpeedDriver(Node):
    """Drives in a circle. The speeds are PARAMETERS, so you can change them without editing code."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('speed_driver')
        self.declare_parameter('robot_name', 'chiku')     # name, default value
        self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0)              # forward speed, m/s
        self.declare_parameter('turn', 0.5)               # turn rate, rad/s
        name = self.get_parameter('robot_name').value
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info(f'{name} is ready to drive')

    def on_timer(self):
        speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value        # read the newest value every tick
        turn = self.get_parameter('turn').value
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = speed
        msg.angular.z = turn
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SpeedDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

blocks.q: The battery level lives only in the node's memory. What happens to it when you stop and start the launch file again? How could a real robot avoid that?
blocks.answer: It starts at 100 % again, because self.level = 100.0 in __init__. A real robot reads the real battery from its hardware driver (a topic like /battery_state with sensor_msgs/BatteryState), so a restart does not lose it.

blocks.text: The C++ battery monitor has exactly the same parts as the Python one: `pub_`, `sub_`, `srv_`, `timer_` and two parameters. blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Two cars of the same model, one with automatic and one with manual gears: the same journey, the same rules of the road, a slightly different way to drive. Python and C++ nodes are the same journey through ROS 2.

items: Publish a pretend battery level on `/chiku/battery` once per second, as **my_robot_interfaces/msg/BatteryStatus**.
The battery empties as the turtle drives: **drain_per_metre** percent for every metre (a parameter).
Log a **WARN** once when the level drops below **low_level** (a parameter).
Offer a **/chiku/recharge** service (std_srvs/srv/Trigger) that fills the battery to 100 %.
Start turtlesim, speed_driver and battery_monitor with **one launch file** that reads **one YAML file** for both nodes.

blocks.text: Requirement by requirement

items: **1**: `create_publisher<my_robot_interfaces::msg::BatteryStatus>("chiku/battery", 10)` and `create_wall_timer(1s, ...)`.
**2**: `on_pose` uses `has_last_` as the "no pose yet" flag (instead of std::optional), `std::hypot` and `get_parameter("drain_per_metre").as_double()`.
**3**: `RCLCPP_WARN(get_logger(), "Battery low: %.1f %%. Please recharge!", level_);`: `%%` prints one % sign.
**4**: `create_service<std_srvs::srv::Trigger>("chiku/recharge", std::bind(..., _1, _2))` fills the response in place.
**5**: `launch/mission.launch.py` in the C++ package: a Python launch file that starts C++ programs.

lessons.title: Time in your nodes: rates, clocks and stopping timers
lessons.summary: Choose a good rate for each job, measure time with the node's clock (Time and Duration), stop a timer after N ticks, and see what use_sim_time changes. Python and C++.

blocks.text: In Week 5 your timer published a Twist 10 times a second. A real robot runs many jobs at **different rates**, and it often needs to know **how much time has passed**: how long has Chiku been driving? Is this sensor reading fresh or two seconds old? When should the countdown stop? Today you learn to use **time** inside a node.

items: Choose a sensible rate for each kind of job
Measure elapsed time with the node's clock (Time minus Time gives a Duration)
Stop a timer after N ticks with `cancel()`
Explain what `use_sim_time` changes and why you never use time.time() in a node

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: **Period** is the time between rings (0.5 s); **rate** is rings per second (2 Hz): rate = 1 / period. The node's **clock** tells the current time (`get_clock().now()` / `now()`). Subtract two times and you get a **Duration**. `cancel()` stops a timer for good.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A heart beats about once per second: the period is 1 s, the rate is 1 Hz. A hummingbird's heart beats about 20 times per second: period 0.05 s, rate 20 Hz. Robots use different rates for different jobs, just like animals.
Choosing a rate

items: **1 to 2 Hz**: status reports, battery level, things people read.
**10 Hz**: motor commands for turtlesim and many mobile robots.
**20 to 50 Hz**: joint states for an arm, smooth motion.
**100 Hz and more**: low-level control loops (usually done in C++ or in ros2_control).

blocks.text: A callback must finish **before** the next ring. If your 10 Hz callback takes 0.3 s, the timer cannot keep up and everything else in the node waits too. Keep callbacks short.
blocks.label: Golden rule

blocks.title: heartbeat: a timer that counts, measures time and stops itself

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException


class Heartbeat(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('heartbeat')
        self.count = 0
        self.start = self.get_clock().now()
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.on_timer)   # every 0.5 s = 2 Hz

    def on_timer(self):
        self.count += 1
        elapsed = (self.get_clock().now() - self.start).nanoseconds / 1e9
        self.get_logger().info(f'beat {self.count} after {elapsed:.1f} s')
        if self.count == 10:
            self.get_logger().info('10 beats done, stopping the timer')
            self.timer.cancel()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = Heartbeat()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: `self.start = self.get_clock().now()` remembers when the node started; every tick subtracts it to get the elapsed time. After 10 beats the timer cancels itself.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: `this->now()` returns an rclcpp::Time; `now() - start_` is an rclcpp::Duration, and `.seconds()` turns it into a double. `timer_->cancel()` stops it.

blocks.text: `use_sim_time` decides which clock `get_clock().now()` returns: the computer's clock (false), or the **simulated** clock from a simulator or a rosbag on the `/clock` topic (true). Your code stays the same; that's why we always ask the node's clock instead of calling `time.time()`.
blocks.label: Why the node's clock?

blocks.q: Match the period to the rate
blocks.why: rate = 1 / period. 1 / 0.02 = 50.
blocks.hint: Read both sides slowly, then try again.

blocks.q: A node started at t = 12.0 s (its clock). Now `get_clock().now()` says 15.5 s. What is `(now - start).nanoseconds / 1e9`?
blocks.why: now - start is a Duration of 3.5 s = 3 500 000 000 ns; dividing by 1e9 gives 3.5 seconds.
blocks.hint: Subtract, then turn nanoseconds into seconds.

blocks.q: Your 10 Hz timer callback calls `time.sleep(1.0)`. What happens to the node?
options: It freezes for a second each time: no messages, no other timers
Nothing, sleep only affects that callback
blocks.why: One spin thread runs one callback at a time. While it sleeps, nothing else in that node can run.
blocks.hint: Who runs the other callbacks?

blocks.q: Fill in the Python call that stops a timer stored in `self.timer`: `self.timer.____()`
blocks.why: `cancel()` stops the timer; it will not ring again (unless you call reset()).
blocks.hint: It is the same word in C++: timer_->cancel().

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Using `time.time()` or `std::chrono::system_clock` in a node: it ignores simulated time. Ask the node's clock.
Forgetting the unit: Duration.nanoseconds is in **nano**seconds; divide by 1e9 for seconds (C++: `.seconds()`).
Sleeping inside a callback to wait: the whole node freezes. Count ticks instead.
Long work inside a fast timer: the next tick comes late.
Pick a rate for each job: about 1-2 Hz for reports, 10 Hz for motors, 50 Hz and more for smooth control.
Time minus Time is a Duration; ask the node's clock, so simulated time works too.
cancel() stops a timer after N ticks.
Keep callbacks short and never sleep inside them.

lessons.title: Logging like a pro: levels, throttle and once
lessons.summary: Use the five log levels, show only what matters with --log-level, avoid flooding the screen with throttle and once, and log the same way in Python and C++.

blocks.text: Your first real robot run prints 200 lines per second. Somewhere in there is the one warning that explains why Chiku stopped, but nobody can find it. Good logging is a superpower: **the right message, at the right level, at the right rate**.

items: Use DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR and FATAL correctly
Switch levels from the command line with --log-level
Limit repeated messages with throttle and once
Write the same logging in Python and C++

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Every log message has a **level**. Normally ROS 2 shows INFO and above, and hides DEBUG. You choose the level when you run the node. **Throttle** prints a message at most once every N seconds; **once** prints it only the first time.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A hospital monitor: it does not beep for every heartbeat (DEBUG), it shows the heart rate on screen (INFO), beeps when something is unusual (WARN), alarms when something is wrong (ERROR), and calls the whole team when life is in danger (FATAL).
The five levels

items: **DEBUG**: details for the developer (raw values, every step). Hidden by default.
**INFO**: normal progress ("goal reached", "node ready").
**WARN**: unusual but the robot can continue ("battery below 20 %").
**ERROR**: something failed ("could not reach the service").
**FATAL**: the node cannot continue at all. Usually followed by shutting down.

tabs.label: Python
tabs.note: Python uses keyword arguments: `throttle_duration_sec=1.0`, `once=True`, `skip_first=True`.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: C++ has one macro per variant: `RCLCPP_INFO_THROTTLE(logger, clock, ms, ...)` (time in **milliseconds**), `RCLCPP_WARN_ONCE`, `RCLCPP_DEBUG`. Note `%%` to print a percent sign.

blocks.text: Choosing the level when you run the node

# show DEBUG messages for every logger in this program
ros2 run chiku_control log_demo --ros-args --log-level debug

# better: DEBUG only for our node, INFO for ROS 2's own internal loggers
ros2 run chiku_control log_demo --ros-args --log-level log_demo:=debug

# only warnings and errors
ros2 run chiku_control_cpp log_demo --ros-args --log-level warn

`--log-level debug` also switches on the internal loggers of ROS 2 itself (rcl, rmw) and you get pages of noise. Use `--log-level <your_node_name>:=debug` to see only your node's details. We tested both on a real ROS 2 Jazzy: the difference is huge.
blocks.label: Tested tip

blocks.title: Try it: stop the flood
blocks.goal: This node logs the battery 10 times per second. Make the INFO line print **at most once per second**, and make the warning print **only once**.

lessons.title: Driving patterns: a square with a state machine (open loop)
lessons.summary: Make a node do a sequence of moves: drive a side, turn a corner, four times. Build it as a small state machine in Python and C++, and see why open-loop driving is never exact.

blocks.text: In Week 5 your node drove a circle: the same command, again and again. Real jobs are **sequences**: drive along the shelf, turn at the corner, drive along the next shelf. To drive a square, the node must remember **what it is doing right now** and **for how long**. That memory has a name: a **state machine**.

items: Turn a speed and a time into a distance and an angle
Build a small state machine (FORWARD, TURN) in Python and C++
Count timer ticks to measure how long a state lasts
Explain why open-loop control drifts

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **state** is what the robot is doing now (FORWARD or TURN). Each timer tick the node does what the state says, counts the tick, and **switches** state when the time is up. **Open loop** means the node never checks where the robot really is: it trusts the clock.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Walking with your eyes closed: "10 steps forward, turn right, 10 steps". You get roughly there, but every step is slightly different, and after a few turns you are off. That's open loop. The next lessons open the robot's eyes (closed loop).
The maths you need (only two lines)

items: **distance = speed x time**: 1.0 m/s for 2 s = 2 m.
**angle = turning speed x time**: pi/2 rad/s (90 deg/s) for 1 s = 90 degrees.

blocks.text: A square needs memory: a state machine

Each timer tick (10 per second) the node asks: which state am I in? FORWARD: publish linear.x = 1.0. TURN: publish angular.z = pi/2. After 20 ticks of FORWARD (2 s = 2 m) it switches to TURN; after 10 ticks of TURN (1 s = 90 degrees) it switches back and counts one side.

blocks.title: square_driver: FORWARD 2 s, TURN 1 s, four times

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class SquareDriver(Node):
    """Open loop: drive 2 s forward, turn 90 degrees, repeat 4 times."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('square_driver')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.state = 'FORWARD'      # the state machine: FORWARD -> TURN -> FORWARD ...
        self.ticks = 0              # how many 0.1 s ticks we spent in this state
        self.sides = 0
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        self.ticks += 1
        if self.state == 'FORWARD':
            msg.linear.x = 1.0
            if self.ticks >= 20:                    # 20 ticks x 0.1 s = 2 s -> 2 m
                self.state, self.ticks = 'TURN', 0
        elif self.state == 'TURN':

blocks.text: Why the square is never perfect

We ran square_driver on a real ROS 2 Jazzy with turtlesim. The Python version ended at (5.54, 5.54) and the C++ version at (5.13, 5.49), both facing -0.15 rad instead of 0. Same code idea, different results! Timers are never exactly 0.1 s, the first message arrives a little late, and small errors add up at every corner.
This is the reason real robots use **closed-loop** control: measure where you are (a sensor, the pose, odometry), compare with where you want to be, and correct. That is the next day's first lesson.

switch state to TURN and reset the tick counter

options: Many robots stop if commands stop arriving (a safety timeout), and the node can change the command at any moment
Twist messages expire after 0.1 s by law
blocks.why: A steady stream lets the robot stop safely when your node dies, and lets the controller react quickly.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Forgetting to reset the tick counter when the state changes.
Mixing degrees and radians: ROS 2 always uses radians (90 deg = pi/2 = 1.5708).
Forgetting to send a stop (all zeros) at the end.
Expecting open loop to be exact.

items.back: remember what the robot is doing now
C++: named states the compiler checks
send commands, never check the result

items: distance = speed x time; angle = turn rate x time; ROS 2 uses radians.
A state machine lets a node do steps in order: do, count ticks, switch.
Always end a sequence with a zero Twist.
Open loop drifts: next we close the loop with the pose.

lessons.title: Closed-loop control: go to a goal by yourself (part 1)
lessons.summary: Combine a pose subscriber, a timer and a Twist publisher into a P-controller that drives the robot to any goal, with gains as parameters. Python and C++.

blocks.text: Now the eyes and the legs work together. You tell Chiku "go to (8, 8)" and it gets there **from anywhere**, even if someone pushes it on the way. The trick is a loop that runs 10 times a second: **look** (read the pose), **think** (how far, which direction), **act** (publish a Twist). This loop is the heart of almost every robot.

items: Compute distance and heading error to a goal
Turn errors into speeds with a P-controller (gains kv and kw)
Keep angles between -pi and pi with atan2
Change the goal live with ros2 param set

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: **Error** = where you want to be minus where you are. A **P-controller** (P for proportional) makes the speed proportional to the error: far away = fast, close = slow, at the goal = stop. Same for turning: big heading error = turn fast.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Parking a car: when the parking spot is far you drive normally; as you get closer you slow down more and more; when you are there you stop. You also steer more when you point further away from the spot. Your brain is a P-controller.

blocks.intro: Click to place a goal, then press Drive. Change Kv and Kw and drive again: see how the path changes.

blocks.text: The four lines of maths

items: `dx, dy = goal_x - x, goal_y - y`: the arrow from the robot to the goal.
`distance = hypot(dx, dy)`: its length (Pythagoras).
`heading_error = atan2(dy, dx) - theta`: the direction of the arrow minus the direction the robot faces.
`v = kv * distance`, `w = kw * heading_error`: the P-controller. Stop when distance < 0.1 m.

blocks.text: atan2(dy, dx) - theta can be bigger than pi (for example 3.5 rad). Then the robot would turn 200 degrees left instead of 160 right. `atan2(sin(e), cos(e))` wraps any angle back into -pi..pi, so the robot always turns the short way.
blocks.label: Why wrap the angle?

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class GoToGoal(Node):
    """Closed loop: read the pose, compute the error, publish a Twist. Repeat 10 times a second."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('go_to_goal')
        self.declare_parameter('goal_x', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('goal_y', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('kv', 1.0)       # speed gain
        self.declare_parameter('kw', 4.0)       # turning gain
        self.pose = None
        self.reached = None                     # the last goal we reached
        # relative names (no leading /) so a launch file can add a namespace
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, 'turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.control)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.pose = msg

    def control(self):
        if self.pose is None:
            return
        gx = self.get_parameter('goal_x').value
        gy = self.get_parameter('goal_y').value
        dx, dy = gx - self.pose.x, gy - self.pose.y
        distance = math.hypot(dx, dy)
        heading_error = math.atan2(dy, dx) - self.pose.theta
        heading_error = math.atan2(math.sin(heading_error), math.cos(heading_error))  # keep in -pi..pi
        cmd = Twist()
        if distance < 0.1:
            if self.reached != (gx, gy):            # say it once per goal
                self.reached = (gx, gy)
                self.get_logger().info(f'Goal reached: x={self.pose.x:.2f} y={self.pose.y:.2f}')
        else:
            cmd.linear.x = min(self.get_parameter('kv').value * distance, 2.0)
            cmd.angular.z = self.get_parameter('kw').value * heading_error
        self.pub.publish(cmd)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = GoToGoal()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: The goal and gains are **parameters**, read every loop, so `ros2 param set /go_to_goal goal_x 2.0` changes the goal while the node runs.

        self.declare_parameter('goal_x', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('goal_y', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('kv', 1.0)       # speed gain
        self.declare_parameter('kw', 4.0)       # turning gain
        self.pose = None
        self.reached = None                     # the last goal we reached
        # relative names (no leading /) so a launch file can add a namespace
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, 'turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.control)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.pose = msg

    def control(self):
        if self.pose is None:
            return
        gx = self.get_parameter('goal_x').value
        gy = self.get_parameter('goal_y').value
        dx, dy = gx - self.pose.x, gy - self.pose.y
        distance = math.hypot(dx, dy)
        heading_error = math.atan2(dy, dx) - self.pose.theta
        heading_error = math.atan2(math.sin(heading_error), math.cos(heading_error))  # keep in -pi..pi
        cmd = Twist()
        if distance < 0.1:
            if self.reached != (gx, gy):            # say it once per goal
                self.reached = (gx, gy)
                self.get_logger().info(f'Goal reached: x={self.pose.x:.2f} y={self.pose.y:.2f}')
        else:
            cmd.linear.x = min(self.get_parameter('kv').value * distance, 2.0)
            cmd.angular.z = self.get_parameter('kw').value * heading_error
        self.pub.publish(cmd)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = GoToGoal()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

No speed limit: a far goal gives a huge speed.

lessons.title: A safety filter node: chaining nodes with remapping
lessons.summary: Write a node that sits between a driver and the robot, limits speed and blocks driving into walls, and connect it with topic remapping instead of changing code.

blocks.text: Chiku's teleop sometimes sends 3 m/s, and one student drove it straight into a shelf. The fix is not to change every driver program; it is to put one small **safety node** in between: it listens to commands, checks them, and passes safe commands on to the motors. Real robots (TurtleBot, Nav2) use exactly this idea.

items: Write a node that subscribes and republishes (a filter)
Clamp values and use the pose to block unsafe motion
Connect nodes with remapping (`-r old:=new`) instead of changing code
Explain relative vs absolute topic names

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **filter** node subscribes to one topic, changes or checks each message, and publishes it on another topic. With **remapping** you can plug it between any two nodes: the driver publishes to `cmd_vel_in`, the filter publishes to the robot's real `cmd_vel`.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A water filter in your kitchen: the tap (driver) sends water, the filter cleans it, and only clean water reaches your glass (the motors). You do not rebuild the tap to add the filter; you just connect the pipes differently. Remapping is connecting the pipes.

blocks.title: safety_filter: clamp the speed and respect the walls

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class SafetyFilter(Node):
    """Sits between a driver and the robot: limits speed and stops before the walls."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('safety_filter')
        self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 1.5)
        self.declare_parameter('margin', 1.0)       # stay this far from the walls (m)
        self.pose = None
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'cmd_vel_out', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Twist, 'cmd_vel_in', self.on_cmd, 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.pose = msg

    def near_wall(self):
        m = self.get_parameter('margin').value
        p = self.pose
        return p is not None and (p.x < m or p.y < m or p.x > 11.0 - m or p.y > 11.0 - m)

    def on_cmd(self, msg):
        limit = self.get_parameter('max_speed').value
        out = Twist()
        out.linear.x = max(-limit, min(limit, msg.linear.x))   # clamp
        out.angular.z = msg.angular.z
        if self.near_wall() and out.linear.x > 0.0:
            out.linear.x = 0.0
            self.get_logger().warn('Too close to a wall: only turning is allowed',
                                   throttle_duration_sec=1.0)
        self.pub.publish(out)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SafetyFilter()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: Topic names without a leading `/` are **relative**: `cmd_vel_in` and `cmd_vel_out` can be renamed at start-up.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: `std::clamp(value, low, high)` (C++17, `<algorithm>`) is the C++ one-liner for max(low, min(value, high)).

blocks.text: Remapping: rewire without rebuilding

# the filter reads /cmd_vel_in and writes straight to the turtle
ros2 run chiku_control safety_filter --ros-args -r cmd_vel_out:=/turtle1/cmd_vel -p max_speed:=1.0

# teleop normally writes /turtle1/cmd_vel; send it into the filter instead
ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key --ros-args -r /turtle1/cmd_vel:=/cmd_vel_in

`-r from:=to` works on topics, services and also on the node name (`__node`) and namespace (`__ns`). In a launch file the same thing is `remappings=[('cmd_vel_out', '/turtle1/cmd_vel')]` (Python) or `<remap from=... to=.../>` (XML).

blocks.text: Relative, absolute and private names

items: `/turtle1/cmd_vel` (starts with /): **absolute**, always exactly this name.
`cmd_vel_in` (no /): **relative**: a namespace is added in front (`/robot2/cmd_vel_in` if the node runs in /robot2).
`~/status`: **private**: becomes `/<node name>/status`, handy for topics that belong to one node.

lessons.summary: Fill nested message fields, lists (arrays) and header time stamps in Python and C++, using sensor_msgs/JointState and geometry_msgs/PoseStamped as examples.

blocks.text: Chiku has a little camera head with two motors: pan (left-right) and tilt (up-down). Other nodes need to know the angle of each motor, **and when** that angle was true. That information has a standard message, `sensor_msgs/JointState`, which has lists and a header. Today you learn to fill any message, however deep.

items: Fill nested fields like `pose.position.x`
Fill list fields (Python lists, C++ std::vector)
Stamp a header with the node's clock
Read a message definition and know how to fill it

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A message is a box that can contain other boxes. `PoseStamped` contains a `header` (with a `stamp` and a `frame_id`) and a `pose` (with a `position` and an `orientation`). You reach inside with dots: `msg.pose.position.x = 1.0`. Lists are filled like normal lists.

blocks.text: A parcel with a delivery note: the **header** is the note on the outside (when it was sent, from which warehouse); inside are smaller boxes, and inside those the items. You never mix up the note and the contents.

blocks.title: head_joints: a JointState with a stamp and lists

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from sensor_msgs.msg import JointState


class HeadJoints(Node):
    """Builds a JointState message by hand: header + stamp + lists."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('head_joints')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(JointState, 'joint_states', 10)
        self.t = 0.0
        self.create_timer(0.05, self.on_timer)     # 20 Hz

    def on_timer(self):
        self.t += 0.05
        msg = JointState()
        msg.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()   # WHEN these values were true
        msg.header.frame_id = ''                             # joint states need no frame
        msg.name = ['head_pan', 'head_tilt']                 # lists: same order everywhere
        msg.position = [0.8 * math.sin(self.t), 0.3 * math.sin(2.0 * self.t)]
        msg.velocity = [0.8 * math.cos(self.t), 0.6 * math.cos(2.0 * self.t)]
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = HeadJoints()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: `self.get_clock().now().to_msg()` turns the node's time into a `builtin_interfaces/Time` for the header.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: In C++ `msg.header.stamp = now();` converts automatically. Lists are `std::vector`, filled with `{a, b}` or `push_back`.

lessons.title: QoS in code: reliable, best effort and latched topics
lessons.summary: Choose QoS profiles in Python and C++: sensor data (best effort), commands (reliable) and latched status (transient local), and see a late subscriber still get the message.
lessons.dayTitle: QoS, safe parameters and launch for two robots

blocks.text: Chiku's map server publishes the map **once**, when it starts. The navigation node starts 10 seconds later and... never gets the map. Meanwhile the laser driver sends 40 scans a second and nobody cares if one is lost. Same ROS 2, very different needs. **QoS** (Quality of Service) lets each topic say what it needs.

items: Pick a QoS profile for sensor data, commands and one-time status
Write QoS in Python (QoSProfile) and C++ (rclcpp::QoS)
Explain why mismatched QoS gives silence
Make a latched topic with TRANSIENT_LOCAL

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Three settings matter most. **Reliability**: RELIABLE (resend lost messages) or BEST_EFFORT (never resend). **Durability**: VOLATILE (new subscribers get only new messages) or TRANSIENT_LOCAL (the publisher keeps the last N messages for late joiners). **Depth**: how many messages to keep.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A TV live broadcast is BEST_EFFORT: a glitch is gone, nobody resends it. A registered letter is RELIABLE: the post office keeps trying. A notice pinned on the classroom board is TRANSIENT_LOCAL: students who arrive late still read it.

blocks.intro: Try combinations and watch which ones connect.

blocks.text: Three profiles you will use again and again

items: **Sensor data** (laser, camera, pose): BEST_EFFORT, depth 5. Python: `qos_profile_sensor_data`. C++: `rclcpp::SensorDataQoS()`.
**Commands and events** (cmd_vel, goals): RELIABLE, VOLATILE, depth 10. The default when you write `10`.
**Latched status** (map, robot description, "ready"): RELIABLE, TRANSIENT_LOCAL, depth 1. C++: `rclcpp::QoS(1).reliable().transient_local()`.

blocks.title: latched_status: publish once, keep it for late joiners

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, DurabilityPolicy, ReliabilityPolicy
from std_msgs.msg import String


class LatchedStatus(Node):
    """Publishes ONE message. Thanks to TRANSIENT_LOCAL, late subscribers still get it."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('latched_status')
        qos = QoSProfile(depth=1,
                         reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
                         durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL)
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, 'map_status', qos)
        msg = String()
        msg.data = 'map of the warehouse is ready'
        self.pub.publish(msg)
        self.get_logger().info('Published the map status once')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = LatchedStatus()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: QoSProfile takes keyword arguments. Python enums: `ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE`, `DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL`.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: C++ chains settings: `rclcpp::QoS(1).reliable().transient_local()`. Easy to read, hard to get wrong.

blocks.title: late_listener: matching QoS on the subscriber side

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, DurabilityPolicy, ReliabilityPolicy, qos_profile_sensor_data
from std_msgs.msg import String
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class LateListener(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('late_listener')
        latched = QoSProfile(depth=1,
                             reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
                             durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL)   # must match the publisher
        self.create_subscription(String, 'map_status', self.on_status, latched)
        # sensor data: BEST_EFFORT, small queue. Newest value matters, old ones do not.
        self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.poses = 0

    def on_status(self, msg):
        self.get_logger().info(f'I joined late but still got: "{msg.data}"')

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.poses += 1
        if self.poses % 50 == 0:
            self.get_logger().info(f'{self.poses} poses received')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = LateListener()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: The latched subscription must also ask for TRANSIENT_LOCAL, otherwise it only gets messages published after it started.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: `rclcpp::SensorDataQoS()` is the ready-made best-effort profile.

blocks.text: The matching rule

items: A **RELIABLE** subscriber cannot connect to a **BEST_EFFORT** publisher (it asks for more than is offered). The other way round works.
A **TRANSIENT_LOCAL** subscriber cannot connect to a **VOLATILE** publisher.
When they do not match: **no error in your code, no messages**. ROS 2 prints a warning about incompatible QoS, and `ros2 topic info -v` shows each side's settings.

blocks.text: We tested this on real ROS 2 Jazzy: late_listener started 2 seconds after latched_status and still logged `I joined late but still got: "map of the warehouse is ready"`, in Python and in C++.

Sent once; every node that starts later needs it.

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Subscribing to sensor topics (best effort) with the default reliable QoS: silence.
Forgetting TRANSIENT_LOCAL on the subscriber side for a latched topic.
A big depth on fast topics: memory grows and old data piles up.
Assuming QoS errors raise exceptions: they only print a warning.

items.back: late joiners get nothing old / get the last N

items: QoS = reliability + durability + depth (and a few more settings).
Sensors: best effort. Commands: reliable. One-time status: transient local.
Both sides must be compatible, or nothing arrives.
C++ chains settings; Python uses QoSProfile keyword arguments.

lessons.summary: Week 5 taught declare, get, set and YAML. Now make parameters safe: describe them with ParameterDescriptor (description, read-only, ranges), validate changes in an on-set callback and react to them at once. Python and C++.
lessons.dayTitle: QoS, safe parameters and launch for two robots

blocks.text: A visitor at the open day types `ros2 param set /cruise_control speed 50`. With a careless node, Chiku races into the wall. With a careful node, the change is **refused** with a clear reason. Today you make your parameters safe: described, limited, checked.

items: Add a description, a range and read_only to a parameter
Validate changes in an on-set parameters callback
Use the new value immediately (no polling)
Understand the three layers that protect a parameter: type, descriptor, callback

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **ParameterDescriptor** describes a parameter: what it means, its allowed range, whether it can change. ROS 2 enforces the range and read_only for you. For any other rule you add an **on-set callback** that can say no.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A cooker's knob: it only turns between 0 and 9 (range); the label says what it does (description); the gas type set by the installer cannot be changed by the cook (read-only); and a child lock refuses dangerous settings (the callback).

blocks.intro: Watch values pass the type check and the callback gate.

blocks.title: cruise_control: described, limited and checked parameters

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rcl_interfaces.msg import ParameterDescriptor, FloatingPointRange, SetParametersResult
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class CruiseControl(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('cruise_control')
        self.declare_parameter('robot_name', 'chiku',
                               ParameterDescriptor(description='Name shown in logs', read_only=True))
        self.declare_parameter('speed', 1.0, ParameterDescriptor(
            description='Forward speed in m/s',
            floating_point_range=[FloatingPointRange(from_value=0.0, to_value=2.0, step=0.0)]))
        self.declare_parameter('turn', 0.5, ParameterDescriptor(description='Turn rate in rad/s'))
        self.speed = self.get_parameter('speed').value
        self.turn = self.get_parameter('turn').value
        self.add_on_set_parameters_callback(self.on_params)    # the gatekeeper
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        name = self.get_parameter('robot_name').value
        self.get_logger().info(f'{name}: speed={self.speed} turn={self.turn}')

    def on_params(self, params):
        for p in params:
            if p.name == 'turn' and abs(p.value) > 3.0:
                return SetParametersResult(successful=False, reason='turn must be between -3 and 3')
        for p in params:                       # all values are fine: use them
            if p.name == 'speed':
                self.speed = p.value
            if p.name == 'turn':
                self.turn = p.value
            self.get_logger().info(f'{p.name} changed to {p.value}')
        return SetParametersResult(successful=True)

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = self.speed
        msg.angular.z = self.turn
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = CruiseControl()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: `ParameterDescriptor(description=..., read_only=True)` and `floating_point_range=[FloatingPointRange(from_value=0.0, to_value=2.0, step=0.0)]`. The callback returns `SetParametersResult(successful=..., reason=...)`.

tabs.label: C++
tabs.note: Store the handle returned by `add_on_set_parameters_callback` in a member: if it is destroyed, the callback is removed.

ROS 2 checked the type (double: OK), then calls our callback.

blocks.text: Three layers of protection

items: **Type**: a double parameter refuses an integer or a string (`speed 2` fails; `speed 2.0` works).
**Descriptor**: read_only and ranges are checked by ROS 2 before your code runs.
**Callback**: your own rules ("turn must be between -3 and 3", "goal must be inside the map").

blocks.text: Since Iron, ROS 2 also has **pre-set** (change the list of parameters before they are set) and **post-set** callbacks (react after they are set). The on-set callback shown here is the classic one and the place to validate.

            if p.name == 'turn' and abs(p.value) > 3.0:
                return SetParametersResult(successful=False, reason='turn must be between -3 and 3')
        for p in params:                       # all values are fine: use them
            if p.name == 'speed':
                self.speed = p.value
            if p.name == 'turn':
                self.turn = p.value
            self.get_logger().info(f'{p.name} changed to {p.value}')
        return SetParametersResult(successful=True)

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = self.speed
        msg.angular.z = self.turn
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = CruiseControl()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import os

from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument
from launch.conditions import IfCondition
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import Node


def generate_launch_description():
    goals = os.path.join(get_package_share_directory('chiku_control'), 'config', 'goals.yaml')
    return LaunchDescription([
        DeclareLaunchArgument('with_monitor', default_value='true'),
        # robot 1: everything inside the namespace /robot1
        Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node', name='sim', namespace='robot1'),
        Node(package='chiku_control', executable='go_to_goal', name='go_to_goal', namespace='robot1',
             parameters=[goals]),
        # robot 2: the same programs, a different namespace, different goals (see goals.yaml)
        Node(package='turtlesim', executable='turtlesim_node', name='sim', namespace='robot2'),
        Node(package='chiku_control', executable='go_to_goal', name='go_to_goal', namespace='robot2',
             parameters=[goals]),
        # an optional extra node, watching robot 1 (remapped to its pose topic)
        Node(package='chiku_control', executable='pose_monitor', name='pose_monitor',
             remappings=[('/turtle1/pose', '/robot1/turtle1/pose')],
             condition=IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration('with_monitor'))),
    ])
tabs.note: `get_package_share_directory()` finds the installed config folder. `IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration('with_monitor'))` starts pose_monitor only when the argument is true.

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class GoToGoal(Node):
    """Closed loop: read the pose, compute the error, publish a Twist. Repeat 10 times a second."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('go_to_goal')
        self.declare_parameter('goal_x', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('goal_y', 8.0)
        self.declare_parameter('kv', 1.0)       # speed gain
        self.declare_parameter('kw', 4.0)       # turning gain
        self.pose = None
        self.reached = None                     # the last goal we reached
        # relative names (no leading /) so a launch file can add a namespace
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Pose, 'turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.control)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        self.pose = msg

    def control(self):
        if self.pose is None:
            return
        gx = self.get_parameter('goal_x').value
        gy = self.get_parameter('goal_y').value
        dx, dy = gx - self.pose.x, gy - self.pose.y
        distance = math.hypot(dx, dy)
        heading_error = math.atan2(dy, dx) - self.pose.theta
        heading_error = math.atan2(math.sin(heading_error), math.cos(heading_error))  # keep in -pi..pi
        cmd = Twist()
        if distance < 0.1:
            if self.reached != (gx, gy):            # say it once per goal
                self.reached = (gx, gy)
                self.get_logger().info(f'Goal reached: x={self.pose.x:.2f} y={self.pose.y:.2f}')
        else:
            cmd.linear.x = min(self.get_parameter('kv').value * distance, 2.0)
            cmd.angular.z = self.get_parameter('kw').value * heading_error
        self.pub.publish(cmd)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = GoToGoal()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


class PoseMonitor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('pose_monitor')
        self.last = None            # the previous pose we received
        self.distance = 0.0         # metres travelled so far
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Pose, '/turtle1/pose', self.on_pose, 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.report)

    def on_pose(self, msg):
        if self.last is not None:
            self.distance += math.hypot(msg.x - self.last.x, msg.y - self.last.y)
        self.last = msg

    def report(self):
        if self.last is None:
            self.get_logger().warn('No pose yet. Is turtlesim running?')
            return
        p = self.last
        self.get_logger().info(
            f'x={p.x:.2f} y={p.y:.2f} theta={p.theta:.2f} travelled={self.distance:.2f} m')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = PoseMonitor()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.summary: Turn the robot's pose into a moving coordinate frame (world -> turtle1) with tf2's TransformBroadcaster, including the yaw-to-quaternion step, in Python and C++.

blocks.text: Chiku's camera sees a parcel "1 metre in front of me". Where is that in the warehouse? To answer, ROS 2 must know **where Chiku is**, as a coordinate frame that moves with it. Today Chiku publishes its own frame, so tf2 can answer such questions for every node.

items: Explain parent frame, child frame and transform
Fill a TransformStamped from a pose
Convert a yaw angle to a quaternion (Python maths and tf2::Quaternion in C++)
Inspect frames with tf2_echo

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **transform** says where a child frame is inside its parent frame: a translation (x, y, z) and a rotation (a quaternion). A **broadcaster** sends it on `/tf`. Every time the turtle moves, we send world -> turtle1 again.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A family tree of positions: the warehouse (world) contains Chiku (turtle1), Chiku contains its camera. If you know each child's position in its parent, you can find any object in any frame by walking the tree. tf2 does the walking.

blocks.intro: The same point seen from different frames.

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import TransformStamped
from tf2_ros import TransformBroadcaster
from turtlesim.msg import Pose


def yaw_to_quaternion(yaw):
    """A robot on the floor only turns around z: roll = pitch = 0."""
    return 0.0, 0.0, math.sin(yaw / 2.0), math.cos(yaw / 2.0)


class TurtleTfBroadcaster(Node):

blocks.q: Match the yaw to the quaternion (z, w)
blocks.why: z = sin(yaw/2), w = cos(yaw/2).
blocks.hint: Read both sides slowly, then try again.

blocks.q: In a TransformStamped from world to turtle1, which is the parent frame?
blocks.why: header.frame_id is the parent; child_frame_id is the frame being described.
blocks.hint: The header says where we measure from.

blocks.q: Why not put the yaw angle directly into the transform?
options: tf2 rotations are quaternions (x, y, z, w), which work for any 3D rotation
Angles are not allowed in ROS 2
blocks.why: Quaternions describe every 3D rotation without the problems of angles (gimbal lock). For a floor robot it is just z and w.
blocks.hint: Robots also fly and climb.

blocks.q: For yaw = 0 the quaternion's w is ____
blocks.why: cos(0) = 1: the 'no rotation' quaternion is (0, 0, 0, 1).
blocks.hint: cos(0)

blocks.label: Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
items: Putting the angle in rotation.z directly (it must be sin(yaw/2)).
Swapping parent and child frames.
Forgetting the time stamp: listeners then see old or invalid data.
Two broadcasters publishing the same child frame (frames must have one parent).
A transform = where a child frame is in its parent: translation + quaternion.
Broadcast it every time the robot moves, with a stamp.
For floor robots: z = sin(yaw/2), w = cos(yaw/2).
Inspect with tf2_echo and view_frames.

lessons.title: Using frames: a tf2 listener that follows another robot
lessons.summary: Ask tf2 where one robot is seen from another (lookup_transform), handle the case where a frame is not there yet, and turn the answer into a chase controller. Launch it all together.

blocks.text: Chiku's little helper robot should always follow Chiku around the warehouse. With tf2 this is surprisingly simple: every 0.1 s, ask "where is Chiku, **seen from me**?" If the answer is "2 m ahead and a bit to the left", drive forward and turn left. No angle maths about the world needed.

items: Create a tf2 Buffer and TransformListener
Call lookup_transform(target, source, time) and catch TransformException
Use a point in your own frame to steer
Start broadcasters and follower together with a launch file

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: The **Buffer** stores all frames it hears on /tf; the **TransformListener** fills it. `lookup_transform('turtle2', 'turtle1', Time())` returns where turtle1 is, expressed in turtle2's frame. In your own frame, steering is easy: angle = atan2(y, x), distance = hypot(x, y).

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: Following a friend in a crowd: you don't think about the city map. You only think "she is 3 metres ahead, slightly left": walk forward, turn a little left. Your own point of view is the easiest frame for control.

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.time import Time
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from tf2_ros import TransformException
from tf2_ros.buffer import Buffer
from tf2_ros.transform_listener import TransformListener
from turtlesim.srv import Spawn


class TurtleFollower(Node):
    """turtle2 chases turtle1, using tf2 to ask: where is turtle1, seen from turtle2?"""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('turtle_follower')
        self.buffer = Buffer()
        self.listener = TransformListener(self.buffer, self)
        self.spawner = self.create_client(Spawn, '/spawn')
        self.spawned = False
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/turtle2/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)

    def on_timer(self):
        if not self.spawned:
            if self.spawner.service_is_ready():
                self.spawner.call_async(Spawn.Request(x=1.0, y=1.0, theta=0.0, name='turtle2'))
                self.spawned = True
            return
        try:
            t = self.buffer.lookup_transform('turtle2', 'turtle1', Time())   # target, source, latest
        except TransformException as ex:
            self.get_logger().info(f'Could not transform turtle1 to turtle2: {ex}',
                                   throttle_duration_sec=2.0)
            return
        x, y = t.transform.translation.x, t.transform.translation.y      # turtle1 in turtle2's frame
        cmd = Twist()
        cmd.angular.z = 1.0 * math.atan2(y, x)
        cmd.linear.x = 0.5 * math.hypot(x, y)
        self.pub.publish(cmd)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = TurtleFollower()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: `Time()` (zero) means "the latest available". The first lookups fail until both frames exist, so we catch `TransformException` and log it, throttled.

import math


def follow(x, y):
    """x, y: turtle1 seen from turtle2. Return (linear, angular)."""
    distance = math.hypot(x, y)
    angular = 1.0 * math.atan2(y, x)
    linear = 0.5 * (distance - 1.0) if distance > 1.0 else 0.0
    return round(linear, 2), round(angular, 2)

lessons.title: Executors and callback groups: waiting without freezing
lessons.summary: Understand what the executor does, why a blocking call inside a callback deadlocks, and how callback groups plus a MultiThreadedExecutor make it safe. Python and C++.

blocks.text: Chiku's battery checker must ask the battery service every 2 seconds **and wait for the answer** before deciding to go home. You tried it in a timer and the node froze forever. Not a bug in your logic: a misunderstanding of who runs your callbacks. Today you meet the **executor**.

items: Explain what an executor does with timers, subscriptions and services
Explain the deadlock of a blocking call in a callback
Use MutuallyExclusive and Reentrant callback groups
Spin with a MultiThreadedExecutor in Python and C++

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: `spin()` hands your node to an **executor**: a loop that picks ready callbacks and runs them. The default executor has **one thread**: one callback at a time. If a callback waits for a service answer, nobody is left to process that answer: deadlock. Give the waiting callback and the answer **different callback groups** and use **several threads**.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A small café with one waiter (single-threaded executor). If the waiter stands at your table waiting for your coffee, nobody makes the coffee: you wait forever. With two waiters (multi-threaded executor) and clear jobs (callback groups: one takes orders, one brings drinks), one can wait while the other works.

blocks.intro: One thread, one callback at a time: see the queue.

blocks.text: Callback groups

items: **MutuallyExclusive** (the default): callbacks in this group never run at the same time. Safe and simple.
**Reentrant**: callbacks in this group may run at the same time (even the same callback twice). Only for code that is safe in parallel.
Every node has a default MutuallyExclusive group. Callbacks you create without a group all land there, so they can never run in parallel, even with many threads.

blocks.title: battery_checker: a timer that safely waits for a service answer

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.callback_groups import MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException, MultiThreadedExecutor
from std_srvs.srv import Trigger


class BatteryChecker(Node):
    """A timer that calls a service and WAITS for the answer, without freezing the node."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery_checker')
        self.level = 100
        self.create_service(Trigger, 'chiku/battery', self.on_battery)   # server (default group)
        self.client_group = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup()             # the client gets its own group
        self.timer_group = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup()              # and so does the timer
        self.client = self.create_client(Trigger, 'chiku/battery', callback_group=self.client_group)
        self.create_timer(2.0, self.on_timer, callback_group=self.timer_group)

    def on_battery(self, request, response):
        self.level -= 7
        response.success = self.level > 20
        response.message = f'{self.level} %'
        return response

    def on_timer(self):
        if not self.client.service_is_ready():
            return
        result = self.client.call(Trigger.Request())     # blocking call: OK here, see main()
        self.get_logger().info(f'battery: {result.message} (ok={result.success})')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = BatteryChecker()
    executor = MultiThreadedExecutor()      # several threads: the answer can arrive while on_timer waits
    executor.add_node(node)
    try:
        executor.spin()
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: The client and the timer each get their **own** MutuallyExclusive group; `MultiThreadedExecutor` provides the threads. Now `client.call()` inside the timer is safe.

tabs.note: `create_callback_group(rclcpp::CallbackGroupType::MutuallyExclusive)`; pass it to `create_client` and `create_wall_timer`. The timer waits on the future with `wait_for(1s)` while another thread delivers the response.

lessons.title: Lifecycle nodes and components: starting robots safely and efficiently (part 1)
lessons.summary: Write a managed (lifecycle) node that only drives after configure and activate, control it from the terminal, then build a C++ component and load it into a container.
lessons.dayTitle: Robust robots and the patrol project

blocks.text: Two problems from a real warehouse. One: when the system boots, the motor driver must **not** move until every sensor is ready; somebody must say "configure, then activate". Two: Chiku's computer is small; 20 nodes as 20 programs waste memory. Lifecycle nodes solve the first, **components** solve the second. Nav2, for example, uses both.

items: Name the lifecycle states and transitions
Write on_configure / on_activate / on_deactivate / on_cleanup in Python and C++
Drive a managed node with ros2 lifecycle
Build a component and load it into a container with ros2 component

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: A **lifecycle node** has states: **unconfigured** -> configure -> **inactive** -> activate -> **active**. You decide what happens in each transition (create publishers, start timers...). A **component** is a node built as a plug-in library that a **container** process loads; many components share one process.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A theatre: the actor arrives (unconfigured), puts on the costume and learns the stage (configure -> inactive), and only acts when the curtain opens (activate -> active). Components are like several small shows sharing one theatre building instead of each renting its own.
States and transitions

configure            activate
unconfigured -----> inactive -----> active
             <-----          <-----
              cleanup         deactivate

shutdown from any of them -> finalized

blocks.title: lifecycle_driver: a node that waits for permission

tabs.label: Python
tabs.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.lifecycle import LifecycleNode, State, TransitionCallbackReturn
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


class LifecycleDriver(LifecycleNode):
    """A managed node: it only drives after someone configures AND activates it."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('lifecycle_driver')
        self.pub = None
        self.timer = None

    def on_configure(self, state: State) -> TransitionCallbackReturn:
        self.pub = self.create_lifecycle_publisher(Twist, '/turtle1/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.get_logger().info('configured: publisher created, not driving yet')
        return TransitionCallbackReturn.SUCCESS

    def on_activate(self, state: State) -> TransitionCallbackReturn:
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.on_timer)
        self.get_logger().info('activated: driving')
        return super().on_activate(state)          # also activates the lifecycle publisher

    def on_deactivate(self, state: State) -> TransitionCallbackReturn:
        self.destroy_timer(self.timer)
        self.get_logger().info('deactivated: stopped')
        return super().on_deactivate(state)

    def on_cleanup(self, state: State) -> TransitionCallbackReturn:
        self.destroy_publisher(self.pub)
        self.get_logger().info('cleaned up')
        return TransitionCallbackReturn.SUCCESS

    def on_timer(self):
        msg = Twist()
        msg.linear.x = 1.0
        msg.angular.z = 1.0
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = LifecycleDriver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
tabs.note: `rclpy.lifecycle.LifecycleNode`; `create_lifecycle_publisher` makes a publisher that only sends while active. Call `super().on_activate(state)` to activate it.

lessons.dayTitle: Robust robots and the patrol project

blocks.text: You improve go_to_goal on Friday evening; on Monday the robot turns the wrong way at one corner. A tiny **unit test** would have caught it in one second. Professional robot teams test every change, automatically. Good news: the most important tests need no robot and no simulator.

items: Separate pure logic from ROS plumbing
Write pytest tests with assert and pytest.approx
Write gtest tests with TEST and EXPECT_NEAR
Run colcon test and colcon test-result

blocks.label: In plain words
blocks.text: Put the maths (wrap an angle, compute speeds) in **pure functions**: no ROS, just numbers in and numbers out. Then a **test** calls the function with known inputs and checks the outputs. If someone breaks the maths later, the test fails and tells you exactly where.

blocks.label: In the real world
blocks.text: A calculator factory does not test each calculator by building a whole office. It presses 2 + 2 and checks for 4, then a few tricky cases. Unit tests are those button presses for your robot's brain.
